title: UPDATE 1-No  Romania fx intervention  recently-cbank economist
text:
BUCHAREST, July 11 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank has not intervened on the forex market in recent days to curb a strong appreciation of the leu currency, chief economist Valentin Lazea said on Wednesday.   

Asked whether the bank stepped in recently to temper the high-yielding currency's rise, Lazea told reporters:   

"No, it did not intervene."   

The leu soared to its highest level against the euro in five years last week, boosted by robust foreign and local demand for the high-yielding unit and ignoring warnings from international observers about future risks to the sizzling economy.   

It has since lost some ground and several local players said the central bank may have intervened covertly.   

Lazea, who attended a meeting of Romanian exporters, who complained that a strong leu hurts their business, said the bank had two levers to temper a steep rise and may have to use one.   

"We have two options: lowering interest rates and intervening in the foreign exchange market. Both remain open. We cannot say when and how we will action.   

"There is always the option to have a wait-and-see attitude, but in the context we spoke of, I suggested that we may need to pick one of the two options," Lazea said.   

By 1500 GMT, the leu was quoted at 3.1265/25 per euro <EURRON=> compared with a five-year high of 3.0870 hit last Monday.

title: INTERVIEW-Romania cenbank gov-prefer  currency  to find own level
text:
ZURICH, June 22 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank is concerned that the strength of the leu will prove unsustainable but would prefer the currency to find its own level, its governor said on Friday.   

In an interview with Reuters, Mugur Isarescu played down a jump in the leu to a fresh 4-1/2 year high against the euro on Friday, and said the central bank was focused on longer-term trends.   

Intervention was a last resort, although always an option.   

"As long as it's possible to not intervene in the market, the National Bank of Romania would like the currency to find it's own level," he said. "But we have a managed float and we could intervene at any time, if necessary."   

Isarescu confirmed earlier comments that the central bank would not intervene to stem the leu's rise unless it was "deeply concerned", but declined to name a precise level which would set alarm bells ringing.   

"We are concerned generally that levels will prove to be unsustainable," he said. "I don't know if I am deeply concerned and I can't say exactly when I would be deeply concerned."   

"One day's movement is not enough ... let's see where we are on Monday or Tuesday."   

Isarescu said policymakers would take the rise in the leu into account in their June 25 interest rate decision but declined to say whether it made another cut more likely.   

The central bank has cut benchmark interest rates by 150 basis points so far this year, in part due to currency worries, to 7.25 percent.   

"It's one element but the key element is our forecast for inflation as so far its well within target," he said.   

In the longer term, however, inflation pressures could reappear. "Wages are rising more rapidly than productivity growth, I do not consider this is sustainable," he said.   

NO RUSH FOR EURO   

Isarescu said the government's recent pledge to cut the budget deficit was a sound move in the lead-up to preparations to adopt the euro early next decade.   

"This is very welcome, it will be good for inflation and for the sustainability of economic growth, it's good for the current account deficit in a period of such rapid economic growth that the budget deficit should be as low as possible."   

But he said Romania was not in a hurry to adopt the common currency. Bulgaria, which also joined the European Union in January, hopes to join euro proving ground ERM-2 this year but Romania is aiming for 2010-2012.   

"We are not in a currency board so we have no urgency," Isarescu said. "Personally I do not consider it good to enter into a race to adopt the euro."   

He declined to comment on renewed calls for a change to the inflation test for euro entry.   

Isarescu said Romania had the necessary rules and regulations in place for fully-functioning capital markets and the central bank was doing its bit by keeping inflation low.   

"I am sure that this time next year we will have a well-functioning capital market in Romania," he said.   

Romania has a small stock exchange and a nascent bond market with virtually no secondary trade.   

Some analysts say it needs to create more opportunities for foreign players eager to invest their cash in long-term instruments to help offset a vast current account deficit.   

ROMANIA/CENBANK (INTERVIEW)|LANGEN|ABN|M|E|RBN|D|RDN|BNX

title: Short-term outflows cannot hurt Romania-c.banker
text:
BUCHAREST, May 25 (Reuters) - Romania's financial stability is not threatened by current short-term capital inflows, central bank governor Mugur Isarescu said on Friday, calling the level of hot cash in the country "reasonable".   

Analysts have warned Romania could be at risk of sudden capital outflows if its gaping current account deficit widened sharply or there were signs that foreign investment cash is not sufficient to cover the shortfall.   

"We have 2 billion euros in short-term capital by non-residents, mostly bank deposits. If we compare that with any indicator, they are at a reasonable level," Isarescu told a banking seminar.   

Foreign investors have snapped up Romania's leu currency, which has firmed 3 percent against the euro since the start of the year, when Romania joined the European Union. Most of the inflows land in deposits or the vibrant real estate market.   

Hot cash is the equivalent of around 2 percent of last year's gross domestic product and some 10 percent of the central bank's hard currency reserves.   

"I don't see a serious problem if that amount leaves ... we have a liquidity surplus in the market and we continue to sterilise ... Making a quick assessment of a current account correction based on monetary levers, risks are limited," Isarescu said.   

The current account deficit, which poses a major risk for Romania's fast growing economy, more than doubled in the first quarter compared with the same 2006 period. It was covered 43 percent by foreign investment.   

The International Monetary Fund sees the deficit widening to around 12 percent of GDP this year against 10 percent in 2006.   

Isarescu said sharp outflows can potentially trigger a central bank intervention, in theory.   

"If capital outflows occur, a central bank bank can take that into accont and possibly react through the rate policy. If that cannot temper the amplitude of the currency depreciation, I believe that a bank can take into account a potential intervention. But I'm not making any projections."

title: UPDATE 2- Intervention  talk briefly hurts buoyant leu
text:
(Adds details, quotes)   

BUCHAREST, April 27 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu lost one percent against the euro on Friday, sliding away from its highest level in nearly five years amid speculation of central bank intervention, later denied by the bank.   

The currency rebounded in later trade as investors rebuilt positions in line with broadly positive sentiment towards the currency, which is benefiting from strong economic growth prospects in the wake of Romania's European Union entry.   

"At some point, we all knew it was just a rumour and this made the leu recover," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Bucharest. "The rumour was spread by somebody from the market and he took good profit from it."   

The leu fell as low as 3.3350 per euro <EURRON=>, compared to highs of around 3.30 which it hit on Thursday and tested again on Friday.   

By 1215 GMT, it had recovered some ground to trade at 3.3098/58.   

"You get scared at some point, but after several minutes you realise the central bank had no reason to intervene. If the leu is on an emerging markets firming trend, an intervention can't hold it from firming but for a few hours," a dealer said.   

Romania's central bank last intervened openly in currency markets in late 2005, when it tried to bring down a soaring leu. Before Friday's speculation, it said it had not been in the market since.   

But it has said interest rate cuts this year were in part driven by concerns that a rapid leu rise posed a threat of a sharp reversal that could reignite inflation.   

On Friday, the bank's spokesman Mugur Stet told Reuters:   

"The central bank did not intervene on the foreign exchange market. (Today's) evolution of the leu's exchange rate is not related to the presence of the central bank on the market."   

The leu is supported by investors' optimism towards Romania which joined the European Union this year, and prospects for strong inflows of direct investment and EU cash.   

Its latest surge was also helped by a jump in overnight money market rates to their highest level since January 2005 at 28.50/54.13 percent.   

Dealers said the spike in rates followed the central bank's move this week to drain more liquidity from the market than expected.

title: Romania  cbank: limited reasons for  fx intervention
text:
BUCHAREST, May 25 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank would only intervene in currency markets to protect "financial stability" and thereby its efforts to curb inflation, governor Mugur Isarescu said on Thursday.  

The bank, which started to target inflation rates in 2005, has come under heavy criticism from foreign observers such as the IMF for weakening its anti-inflation efforts by curbing the leu currency.  

"Everybody looks at the exchange rate ... the exchange rate has a visibility and a big impact on the economy," Isarescu told a financial seminar.  

"If we intervene that means that we are protecting financial stability...This way we give sustainability to disinflation," Isarescu said.  

Inflation fell to a post-communist low of 6.9 percent on the year in April and is widely expected to rise in coming months due to tax hikes, before subsiding slightly later this year.  

The central bank has recently raised its end-year forecast to 6.8 percent from 6.5 percent, further above its December target of 4-6 percent. It expects inflation to move within its 3-5 percent goal next year.  

It raised its key rate by 100 basis points to 8.5 percent in a surprise move in February to keep inflation at bay.  

But it kept credit costs on hold for two meetings in a row afterwards, including earlier this month, with some analysts saying its inflation-fighting credibility was on the line because of expectations of higher price growth in coming months.  

On Wednesday, Isarescu said the fight against inflation is safe from any impact of this month's sharp fall in the leu currency against the euro.  

The leu <EURRON=> has hit its lowest level against Europe's single currency since early February as other emerging market currencies tumbled while the euro gained across the board.  

Isarescu reiterated that his bank has not intervened in the foreign exchange market since last autumn. "We did not have a free float (regime), we did not declare that the exchange rate is perfectly free. However, over the past seven months we haven't intervened," Isarescu said.  

"We have a managed float which implies that we maintain the right (to intervene) when conditions go against what the central bank wishes."  

A free float would imply a commitment by the bank to refrain for ever from intervention, he said, adding "We are not there."

title: EBRD-Romanian c.banker expects tight monetary stance
text:
LONDON, May 21 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) will maintain its hawkish interest rate stance for a while but its message to markets is "balanced," deputy central bank governor Cristian Popa on Sunday.  

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London, Popa told Reuters high credit growth and stubborn inflation required tight monetary policy but he declined to comment if a new rate hike was in the cards.  

He said the bank was sending a "balanced" message to domestic markets, which had been rattled in recent weeks after rapidly changing their interpretation of a series of BNR comments.  

"We are saying: 'do not rejoice' regarding inflation," Popa told Reuters in an interview.  

"We are continuing the hawkishness from February ... We have been tightening policy since November. This continues by keeping the broad monetary conditions tighter for a longer period than envisaged in February," he said.  

The BNR, which adopted inflation targets last year, raised official lending costs by 100 basis points to 8.5 percent in February and has continued to mop up excess liquidity from the interbank market.  

But it kept interest rates on hold for two meetings in a row afterwards, including earlier this month, and some analysts said its inflation-fighting credibility was on the line because of forecasts of higher price growth in coming months.  

STUBBORN INFLATION  

Romanian inflation fell to a post-communist low of 6.9 percent on the year in April and is widely expected to rise in coming months due to tax hikes, before subsiding slightly later this year.  

The BNR has recently raised its end-year forecast from 6.5 percent to 6.8 percent and further above the December target of 4-6 percent.  

But Popa defended the bank's decision to keep rates unchanged, saying the mopping up of excess liquidity helped create tight monetary conditions, and said the bank was no longer as concerned about possible gains in the leu currency due to rate hikes as it was last year.  

"What we are saying is that we are keeping monetary conditions tight even as disinflation progresses," he said.  

"We are also seeing the elimination of excess demand not at the end of 2006 anymore but in the beginning of 2007, which means tightening is required ... We will not have a cut for some time. But I am not sure about a hike," Popa said.  

Some analysts have said the BNR has not been raising interest rates aggressively this year despite stubborn inflation because of continued worries about currency appreciation.  

Last year, such concerns drove the BNR to intervene massively in currency markets to keep the leu in check. The currency still gained some 7 percent in 2005 and is widely expected to continue appreciating this year.  

"Those concerns are much less pronounced than last year. We have not been intervening. The preoccupation with currency strength remains, but it is far weaker than the preoccupation with inflation," Popa said.  

He added, echoing recent comments by BNR governor Mugur Isarescu, that the bank did not rule out further intervention in currency markets "if exceptional conditions warrant it, for example large swings in currency exchange rates."  

"We can intervene and we could do it in either direction ... But the pressure is still towards appreciation of the leu. What we don't want is unsustainable appreciation accumulating because when the market shifts that could result in sudden depreciation and that could hurt disinflation."  

Popa also said a recent weakening of the leu against the euro was temporary.  

"The recent weakening of the leu happened in an international context but the leu was one of the least hit currencies and it has already rebounded. So the weakening does not require intervention," he said.

title: UPDATE 4- Romania  moves to inflation targeting,restrains leu
text:
(Updates with intervention on leu currency, analyst comment)  

BUCHAREST, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank on Monday announced a shift to inflation targeting to strengthen its fight against rising consumer prices as the country moves closer to European Union entry.  

But while central bank governor Mugur Isarescu gave details of the policy -- which switches focus from the exchange rate -- the bank intervened in the market to stop a steep appreciation of the leu, dealers said.  

Analysts said the bank risked undermining its own policy.  

"They're in a policy dilemma. There's a clear risk that they can undermine the credibility of inflation targeting policy by paying too much attention to what happens in the forex market," said Danske Bank analyst Lars Christensen.  

Isarescu announced the central 2006 inflation target would be 5.0 percent with a 1 percent band and this year's target 7.5 percent, with the same band on either side. Year-on-year inflation was 9.3 percent in July, the same as end-2004.  

The governor said next year's target was conditional on the centrist government not hiking the value added tax (VAT) rate to 22 percent from 19 to boost state revenues.  

"We believe that next year's inflation will probably rise to 6.5 percent if the government raises VAT to 22 percent," he told a news conference.  

FIGHTING INFLATION  

The long-anticipated announcement marked the official shift from monetary to direct inflation targeting, which the central bank says will make fighting inflation more effective, enhance its policy transparency and reduce inflation expectations.  

Analysts said the targets were realistic but warned the bank must work hand in hand with the government, which must gradually raise energy prices to EU levels, for the policy to work.  

"Both this year's and next year's targets are attainable," said independent financial analyst Florian Libocor. "But I think the bank's mission to ensure lasting disinflation towards the desired levels would be eased if they continue to work together as a team with the government."  

Isarescu said the targets hinged on tight fiscal policy and warned the bank would not hesitate to resort to monetary tools to attain its goal.  

"By all means, Romania must avoid granting further incentives that might boost demand," he said. "To reach its main objective (lasting price stability) the BNR will resort to all monetary policy instruments at its disposal."  

Economists say the policy shift, part of efforts to curb price growth in preparation for EU entry in 2007, should push the bank to allow the leu to strengthen.  

But the central bank has said it will keep its managed-float regime for the leu for a few more years. In recent months, it has sporadically intervened through commercial banks to check the leu, which has appreciated by about 11 percent this year.  

Dealers said the bank moved directly on the market to keep the leu close to 3.53 to the euro, buying about 70 million euros on Monday. It was the second such intevention in consecutive trading days, after it bought 200 million euros on Friday.  

The bank would not comment on the interventions but Isarescu said the bank would continue to move on the leu.  

"Romania cannot afford to give up its managed float at this time," Isarescu said. "When we intervene we don't have a specific exchange rate target. And it's well known that an excessive appreciation doesn't help disinflation and it could trigger credibility problems."  

But analysts said the bank should be careful because a strong presence in the market could backfire, making the leu attractive to speculators and luring hot money.  

"The idea is that massive interventions on the forex market boost unwanted volatility in the unit, thus creating the perfect playground for currency speculators," Finansbank analyst Omer Tetik told Reuters.  

And Christensen added: "They must be very careful. They should not enter in a game with market forces, because they'll eventually lose."

title: UPDATE 2- Romania  c.bank  intervenes  to hold back leu
text:
(Adds leu close, analyst's quote, background)  

BUCHAREST, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) stepped into the foreign exchange market on Friday, soaking up hefty hard currrency surpluses in a bid to cap a leu currency appreciation against the euro, dealers said.  

It was the first time in months that dealers had spotted the central bank moving directly on the leu -- which firmed to the sensitive level of 3.4 against the euro this week -- after sporadic interventions through commercial banks.  

Analysts said the move was aimed at weakening the currency as much as possible before Monday, when the bank shifts to direct inflation targeting, which would limit its intervention powers to increasingly focus on rates.  

"It (the BNR) intervened in waves when the leu hit bids of 3.4500," said one dealer with a commercial bank in Bucharest.  

The leu has been under pressure mostly from non-bank exchange houses unloading excess euros from Romanians working abroad and export-related inflows.  

Dealers said the leu's quick advance to around 3.4500 at midday prompted the BNR to intervene. BNR officials were not available for coment.  

CHECKING THE LEU  

The bank, which rarely comments on its interventions, was last suspected of purchasing moderate volumes of euros via commercial banks on July 19. It has sporadically moved over the past months to check the rise of the leu, which gained about 11 percent since the start of the year.  

The leu slipped to 3.5350/00 after the intervention, which some dealers estimated to be worth up to 200 million euros. It closed at 3.5390/50 against Thursday's 3.4570/25.  

The BNR switches to inflation-targeting next week as part of efforts to curb price growth in preparation for EU entry in 2007. Economists said the new policy would put more pressure on the bank to allow the leu to strengthen.  

Romania aims to cut consumer price inflation to 7-7.5 percent this year from 9.3 in 2004, and 2-3 percent in the next three-four years, but analysts see the target as optimistic given mainly the energy price adjustments needed for EU entry.  

Last week, BNR vice-governor Cristian Popa told Reuters the bank would keep its managed-float regime for the leu for at least a few more years after the shift to inflation targeting.  

"Today's intervention illustrates the bank's policy dilemma. It is worried about increasing inflationary pressures that could be reduced by accepting a leu appreciation," said Lars Christensen of Danske Bank. "On the other hand it sees the recent appreciation as excessive."  

Analysts said the bank will not let the unit breach the 3.4000 level in the weeks following the policy shift.  

"In the coming weeks the BNR will be reluctant to see the euro/leu rate move below the 3.4000 mark. I would expect them to sporadically intervene," said Bank Austria Creditanstalt analyst Simon Quijano-Evans.

title: Romania July  Forex  Reserves EUR14.85B, +EUR1.082B On Mo
text:
BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Romania's foreign-exchange reserves rose EUR1.082 billion in July, to EUR14.85 billion, the bank said Wednesday.  

The central bank didn't release a breakdown of the monthly inflows and outflows, but said inflows totaled EUR1.663 billion, while outflows totaled EUR580.2 million.  

Last month, National Bank of Romania Governor Mugur Isarescu said the central bank continues to intervene in the local foreign-exchange market, albeit less frequently than in the past, to keep the local currency's appreciation in check.  

With the government unable to stem the widening of the current account deficit through fiscal measures, Isarescu said the central bank would be "irresponsible to stimulate the current account deficit through an excessive appreciation of the leu."  

The leu (EUR1=RON3.4776) has appreciated by some 14% against the euro this year.  

In addition to foreign-exchange reserves, the central bank reported holdings of 105 metric tons of gold, with a total market value of EUR1.192 billion.  

Romania's remaining foreign debt service for 2005 totals EUR723 million.

title: Romanian leu flat, c.bank  intervention  suspected
text:
BUCHAREST, July 25 (Reuters) - Romania's leu <EURRON=> closed flat in quiet trading on Monday after a suspected central bank (BNR) intervention knocked it off its more than a five-month maximum of 3.5400 to the euro, dealers said.  

The leu firmed early on Monday as corporates sold hard currency but retreated back above 3.5500 in the middle of the day in what traders said looked like a covert intervention by the BNR. It ended at 3.5490/45, unchanged from Friday.  

"The RON was appreciating in the morning until reaching 3.5400 (per euro)," one dealer said.  

"Then someone started buying euros and the exchange rate went up (weakened) to 3.5055. It could have been the NBR perhaps, because it happened at around noon ... as was the case last week," he said.  

The monetary body has been repeatedly trying to slow down quick rise of the leu with modest interventions through banks in July, saying it wanted to prevent excessive exchange rate moves. Central bank officials were not available to comment.  

The leu, which is up roughly 9.8 percent this year, resumed firming after its redenomination on July 1 as the BNR eased slightly its exchange rate policy, which had kept the unit locked above 3.6000 per euro since mid-March, dealers said.  

Market watchers expected firming pressure on the leu to continue in the coming days, but some said the central bank would probably try to stabilise it at around 3.5500 per euro in the short term.  

Short-term money market rates were at 7.02/8.06 percent from Fridays 6.97/8.04 percent.  

The BNR drained 2.6 billion lei worth of one-month deposits from the market at an average rate of 8.0 percent <BNR13>.

title: UPDATE 2- Romania  cbank eyes prices, reserves for  intervention .
text:
BUCHAREST, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank said on Thursday it would keep intervening in currency markets to maintain stable prices and reserves, and was watching the leu's moves against the euro rather than a euro/dollar basket.  

In a rare confirmation that the central bank (BNR) drained euros to cool a firming leu, governor Mugur Isarescu said the bank bought more than 520 million euros from the foreign exchange interbank market over the past two days.  

"We will continue to intervene in the future," Isarescu told reporters. "Our goal is to keep foreign exchange reserves at an optimal level to cover five months of imports."  

"We do not have specific targets for the (leu's) exchange rate. Our objective is price stability," he added.  

The Balkan country has promised the International Monetary Fund to cut inflation, one of the highest in the region, to 7.0 percent this year from 9.3 percent in 2004.  

Until it shifted to a more flexible managed currency float last year, the central bank used to announce forecasts on how much the leu was likely to appreciate in real terms against a euro/dollar basket with 75/25 weighting.  

The bank has been steadily reducing the dollar weighting in the basket as Romania prepares to join the European Union in 2007.  

Isarescu said the bank had switched to watching only the euro from the start of this year. "We weigh the leu a hundred percent against the euro from January the first."  

Isarescu said the BNR bought more than 220 million euros directly in the latest forex intervention this week to cool the leu which has gained 12 percent this year reaching 34,900 to the euro. The bank also bought another 300 million euros indirectly from banks.  

Analysts said the central bank was looking to discourage speculators attracted by its plans to give foreigners access to leu deposits, a move expected to attract billions of euros in hot money.  

"The central bank sent a signal that it wishes to calm down the market," said financial analyst Florian Libocor.  

"It also tried to make the players understand that what's happening now on the forex market (the leu's fluctuations) is something we should all get used to," he added.  

GREATER EXCHANGE RATE FLEXIBILITY  

Isarescu did not want to say exactly when the next phase of capital account liberalisation would take place, but said greater flexibility of the exchange rate was likely to fend off speculative inflows.  

He did not offer any estimate of the hard currency inflows expected after the move, scheduled for the first half of this year. Some estimates have put the inflows at around 3 billion euros.  

Isarescu warned foreigners eager for quick gains that the bigger the hard currency inflows, the bigger the risk the small Romanian foreign exchange market would not be able to absorb them. That could make the exchange rate unattractive.  

"They may want to come in with a long train, but we have quite a short platform for it," he said.  

Analysts said Isarescu's comments were also meant to signal to exporters, who have complained about the leu's strength over the past months, that they should become more competitive and that he was not worried about a bulging current account gap.  

"He is telling exporters to turn to products and services with more added value," said ABN Amro senior analyst Radu Craciun.  

Isarescu said foreign direct investments, including capital transfers, covered about 98 percent of last year's current account deficit of 7.7 percent of gross domestic product and that he saw exports rising by 10 percent this year. "I don't think Romania needs a major adjustment of the current account deficit this year because FDI is high," he said.

title: CORRECTED - ANALYSIS-Foreign investors turned on by Romania.
text:
In London story headlined "ANALYSIS-Foreign investors turned on by Romania, fuel FX rally" please read in paragraph 7 "the key deposit rate is at 17.75 percent" ... instead of ... "the key deposit rate is at 18.25 percent." (corrects level of deposit rate).  

A corrected version follows  

By James Thornhill  

LONDON, Dec 7 (Reuters) - It's difficult for foreign investors to get exposure to Romania's soaring currency, but that hasn't stopped some of them and the attraction of high yields and EU entry in 2007 means more are likely to follow.  

The leu is up around six percent against the euro since November 3 - when the central bank announced a shift to a flexible managed float currency regime - driven, at least in part, by speculative foreign inflows.  

Romania's central bank intervened aggressively on Monday to stem the leu's charge, but analysts say it can probably only slow the pace of gains, given the growth of interest in Romania.  

Romania's benchmark Eurobond maturing in 2012 also underlines the strength of interest, with the risk premium having dropped to 4.0 percent, from 6.285 percent in May.  

Investors' confidence that Romania will remain on track for EU entry has insulated markets against a bout of political turbulence in the wake of last month's inconclusive parliamentary elections.  

"In spite of capital restrictions, Romania has benefited from the plentiful global liquidity chasing yield and, with better macro policies, approaching EU membership and high domestic rates, money has moved in," said Erik Nielsen, head of new European markets research at Goldman Sachs.  

The central bank's reduced participation in the market since November has encouraged leu bulls, salivating at the prospect of Romania's high yields - the key deposit rate is at 17.75 percent - and the convergence anchor of European Union entry in 2007.  

"People are looking for vehicles to express their bullish leu view. Interest rates are only a couple of percent below Turkey, but Romania is a lot closer to EU entry. From that perspective it's very attractive," said Koon Chow, emerging markets currency strategist at CSFB.  

Domestic traders corroborate the view from outside: "Foreign inflows are picking up and are set to grow on expectations of further liberalisation of capital flows, maintaining upward pressure on the leu," said one senior dealer in Bucharest.  

STRICT DOOR POLICY  

The attraction of Romanian markets to foreign investors are obvious. The trouble is, as Chow at CSFB puts it, it's still "hard as hell" for foreigners to buy leu assets and get in and out of the market easily.  

"It's definitely nowhere near as liquid as other parts of central Europe, there is an NDF (non-deliverable forward) market, but investors tend to take very small positions," said Ivailo Vesselinov, emerging markets analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein.  

NDF markets allow investors to take forward positions in non-convertible or thinly traded currencies, like the leu, with contracts settled in hard currency.  

"They're still testing the waters, but we expect the market to develop quite rapidly over the next year," Vesselinov added.  

That development should be enhanced by the gradual lifting capital controls, in line with EU entry requirements.  

Romania has promised to allow foreigners access to leu deposits starting next April, with the full liberalisation of the capital account to take effect in time for EU membership in 2007.  

Bankers in London say hedge fund involvement in leu markets so far has been very limited, but that could change if these markets are opened up.  

"If these opportunities were there with an open market, people would be a lot more interested," said Goldman's Nielsen.  

FDI PICKING UP  

It's not just speculative investors who are taking a greater interest in Romania. A string of privatisations has helped fuel a strong pick up in foreign direct investment this year, with the trend set to continue.  

FDI inflows into Romania have badly lagged other countries in former communist eastern Europe since 1990, with investors deterred by weak institutions, red tape and widespread corruption.  

But a corner may have been turned in 2004, thanks to progress on economic reform and Romania finally gaining "functioning economy" status from the EU.  

"We haven't seen any particular FDI inflows since the (currency) change, most of it has been speculative inflows. But the outlook for next year is quite positive, driven by ongoing progress towards EU entry," said Vesselinov at Dresdner.  

Progress on privatisation is indicative of the improved investment climate.  

The lower house of parliament approved last month the sale of leading oil company Petrom (SNPP.BX), two gas distributors and two electricity companies, all to foreign firms.  

Austrian energy group OMV (OMVV.VI) is expected to pay around 1.5 billion euros to take a 51 percent stake in Petrom by December 20, in a landmark deal that will double total FDI into Romania to 3.3 billion euros this year.  

Political uncertainty has so far failed to dampen investor enthusiasm for Romanian assets.  

The ruling ex-communists lost their majority in the poll, but could remain in power via an alliance with ethnic Hungarian parties. Romania also holds a presidential election on Dec. 12, which Prime Minister Adrian Nastase is favourite to win.  

(Additional reporting by Mirela Roman in Bucharest).

title: Romania c.bank buys euros to curb leu rise.
text:
BUCHAREST, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank has intervened on the local interbank foreign exchange market to temper a steep appreciation of the leu after it announced a more flexible currency regime, dealers said on Wednesday.   

"It started buying euros when the leu went as low as 39,430/450," said one dealer with a private commercial bank.   

They could not immediately estimate the size of the intervention. A BNR spokesman did not comment.

title: INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1- Romania  c.bank  fx - intervention  not ruled out.
text:
BUCHAREST, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) said on Wednesday it will limit but not scrap its interventions in the foreign exchange market a day after it moved to relax its managed float currency system.   

On Tuesday the BNR announced it will let the leu fluctuate in line with market trends, a major step towards opening up to short-term foreign capital inflows ahead of Romania's 2007 EU entry.   

It also cut its key interest rate, which it uses to drain money market funds, by 50 basis points to 18.25 percent.   

"It's important for the exchange rate to fully reflect market forces," central bank vice-governor Cristian Popa told Reuters by telephone from Brussels.   

"The BNR has not completely eliminated intervention as a possibility but you will see these limited. And of course the predictability of such interventions should be substantially lessened in the future," he said.   

Popa said a more flexible float, aimed at inflation targeting and ahead of freeing up capital flows early next year, would not have a "serious negative" impact on the current account gap, seen widening towards six percent of GDP this year.   

"We do not believe it will have serious negative consequences on the current account primarily because exports have a good performance despite real appreciation against the basket (so far this year) which is higher than the initial forecast of the central bank," said Popa.   

"The current account performance can go up to close to six percent of GDP. That is independent of the change in the exchange rate policy as of yesterday," he added.   

The central bank move took the market by surprise and the leu rose to touch 39,430/50 against the euro. Dealers said the bank then stepped in to temper the leu's rise of about 2.5 percent since the announcement.   

Until Tuesday, the BNR had been steering the leu along a gradual course of appreciation through frequent interventions under its managed float system.   

The policy change was also aimed at helping curb inflationary pressures, which have risen recently on the back of high world oil prices and demands for wage increases. Romania wants to cut inflation to under 10 percent this year, from 14.1 in 2003.   

"Our ultimate responsibility is inflation," Popa said. "That's the overriding goal of our policy."

title: Romania approves law to slash four zeros from bills.
text:
BUCHAREST, June 29 (Reuters) - Romania's parliament on Tuesday approved a law which will lighten the burden on shop assistants and book keepers by creating a new "heavy" leu worth 10,000 times the present national currency.  

With the present "light" leu trading at around 40,700 to the euro (33,630 to the dollar), the reform has been long awaited.  

The heavy leu will circulate from July 2005 to the end of 2006 alongside its light counterpart, and light leus will then remain exchangeable for heavy ones at commercial banks until 2009.  

Romania is not the only country to be re-denominating a currency ravaged by the effects of past heavy inflation.  

In January, the Turkish parliament approved a law to create a new lira worth a million times the present unit which currently trades at not far short of 1.5 million to the dollar. The new currency will come in at the start of next year.  

Romania's leu, convertible on current account deals since 1998, will be fully liberalised also for capital account deals in 2007, when the ex-communist state hopes to join the European Union. Romanian officials have said the Balkan country will be able to adopt the euro sometime between 2012 or 2013.  

Romania has a managed float system, with the central bank intervening only in case of increased volatility.

title: INTERVIEW-Romanian FinMin sees euro adoption 2012-2013.
text:
BUCHAREST, May 11 (Reuters) - Romania, which hopes to join the European Union in 2007, will be able to adopt the euro sometime in 2012 or 2013, the ex-communist country's Finance Minister Mihai Tanasescu said on Tuesday.  

Prime Minister Adrian Nastase said last month he hoped Romania will join the euro zone around 2010, earlier than a 2011-2013 timing estimated previously by central bank officials.  

But Tanasescu said Romania would need more time.  

"I see euro adoption in five to six years after Romania joins the European Union," Tanasescu told Reuters in an interview. "It is a realistic view as our economy has to be ready for such a moment."  

Although Romania's budget deficits and public debt are well within the Maastricht criteria at present, the Balkan country has been slow to revamp its economy in 14 post-communist years.  

It is still striving to cut inflation, one of the highest in the region, to 9.0 percent this year from 14.1 percent in 2003.  

In the meantime, Romanians will slash some zeros from the leu currency, now trading about 40,500 to the euro.  

Tanasescu said a long-awaited draft bill on a planned re-denomination - making the 10,000 "light" lei worth one "heavy" leu" - will be discussed by the government this week.  

Romanian bankers have repeatedly asked for a redenomination to ease bookeeping and costs of handling cash in circulation.  

"That move needs about 12 months of preparation, therefore the heavy leu will be on the market sometime between mid-2005 to early 2006," Tanasescu said.  

The leu, convertible on current account deals since 1998, will be fully liberalised on the capital account in 2007. Romania has a managed-float system, with the central bank intervening only in cases of increased volatility.

title: UPDATE 2- Romania central bank intervenes  again as leu slides.
text:
BUCHAREST, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) sold euros on the local foreign exchange market on Monday for the third time in 10 days to temper a slide of the leu, caused mostly by seasonally high imports, dealers and analysts said.   

The leu was under pressure from a shortage of euros, triggered by both robust winter imports and a weakening dollar which prompted local traders to boost their euro positions, foreign exchange dealers said.   

"It (the BNR) entered the market as the leu slid towards 40,020/60," said a dealer with a Bucharest bank. The unit, which closed at 39,955/995 to the euro on Friday firmed to 39,920/950 after the intervention and subsequently traded at 39,930/960.   

Dealers estimated Monday's intervention at 10 million euros.   

They said the BNR, which runs a managed-float system letting the leu move according to market demand but intervening in cases of increased volatility, might have spent up to 50 million euros in its recent interventions.   

Analysts said the slide of the leu, which is not traded internationally, was only temporary because after importers stock up for the harsh winter, expatriates' Christmas remittances will boost it again in December.   

"Today's intervention is surprising, given that the pressure on the leu is related not only to hard currency deficits but to the significant strengthening of the euro on world markets as well," ABN Amro senior analyst Radu Craciun said.   

"Traditionally, there is a surplus of hard currency on the market in December," he added. "Companies sell hard currency to pay end-year taxes and bonuses, and Romanians working abroad send their savings home."   

LEU SLIDING   

He said the leu has depreciated 14.3 percent against the euro since the beginning of the year and 0.8 percent against the dollar.   

"The central bank's interventions are aimed at stabilising the market," the BNR's communication manager Adrian Vasilescu told Reuters. He said the leu/euro rate "is now within the BNR programme".   

He dismissed media reports that the BNR was trying to prevent the euro from breaching through a 40,000 lei "psychological barrier".   

"There are no such barriers...We intervene whenever the leu gets weaker too quickly or it firms too fast," Vasilescu said.   

Romania switched to the euro from the dollar as its reference currency in March to reflect the weight of the euro zone in its foreign trade better.   

Analysts said a stronger leu would not help reduce the country's bulging current account and trade deficits because it would contribute to a rise in imports.   

Romania's January-September trade deficit rose to $2.67 billion from $1.71 billion in the first nine months of last year, with year-on-year imports surging by 32.5 percent and exports by 28.7 percent.   

It has been the key factor in widening the current account gap by 48.1 percent to 1.395 billion euros ($1.64 billion) over January-August from the same 2002 period.   

The euro's strength on world markets has helped Romanian exports in 2002, when the country recorded a robust 4.9 percent GDP rise, mainly due to exports to its traditional trading partner, the European Union.   

The leu currency, convertible on current account deals since 1998, will be fully liberalised on the capital account in 2007, the year when Romania hopes to join the European Union.

title: ANALYSIS-Romania's rush to free capital flows brings risks.
text:
BUCHAREST, May 28 (Reuters) - With its sights set on joining the European Union in 2007, Romania is pulling down barriers to the flow of capital, but analysts warn rushing deregulation before truly reforming its ex-communist economy may leave it vulnerable. 

 Liberalising the movement of capital is a key part of the Balkan state's drive to win the EU's "functional market economy" tag - a signal that it is ready to move closer to the wealthy bloc. 

 Romania began freeing up various capital flows in 2001. Next year it plans to admit foreign securities on domestic markets, and to make it easier for foreigners to operate local currency deposits in Romanian banks. 

 Freeing up the most sensitive flows - operations with short term money market instruments and current and deposit accounts of residents abroad - is left for when Romania joins the EU. 

 The leu, convertible on current account deals since 1998, will be fully liberalised on the capital account in 2007, the year Romania hopes to join the EU. 

 But analysts say this may open the leu to speculative attack, a scenario already fought off this year by fellow EU aspirant Hungary, even though Romania too could intervene to defend the currency under its flexible exchange rate system. 

 "I don't think our economy is ready for such a calendar," former reform minister Ilie Serbanescu said. "We may have a wonderful exchange rate management and billions in foreign exchange reserves, but our economy is not prepared." 

 The central bank runs a managed-float system, letting the leu move according to market demand, but intervening in case of increased volatility. 

 "We're rushing a bit with some deregulation," said analyst Liviu Voinea, noting the poor monitoring of private debt flows and the absence of limits on the use of state securities as collateral for short-term borrowing by residents abroad. 

 GRADUAL PROCESS 

 Analysts also said high inflation, low levels of financial intermediation by banks between borrowers and lenders, weak law enforcement and possible currency appreciation posed ongoing risks. 

 "Even though Romania's economy recovered over the past years and a series of macroeconomic indicators look good, there are persistent vulnerabilities that cannot be ignored," said Daniel Daianu, an economics professor and former finance minister. 

 Inflation halved to 17.8 percent last year and could be down in single digits from next year. The budget deficit target is 2.65 percent of GDP this year - well within the Maastricht criteria for euro zone membership, though the most optimistic date for Romania joining the euro single currency is 2010. Bank and government officials admit structural reforms must be in place to prevent a currency crisis, but insist capital account liberalisation is seen as both gradual and prudent. 

 "For each stage there will be a careful assessment...and the EU allows intervention if there are disturbances," said Romania's chief EU negotiator Vasile Puscas. 

 Valentin Lazea, chief economist at the central bank, noted that most foreign inflows into Romania were direct investments - seen at $1.4 billion this year, up from $1.1 billion in 2002, when Romanians working abroad sent back $1.25 billion. 

 He said falling real interest rates on Romanian bonds would also make speculation less attractive. 

 "All other (EU) candidates freed up capital flows four to five years ahead of accession," he said. "To postpone that calendar indirectly means to assume a delay in accession." 

 "But, if Romania does not tackle all the other aspects of (EU) integration, the risks are greater."

title: Emerging  FX -Weaker amid Slovak  intervention .
text:
LONDON, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Emerging European currencies were slightly weaker on Tuesday as intervention by the central bank of Slovakia drew more attention than the dismissal of the Romanian prime minister. 


The Slovak crown	 , boosted to record highs against the euro amid hopes for increased foreign investment next year, eased only a touch after dealers said the central bank intervened to weaken the currency.
The bank bid down the crown	     to 42.15 to the euro and then 42.20 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data.


 Soon after the intervention it was bid at 42.168 compared with 42.10 late on Monday. 

 "I'm not sure how great a success they're going to have given the euro's broad-based weakness," said Jake Moore, emerging market currency analyst at Barclays Capital. "It (the intervention) will only be of limited impact." 

 The central bank's moves came despite Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova saying on Monday she would prefer the central bank did not intervene before the end of the year as it could complicate exchange rate risks for companies. 

 Her comments boosted the crown to record levels, adding fuel to a rally driven in recent days by expectations the European Union's invitation for membership talks will boost foreign business investment in Slovakia. 

 ROMANIAN DISMISSAL 


The central bank of Romania was also expected to intervene after resuming dollar purchases on Monday to prevent an appreciation of the leu	 .



That prospect weakened the currency against the dollar and overshadowed the dismissal late on Monday of Prime Minister Radu Vasile.



Vasile was ousted following a revolt in his Christian Democrat party over slow economic reform and hopes that fresh leadership would speed admission to the EU.



The leu was bid weaker at 17,935 to the dollar from 17,895 on Monday.



The zloty	  continued to weaken amid dampened hopes for a fast decision on a full float of the zloty.



The currency fell to 1.08 percent stronger than the central bank's parity level, compared with 1.44 percent on Monday and more than two percent after comments by the finance minister last week triggered hopes for a quick move to a float.



Against the euro	     the zloty was bid at 4.221 to the euro from 4.212.



The focus is likely to shift to inflation on Wednesday, when consumer price data is expected to show annual inflation accelerated to 9.25 percent in November from 8.7 percent in October.



Czech third-quarter gross domestic product figures are also due on Wednesday, and expected to show about 0.7 percent growth from a year earlier.



The crown			was in the meantime little changed, bid at 35.86 to the euro against 35.88 on Monday.
Hungary's forint	  showed little reaction to news consumer prices rose 10.6 percent year-on-year and 0.4 percent month-on-month in November, broadly in line with market expectations.

BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--The Romanian leu (ROL) is slightly lower against the dollar early Monday, with dealers reluctant to forecast a pattern for the day as they try to make sense of a rise in the minimum reserve requirement for banks. 

 At 0730 GMT, the dollar was trading at between ROL15,960 and ROL15,990, up from between ROL15,955 and ROL15,980 late Friday. 

 Market participants said the money market is still unstable as banks try to adapt to the new minimum reserve requirements which came into effect Friday. The rise in commercial banks' minimum reserve requirements to 20% from 15% has drained leu liquidity and increased money market rates to levels around 100%. 

 The overnight money market rate was quoted early Monday at between 95% and 125%, while the one-week deposit rate was quoted at between 80% and 125%. 

 On the foreign exchange market, the leu has been seen supported by a slight intervention from the National Bank of Romania, which sold few million dollars Friday as the dollar traded above ROL16,000, dealers said. 

 Market players said the central bank would allow just a slow depreciation of the leu, which must be in line with the level of inflation. June inflation rose by 5.1% on the month, following a 5.3% raise in May.

 Market participants said the leu fell in early trading as some banks bought dollars to fill their hard currency positions ahead of weekend. They also said the National Bank of Romania might intervene in the market to buy dollars in order to restore its foreign exchange reserves, which were depleted to around $852 million at the end of June due to heavy foreign debt payments. 

 Dealers said the central bank might encourage a depreciation of the leu in line with inflation, to prevent a real appreciation of the currency. Romanian inflation rose 5.1% in June on the month, compared with a rise of 5.3% in May, the National Commission for Statistics said Wednesday. 

 Year-on-year inflation at the end of June was 48.2%. 

 Dealers' attention will continue to be focused on the money market, ahead of an increase in commercial banks' minimum reserve requirements to 20% from 15% on July 16. 

 Market participants said that interest rates are expected to go up following the increase in minimum reserve requirements, as banks will need time to adapt to the higher level. 

 On Thursday, the overnight money market rate was quoted between 15% and 30%, while the one-week deposit rate was quoted between 35% and 60%.

title: EBRD/ Romania  Central Banker -2: Won't  Intervene  In  Forex
text:
International bankers have speculated that Romania may try to raise short-term loans by pledging its gold reserves, which are worth an estimated $900 million, as collateral. But Popa said that under the terms of its Samurai bond issue, which matures on May 28, the government can't use its gold for this purpose. 

 Popa said the bank may instead deposit some of its gold overseas in order to earn some interest. 

 Although Popa earlier pledged that the country wouldn't default on its bonds and would try to protect its foreign exchange reserves, the country's foreign currency markets are expected to be volatile throughout May and June. 

 But speaking to Dow Jones Newswires, Popa said the central bank has no plans to intervene in the markets to support the currency. He added that the central bank will confine itself to periodic interventions in the money markets. 

 "We don't want to intervene in the foreign exchange market, since that would involve a lot of reserves," he said. "We will continue to do what we have been doing up till now and intervene in the money market to defend against speculative attacks." 

 By raising short-term interest rates, the central bank can limit the availability of leu (ROL) with which to buy dollars. 

 Popa said he believed the leu is now at "equilibrium levels." 

 In addition to loans from the IMF, the World Bank and foreign banks, Popa hopes the government will be able to ease its financial problems through sales of state-owned companies for foreign currency. Popa estimated that the government will receive between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion from this source in 1999. 

 Popa told Dow Jones Newswires that the crisis in Kosovo won't affect the government's ability to reach that target. 

 "Some investor prudence is warranted, but I don't see sizable adverse effects (from Kosovo)," he said. 

 Other countries affected by the Kosovo crisis are less optimistic. A Bulgarian government minister Friday said he expects foreign direct investment in the country to be halved as a result of the war.

BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--The Romanian leu (ROL) is steady against the dollar early Thursday, but dealers predict it will depreciate by the end of the day. 

 At about 0747 GMT, the dollar was between ROL14,950 and ROL15,000, little changed from late Wednesday. 

Currency dealers said the leu is likely to depreciate slightly by the end of the session amid falling money market rates. The overnight money market rate was quoted between 20% and 80%, down from 40% and 100% Wednesday, while the rate for one-week deposits was quoted between 50% and 100%, from 50% and 115% Wednesday. 

 The National Bank of Romania was seen intervening in the market Wednesday to halt the leu's rapid fall. The central bank sold "only a few million dollars" when the dollar was trading at more than ROL15,000, dealers said. 

 Market observers predicted the central bank will look to keep tight control over the currency as the government negotiates a new stand-by loan from the International Monetary Fund. Talks are expected to conclude by April 22.

title: Romanian Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  To Halt The Leu's Fall -Dealers
text:
BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Romania intervened on the foreign exchange and money markets Wednesday in an attempt to halt the fast depreciation of the leu (ROL), currency dealers said. 

 The central bank was seen selling a "few million" dollars on the forex market as the dollar was traded at between ROL15,450 and ROL15,650, dealers said. They also noted that the central bank attracted leu deposits at high rates to drain the leu liquidity and prevent banks from investing in dollars. 

 The central bank attracted one week deposits at rates between 150% and 200%, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the leu depreciation sharpened midday Wednesday amid increasing dollar demand from importers. They said the heavy demand for dollars will maintain the pressure on leu in the coming days. 

 After central bank intervention, the dollar was traded at between ROL14,700 and ROL15,150 but the leu resumed its depreciation trend later and the market closed at between ROL14,800 and ROL15,300 a dollar. 

 So far this year, the leu has depreciated 27.3%, compared with the central bank's official target of 40% depreciation for the whole of 1999. 

 Analysts said the central bank will have a difficult task trying to support the leu in the coming three months when Romania must repay almost $1 billion in foreign debts. 

 The central bank foreign exchange reserves were quoted at $1.5 billion at the end of last week.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Romania on a knife-edge.
text:
LONDON, March 19 (Reuters) - Romania is on a knife-edge, caught up in an ethical argument between foreign banks and the International Monetary Fund that could cost it crucial external funding and plunge it into further economic turmoil. 

 Overseas analysts said the eastern European country desperately needed foreign finance to stave off debt default and economic collapse, but an IMF diktat that banks must shoulder their share of the burden had put that support at risk. 

 "You've got private finance saying it doesn't want to lend money, and the IMF saying 'If you don't want to lend money, why should we?'" said Charles Robertson, emerging Europe economist at ING Barings in London. "The Romanian authorities are stuck in the middle." 

 A current account deficit of around seven percent of gross domestic product combined with a spike in debt service obligations mean Romania must bridge an external financing gap of at least $5 billion this year, analysts said. 

 Maturing debt amounts to $2.8-3.0 billion, of which about $1.0 billion falls due in May and June alone. 

 Lined up against that, Romania has foreign currency reserves of about $1.5 billion and gold reserves worth $900 million. 

 A privatisation programme is under way, but deals so far on companies such as telecom operator Romtelecom or oil refinery Petromidia have brought in little hard cash after debt write-offs and investment obligations are taken into account. 

 The country is seeking funding of around $1 billion from the World Bank and IMF this year, with approval needed from both institutions to unlock either loan. These would then pave the way for other multilateral funding. 

 But the IMF has told Romania it should refinance or roll over some $800 million in principal and interest coming due this year on two Eurobonds and a yen Samurai bond, arguing that it cannot be expected continually to bail out private investors. 

 Analysts said Romania was determined not to default on the bonds, and bankers said it had made no approach to that end. 

 But foreign reserves are already under siege from the sliding leu currency, currently bid on the interbank market at around 15,000 to the dollar against 11,000 at the start of 1999. 

 The central bank said on Thursday it would intervene to support the currency when and where needed. 

 "Romania is in real trouble," said Nick Douch, emerging markets analyst at Barclays Capital. "It's a classic case where if they continually intervene they worsen the credit risk." 

 Analysts said Romania needed a weaker leu to ease its current account problems, but a currency freefall would spook investors and Romanians alike and could topple the fragile coalition government even before general elections next year. 

 One possible way through the May-June debt crunch is for Romania either to sell some gold reserves or - more probably - to use the gold as collateral for fresh commercial borrowing. 

 But Robertson at ING Barings said the IMF was likely to object to such an arrangement, arguing it would effectively run down Romania's reserves while insulating the banks from risk. 

 To gain IMF support the centre-right government must also press on with sweeping structural reforms, but the social pain that these inevitably cause is eroding its popular support. 

 Analysts said former communist and nationalist parties were waiting in the wings and could form a new government hostile to foreign investors. (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: =Exotic  Currency  Focus: Romanian Leu's Fate Linked To Debt
text:
BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--A deep economic recession and fears the country may default on its foreign debts sent the Romanian leu (ROL) tumbling against the dollar this week. 

 The leu's fate now hinges on the National Bank of Romania's dwindling ability to intervene on the foreign exchange markets, and the government's success in negotiating fresh loans from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. 

 The leu has fallen 10.3% against the dollar so far this week, and closed at ROL16,000 Thursday. A further sharp depreciation of the currency could lead to inflation in excess of the 32% targeted by the government for 1999. 

 But the National Bank of Romania insists it has the power to halt the leu's decline. 

 "The central bank will intervene both on the money market and foreign exchange market to steady the leu," the bank's chief economist, Valentin Lazea, told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 So far this year, the leu has depreciated by 28.2%. The central bank had planned to allow the currency to depreciate by 40% during the whole of 1999. 

 Lazea said that the leu's depreciation was "normal" until this week. But he said the currency's decline since Monday was being driven by speculators. 

 "The normal value for the dollar would be between ROL14,000 and ROL15,000," he said. 


     Debt Repayments In May And June Crucial



But with the government set to draw on central bank currency reserves
to meet heavy debt repayments this year, many market participants doubt
the central bank's ability to defend the currency.



"The (central) bank can not afford to spend the reserves," said Serban
Ionescu, an analyst at Erste Bank in Bucharest.



The country must repay $1.54 billion of foreign debts this year, and
find the money to cover a $2.3 billion current account deficit. But the
central bank had only $1.59 billion at the end of February.



More than $800 million in principal and interest matures in May and
June, when analysts and officials see another hard time for the leu.



Lazea didn't exclude major fluctuations of the currency at that time,
similar to those experienced this week.



However, he said Romania will meet its May repayments, which include
$430 million in yen-denominated Samurai bonds lead managed by Nomura
International and a $250 million Eurobond lead managed by Merrill Lynch.
He said revenues from privatization will help preserve the central bankforeign exchange reserves.



But in order for the government to be able to meet its debt payments
and maintain some semblance of stability in the foreign exchange market,
it will have to persuade the International Monetary Fund and the World
Bank to resume lending.



The government is currently negotiating with the World bank a $300
million loan to support the country's badly needed structural reforms.
Conditional on the success of negotiations with the World Bank, an IMF
team will return to Bucharest in April, when a letter of intent for a
new stand-by loan might be signed.



     Officials Stand By Inflation Forecasts



Until there is clear sign of progress in these negotiations, the leu
is likely to remain weak, analysts said. But further leu weakness will
further damage an already stricken economy.



"The leu's decline is threatening the (country's) macroeconomic
stability," the central bank's Lazea said.



Speaking on national radio Thursday, National Bank Governor Mugur
Isarescu said the leu's weakness was in part a response to the
repatriation of $60 million of foreign investments in the Treasury bill
market. He said foreigners no longer want to hold the country's domestic
debt.


Currency dealers said the leu rallied against the dollar midday
Thursday amid dollar sales by some state-owned banks. The leu resumed
its depreciation trend later while the dealers predicted the market
might calm down in the next days if the central bank intervenes on the
market.



It may already be too late to meet the central bank's depreciation and
inflation targets for this year, however, although officials are
sticking to their forecasts for the time being.



"We remain at the same targets. Officially," the central bank's Lazea
said.

title: FOCUS- Romania  C.Bank vows to  intervene  on  currency .
text:
BUCHAREST, March 18 (Reuters) - The governor of Romania's central bank (BNR) pledged on Thursday to intervene whenever required to support the leu currency after its sharp plunge this week on volatile markets. 

 "We will intervene when and where it is needed," Mugur Isarescu told parliament's upper house, the Senate, a day after the leu sank more than five percent against the dollar, its largest single-day decline this year. 

 Separately, Finance Minister Traian Remes said the country will "categorically" not default on debt servicing payments this year. 

 The leu started the day by resuming its fall from Wednesday's close of 15,500/17,000 to the dollar, and swung between 11,000 and 16,000/18,000 at midday before being quoted at 15,000/17,000 in mid-afternoon. 

 Most dealers said the BNR was trying to sell some treasury notes from its portfolio but no deals appear to have been done. There was no apparent direct foreign exchange intervention. 

 The currency, which started the New Year at about 11,000 to the dollar, has been battered by poor economic performance and large trade deficits. Central bank officials say a correction is required as the currency has appreciated in real terms in the past two years due to high capital inflows. 

 Remes told reporters a promised plan to redress the leu's situation would be ready next week. He said he had "no moral right" to disclose details as this could affect markets at a critical point for the leu. 

 Isarescu said the bank had taken no action during Wednesday's big drop. The Finance Ministry had had to honour redemption of $60 million in domestic bonds, he said. 

 He said the central bank was now working with a projected leu depreciation of about 40 percent, compared to 31-32 percent as set down in the 1999 budget. Markets would quickly calm down and the depreciation would be more gradual from next month. 

 Analysts have expressed concern about Romania's ability to meet servicing of more than $2 billion in public debt, with a peak in May and June. The government is negotiating a new loan arrangement with the World Bank, a pre-requisite for further credits from the International Monetary Fund. 

 On Bucharest streets, the leu rebounded slightly at exchange offices from Wednesday's selling quotes of up to 23,000. 

 Passersby gaped at rates posted on billboards and calculated out loud the prices of imported goods. Dozens of shops selling appliances shut their doors and declared a day of stock-taking. 

 "How much do you think they will push up the price of a mobile phone?" one young man asked a friend. 

 Small queues formed outside banks of depositors trying to change leu deposits into hard currency. 

 Former Prime Minister Petre Roman, now Senate Chairman and leader of the Social Democrats, said the central bank had to intervene to protect the currency against speculation. 

 "The central bank must intervene firmly to stem speculation and stabilise the currency," Roman told a news conference. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Romania  C.Bank vows to  intervene  to boost  currency .
text:
BUCHAREST, March 18 (Reuters) - The governor of Romania's central bank (BNR) pledged on Thursday to intervene whenever required to support the leu currency after its sharp plunge this week on volatile markets. 

 "We will intervene when and where it is needed," Mugur Isarescu told parliament's upper house, the Senate, a day after the leu sank more than five percent against the dollar, its largest single-day decline this year. 

 "The situation reflects tension accumulated within the economy and in public life. At the moment, there is a big psychological component reflected by big spreads on markets." 

 The leu started the day by initially resuming its fall from Wednesday's close of 15,500/17,000 and then regained some of the lost ground. At mid-day, it was swinging wildly from quotes of 11,000 to 16,000/18,000 and by mid-afternoon, quotes were standing at 15,000/17,000. 

 Most dealers said the BNR was trying to sell some treasury notes from its portfolio but no deals appear to have been done. There was no apparent direct foreign exchange intervention. 

 But the currency was helped by dollar selling orders from corporate clients at mid-day. Orders were relatively moderate, but in the tumult even small amounts were prompting big swings. 

 The centrist coalition government cut its weekly meeting to 90 minutes and put off a discussion on a privatisation bill. Leaders of the four coalition parties agreed to meet next week to discuss the outlook for the currency. 

 Finance Minister Traian Remes told reporters a promised plan to redress the leu's situation would be ready next week. He said he had "no moral right" to disclose details as this could affect markets at a "critical" point for the leu. 

 Isarescu said the bank had taken no action during Wednesday's big drop. The Finance Ministry, he said, had had to honour redemption of $60 million in domestic bonds. 

 He said the central bank was now working with a projected leu depreciation of about 40 percent, compared to 31-32 percent as set down in the 1999 budget. Markets would quickly calm down and the depreciation would be more gradual from next month. 

 The leu, which started the New Year at about 11,000 to the dollar, has been battered by poor economic performance and large trade deficits. Central bank officials say a correction is required as the currency has appreciated in real terms in the past two years due to high capital inflows. 

 Analysts have expressed concern about Romania's ability to meet servicing of more than $2 billion in public debt, with a peak in May and June. The government is negotiating a new loan arrangement with the World Bank, a pre-requisite for further credits from the International Monetary Fund. 

 On Bucharest streets, the leu rebounded slightly at exchange offices from Wednesday's selling quotes of up to 23,000. 

 Passersby gaped at rates posted on billboards and calculated out loud the prices of imported goods. Dozens of shops selling appliances shut their doors and declared a day of stock-taking. 

 "How much do you think they will push up the price of a mobile phone?" one young man asked a friend. 

 Small queues formed outside banks of depositors trying to change leu deposits into hard currency. 

 Former Prime Minister Petre Roman, now Senate Chairman and leader of the Social Democrats, said the central bank had to intervene to protect the currency against speculation. 

 "The central bank must intervene firmly to stem spculation and stabilise the currency," Roman told a news conference. 

 Isarescu said the bank's strategy called for a faster depreciation in the first months of the year and a more gradual decline from April. 

 After closing on Wednesday at 15,500/700, the currency was traded in volatile conditions through the morning. 

 The leu initially resumed its fall and then regained some of the lost ground. By mid-day, quotes ranged from 16,000/18,000 to 14,000/17,000 and most dealers said the central bank had taken no action on the market. 

 But the currency was helped by some dollar selling orders from corporate clients at mid-day. Orders were relatively moderate, but in the tumult even small amounts were prompting big swings. 

 The leu started the week at 13,850 to the dollar. At the New Year, it was trading at about 11,000.

title: Romanian Leu's Sharp Depreciation Spreads Panic
text:
BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--The depreciation of the Romanian leu has become critical after the currency fell sharply again Wednesday, market participants said. 

 The leu dropped 5.8% against the dollar in hectic trade Wednesday after a 2.5% fall Tuesday. So far this year, the leu has depreciated 27,2%, clearly overshooting the central bank's official target of 40% depreciation in 1999. 

 "Everybody is desperate to buy dollars, at any price," a dealer at a foreign bank in Bucharest said. "Somebody must do something to halt the trend, if it can or if it has the interest to do it," he said, referring to a possible intervention from Romania's central bank. 

Currency dealers said the fast depreciation trend could be stopped only by a massive intervention from the central bank. They said the longer the intervention is delayed, the higher the costs in terms of the value of the currency. 

 "It is a moment of panic," said a top official at a foreign bank in Romania, adding that the leu's depreciation has been caused by speculative trading. "The next two weeks will be crucial in proving whether the Romanian market is mature enough to return to normal," he said. 

 The leu's depreciation Wednesday also sparked panic among ordinary Romanians, who rushed to exchange savings in lei for dollars. In Bucharest, the exchanged houses bought the dollar at ROL16,000 and sold it at more than ROL18,000. 

 On the interbank foreign exchange market, the dollar closed at between ROL15,500 and ROL18,000, up from ROL14,400 and ROL14,500 early Wednesday and ROL14,200 and ROL14,600 late Tuesday. The National Bank of Romania quoted its reference rate at ROL14,900, from ROL14,040 Tuesday. 

 The leu's depreciation initially was seen as a positive sign by analysts. A weaker leu was expected to help the government narrow its current account deficit, which was estimated at $2.3 billion in 1998. Adding the $2.2 billion in foreign debts that must be repaid this year, it become clear that the central bank would have to choose between meeting payments and supporting the leu. 

 But the leu fall in the past days boosted concerns about the central bank's ability to halt the leu from disaster. 

 The official at the foreign bank said that the central bank is expected to intervene and calm the market by attracting leu deposits on money market and diverting banks from investing in dollars. A central bank intervention on the foreign exchange market, however, is unlikely as the central bank needs its foreign exchange reserves - quoted at $1.59 billion at the end of February - to pay back foreign debts. 

 But if the leu continues to fall, the central bank might need to intervene via administrative measures, such as implementing the crawling peg, the official said. 

 The central bank spokesman Adrian Vasilescu said in a radio interview Wednesday that the leu's depreciation trend won't continue in the coming days.
