title: FOCUS-Romania c.bank calms pressure on the leu.
text:
BUCHAREST, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) on Wednesday said it had intervened on the local interbank and money markets to brake a decline in the leu and promised a close watch on the currency's further movements. 

 "The BNR will intervene whenever the market needs to be calmed down," BNR spokesman Mugur Stet said. 

 He said the BNR's policy would maintain its focus on controlling the money supply and on keeping a market-determined exchange rate as an "element of credibility". 

 Dealers earlier said the BNR had sold dollars and drained money market funds after the unit had slumped to 12,100 to the dollar from Tuesday's close of 12,020/50 amid speculative purchases by banks and increased corporate hard currency demand. 

Intervention had helped the leu firm at mid-day to quotes near 11,965/12,040 and propelled money market prices towards 100/140 percent against 70/80 percent at the opening. 

 But the recovery was shortlived. The unit weakened again in afternoon trading to close at 12,040/060. 

 "The BNR moves were more decisive on the money market," said a dealer. "But if you look at the closing prices that's an indication that the market preferred to stay long on dollars." 

 Stet gave no figure on what the foreign exchange intervention had cost. Some traders estimated it at some $15 million. They also said the bank paid around 130 percent on drainage of one-and two-week funds. 

 Latest data put the BNR's foreign exchange reserves at $1.97 billion at end-January. 

 Stet noted the BNR had paid earlier this week around $200 million to service debts to the European Union. The amount was a part of February's total payments on the public and public-guaranteed debt of around $388 million. 

 Operators saw the leu likely to stay under pressure on Thursday when position adjustments were likely to continue, probably linked to week-end money deals. They also said short-term rates were expected to remain near current levels. 

 "I believe the leu could finish the week near 12,100/150 despite some support from the money market side," said one dealer, adding that the unit might quote near 12,500 at end-February. 

 The leu has weakened around three percent this week and by more than nine percent since the New Year. 

 The decline came against the background of poor economic indicators, with gross domestic product estimated to have slumped 5.5 percent in 1998 after a 6.6 percent plunge the previous year. Forecasts have it contracting this year too. 

 Data issued on Monday also showed the 11-month trade balance in FOB prices showed a deficit of $2.24 billion against around $1.6 billion in the same 1997 period. 

 Traders said the indicators had no direct impact on trading. 

 "The poor results have been priced in by the market even before they were issued," said one. "And the leu decline in the recent period had only confirmed that pessimism." 

 Overnight and one-week prices rose to 100/140 percent after the BNR actions, against 70/85 percent in early trading. 

 BNR officials were not immediately available for comment. 

 Dealers said increased pressure on the leu had come from speculative position adjustments by banks. Some said the BNR had spent about $15 million in Wednesday's intervention. 

 The leu has depreciated by more than 2.5 percent since end-January due to banks' speculative moves and increased hard currency demand from corporate clients.

title: FOCUS-Romanian  central bank intervenes  to prop leu.
text:
BUCHAREST, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) intervened on the interbank market on Thursday, selling dollars to prop the leu currency for the first time since it slipped past 10,000 to the dollar four days ago. 

 Dealers said the action, in two waves, could ease pressure on the currency in coming days. 

 They said the BNR took action after the leu dived to about 10,193 to the dollar in early trade from about 10,140 at Wednesday's close. The second wave of interventions came at midday, hoisting the leu to about 10,060 from 10,143. 

 "We've been waiting for such action through the week since the leu moved into five digits," said one dealer. "The dollar surge was driven by position adjustments and some import bills, but the market calmed down on BNR support for the leu." 

 The leu's passage through the sensitive 10,000 level took place in calm interbank trading. But Romanian consumers, who have seen the leu sink from 21 to the dollar when the communist era ended nine years ago, feared new bouts of inflation. 

 The indicative rate calculated by the BNR firmed to 10,053 from Wednesday's 10,080. But it was down from 9,877 a week ago. 

 Some traders said sliding short-term money market rates might have been behind a faster leu fall in recent days. Rates hovered near 50/80 percent against some 110/120 a week ago. 

Central bank officials declined comment on Thursday. But BNR officials had been at pains previously to point to a combination of factors behind the leu's decline - a large current account deficit, inflation and poor productivity. 

 The market has been unmoved by the most recent outbreak of Romania's recurrent political infighting, with leftist and nationalist opposition parties boycotting parliamentary debates. 

 The assembly on Thursday postponed a vote on a new BNR board, though parliamentary commissions agreed on its composition, with Mugur Isarescu retaining the post of governor which he has held since 1990. 

 "We have seen continuous political rows this year and the market failed to react," said one. "And as we are keeping nearly the same team at the BNR, I don't see a major worry." 

 Dealers said the leu might stay relatively stable for a while but the near-term outlook was fpr a further slide, with interbank prices seen between 10,500 and 10,800 in the new year. 

 "I don't think the BNR will allow it to slip below 11,000 this year," said a dealer with a foreign bank. "For a while, the leu might gain some support from an expected pick up in money market rates ahead of the end of this month." 

 The leu opened the year at about 8,000 to the dollar and lost ground gradually over several months. It has sunk more than four percent since October and the BNR intervened repeatedly early in November to cushion its fall. ((Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 312-0264, fax +40 1 315-8448, bucharest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

Exports rose 9.9% from January 2022 to 238K units, and domestic new-car sales were up 20% at 94K units. Auto industry association AMIA projects production in 2023 to increase 6.6%, and exports to grow 7.2%. In 2022, production rose 9.2% from the previous year, and exports were up 5.9%. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

0835 ET - Canada logged only its second annual goods-trade surplus in recent years in 2022, widening to C$20.1B from a C$4.6B surplus in 2021. That followed yearly merchandise-trade deficits from 2015 to 2020. Last year saw a big jump in exports, up 22.1% thanks in large part to strength in prices, while imports rose 19.8%, with higher prices also playing a significant role, Statistics Canada says. Goods exports in 4Q22 fell 2.5%, a second consecutive quarterly drop, led by lower energy products, while imports were down 1.4%, the first decline since 2Q20. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0825 ET - Treasury yields give up some of their post-jobs report gains, ahead of Chair Powell's speech later today and as investors seem to scramble to guess when the Fed will pivot. Powell will speak at the economic club in Washington, his first chance to address Friday's surprisingly high employment gains. "With investors pricing in a significantly more hawkish policy response, all eyes will be on [Powell's] interview," Deutsche Bank analysts say in a note. "Clearly any implication that there are upside risks to the Fed's rate outlook would validate the shift in market pricing over the last couple of days." The two-year yield is at 4.437% and the 10-year at 3.732%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0821 ET - The U.K.'s 4Q 2022 GDP is expected to flatline with December's GDP shrinking to a more sizeable 0.4% month-on-month, driven by broad-based weakness across the construction, manufacturing and services sectors, Deutsche Bank analyst Sanjay Raja says in a note. Although 2022 GDP growth is expected at around 4.1% the U.K. is still on course for a 2023 technical recession with activity expected to fall in the first two quarters, Raja says. Expectations are for 2023 GDP shrinking by 0.5% and expanding by 0.8% next year, with GDP crossing its pre-pandemic peak in 4Q, 2024, he says. "While the U.K. remains firmly on course for a negative growth year in 2023, we now think that the oncoming recession will be shorter and shallower," Raja says. (anthony.orunagoriainoff@dowjones.com)

0743 ET - The Bank of England could cut the bank rate as soon as in the last quarter of 2023 as the U.K.'s economic activity slows, rate of unemployment rises, and inflation falls, UBS Research economist Dean Turner says in a note. "With the economy slowing, inflation falling, and unemployment rising, we expect the BOE to unwind some of the policy tightening from the past 10 meetings," he says. Turner expects the BOE base rate to peak at 4.25% in March. "With labour market data still signalling tightness, the BOE will likely deliver another small--25 basis points--hike in March, lifting base rates to 4.25%," he says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0701 ET - The euro's downward correction against the dollar is likely to prove limited, Argentex says. The Federal Reserve's modest 25 basis points interest rate rise last Wednesday lifted EUR/USD above 1.10 but the exchange rate suffered a correction after Friday's strong U.S. nonfarm payrolls report prompted investors to close out short dollar positions that bet on its fall, Argentexforex analyst Joe Tuckey says in a note. However, the data merely prolongs, not cancels, the gradual erosion of dollar strength, he says. "We think deeper pullback toward [EUR/USD] 1.05, if it were to happen, would be met with buyers," he says. "Trendline support at 1.0680 may arrest the downside move first." EUR/USD falls 0.2% to 1.0707. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0628 ET - U.K. house prices were flat in January and on-year growth slowed, according to new data from Halifax, as demand was burdened by the Bank of England's consecutive rate rises, Interactive Investor says. However, looking ahead, the central bank could pause or even cut rates later this year, which is good for the housing market, particularly if the economic downturn is less devastating than feared, Interactive head of investment Victoria Scholar says in a market comment. "The U.K. housebuilders suffered painful stock market losses last year but shares in Taylor Wimpey and Persimmon are both up by around 15% so far in 2023, reflecting the prospect we could be approaching the peak for U.K. interest rates," Scholar says. Barratt Developments is down 0.9%, Taylor Wimpey is up 0.1% and Persimmon is up 0.7%. (joseph.hoppe@wsj.com)

0603 ET - The euro versus sterling saw a sharp increase in negative sentiment among European retail investors before the last interest rate decisions from the European Central Bank and Bank of England, Spectrum Markets says. Spectrum's SERIX investor sentiment indictor for derivatives linked to EUR/GBP fell further into negative territory before the ECB and BOE both raised rates by 50 basis points on Feb. 2. "While the eventual rate rises themselves were pretty widely anticipated by markets, there was a significant amount of volatility in the lead up to this which created opportunities for investors to act on short-term price movements, while the euro gained strength overall," Spectrum's Michael Hall says in a note. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

title: Fitch Ratings: CEE QE Supports Coronavirus Response but Brings Macro Risks
text:
Fitch Ratings-London-03 June 2020: Quantitative easing (QE) in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) has aided coronavirus crisis responses, but could bring macroeconomic risks if used excessively, says Fitch Ratings. Risks would be more pronounced if QE undermined perceptions of central bank independence and economic policy framework credibility.

Croatia, Poland and Romania have all debuted QE since the pandemic began, while the Hungarian central bank (MNB) restarted government bond buying. Not all monetary authorities have outlined specific goals, but purchases so far have mostly been small and appear focused on smoothing volatility in domestic government debt markets and lowering longer-dated bond yields. The National Bank of Poland (NBP) has been more active, building a portfolio equivalent to 3.2% of GDP across the yield curve.

All four countries face large financing needs in 2020. Policy rate cuts in Romania and Poland have underpinned lower funding costs - rates in Hungary were already at the zero lower bound (ZLB) - but QE has likely contributed. Indeed, QE purchases may have been calibrated with reference to funding conditions, which have been relatively supportive. Non-resident outflows from core CEE markets during March were proportionately smaller than from other EM regions, and April saw inflows. The MNB initially announced HUF1,000 billion of purchases between May and July, but only bought around HUF150 billion last month, with weekly purchases falling as yields declined.

Lower financing costs are supportive of sovereign ratings in the short-term, as noted in our recent report

What Investors Want to Know: Central Bank Purchases of Government Bonds. However, we also highlighted potential medium-term risks from QE, which are often greater in emerging markets (EMs).

By increasing the money supply, unsterilised QE can put pressure on exchange rates. Croatia and Romania have intervened to support their currencies and Hungary tightened monetary conditions in April, suggesting that awareness of this risk may be limiting the size of their QE programmes. Meanwhile the Czech National Bank (CNB) cited potential exchange rate destabilisation as a reason not to adopt QE, although the CNB can buy Czech government bonds following recent legislative changes.

The exchange rate impact of crowding non-residents out of local currency debt is probably lower, given high local ownership of government debt (75%-80% of the total). The desire to introduce new local demand given high domestic bank holdings may have partly motivated QE.

QE also brings inflation risks through the money supply and exchange rate channels. QE has a mixed record at pushing inflation higher, but research suggests it raised inflation in developed markets (DMs) following the global financial crisis relative to the counterfactual of no QE. The opening of large negative output gaps suggests inflationary pressures will be muted for some time in CEE, but with QE untested in the region, the transmission to prices may be faster than in DMs.

None of the CEE central banks pursuing QE has a mandate for primary market purchases of government debt, which would be tantamount to financing the fiscal deficit, potentially damaging perceptions of central bank independence. However, some NBP operations resemble direct monetary financing.

More broadly, with interest rates likely to stay very low, and as it helps reduce funding costs, QE is likely to become a permanent part of the authorities' policy toolkit in CEE. High funding needs could result in greater political pressure to reduce the threshold for its future use.

title: Romania 's cenbank  intervenes  on  FX  to halt leu fall
text:
BUCHAREST, March 19 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank stepped into the foreign exchange market on Thursday, seeking to rein in the falls in the leu currency over the past few days due to global coronavirus worries, dealers said.

The leu fell as low as 4.8610 to the euro in early session and later firmed about 0.5% on the day to trade at about 4.8450 by 1200 GMT. "It likely shown some bids," said one trader, referring to the central bank. Another said: "It's been there to cushion the slide."

Contacted by Reuters, the bank's spokesman Dan Suciu said: The bank never comments." (Reporting by Radu Marinas; Editing by Alex Richardson)

title: *S&PGR Revises Romania Outlook To Negative
text:
10 Dec 2019 16:57 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Romania Outlook To Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Large spending deviations by the previous government have forced 
Romania's current leadership to revise up its fiscal targets for 2019 and 
2020, against the backdrop of a slowing economy. 
     -- Planned wage and pension increases will contribute to a widening of 
Romania's already substantial current account deficit through 2020. 
     -- While we assume significant fiscal consolidation commences next year, 
the rigid budget structure and volatile policy environment pose risks to that 
assumption. 
     -- We are therefore revising our outlook on Romania to negative from 
stable, and affirming our 'BBB-/A-3' ratings. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On Dec. 10, 2019, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Romania to 
negative from stable. At the same time, we affirmed our long- and short-term 
foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at 'BBB-/A-3'. 
 
As a "sovereign rating" (as defined in EU CRA Regulation 1060/2009 "EU CRA 
Regulation"), the ratings on Romania are subject to certain publication 
restrictions set out in Art. 8a of the EU CRA Regulation, including 
publication in accordance with a pre-established calendar (see "Calendar Of 
2019 EMEA Sovereign, Regional, And Local Government Rating Publication Dates: 
Midyear Update," published July 2, 2019, on RatingsDirect). Under the EU CRA 
Regulation, deviations from the announced calendar are allowed only in limited 
circumstances and must be accompanied by a detailed explanation of the reasons 
for the deviation. In this case, the reason for the deviation is the rising 
risk that delayed policy response could lead to the erosion of Romania's key 
credit strengths: its modest public and external leverage. The next scheduled 
rating publication on Romania will be in 2020, with the exact timing publicly 
available in our next "Calendar Of Sovereign, Regional, And Local Government 
Rating Publication Dates," which will be published later this month. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The outlook revision reflects increasing risks to RomaniaÂ´s economic and 
fiscal stability should policymakers be unsuccessful stabilizing and 
consolidating Romania's budgetary stance, including from plans to implement 
further pension hikes from next year. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower our ratings on Romania within the next 24 months if: 
     -- Fiscal and external imbalances continue to deteriorate and persist for 
longer than we currently anticipate, with the absence of fiscal consolidation 
resulting in higher public and external debt than we currently forecast. 
     -- A lack of economic policy synchronization leads to an overextension of 
real wages and increased exchange rate volatility, with potential negative 
repercussions on public- and private-sector balance sheets. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could revise the outlook to stable if we observed that the government has 
made headway in anchoring fiscal consolidation, leading to a stabilization of 
Romania's public finances and external position. 
 
RATIONALE 
Policymakers have increased their projections for the budgetary deficit for 
2019 and 2020 to 4.3% and 3.5%, respectively, of GDP from 2.8% and 3.0%, 
signifying a major deviation from original targets. These revisions largely 
reflect Romania's new government's transparent decision to settle overdue 
invoices and arrears with suppliers within the 2019 budget while revising 
downward its expectations for revenue growth. 
 
However, we believe there are grounds to question the realism of the revised 
budgetary targets over the 2020-2022 period. First, we understand the 
government intends to stand by the pension hikes mandated in the July 2019 
pension law, leading to over 3% of GDP in cumulative pension spending 
increases in 2020-2022. 
 
Second, in our view, any plans for offsetting budgetary measures are 
complicated by the upcoming election cycle. Given that the general government 
deficit will likely exceed the EU's 3% of GDP Excessive Deficit Procedure 
(EDP) ceiling this year and next, Romania may not be able to avoid the EDP 
determined by the European Commission  under the Stability and Growth Pact. 
Romania was last subject to the EDP from 2009 to 2013. 
 
Third, an economic slowdown would weigh on government revenues, leading to 
further budgetary pressures. Under our base-case macroeconomic scenario, we 
assume growth remaining close to 3% through 2022. 
 
Despite these concerns, we have decided to affirm the rating given 
comparatively low stocks of general government and external debt. The 
affirmation also reflects Romania's EU membership, which benefits its 
institutional framework, in our opinion. Constraints to the ratings include 
low economic wealth, relatively weak administrative capacity, an unpredictable 
policy environment, and only average monetary flexibility relative to peers. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Short-term political considerations 
continue to guide policy 
     -- Economic growth in Romania should remain just below 4% this year 
before weakening in 2020-2021, since external demand and wage growth are 
slowing. 
     -- Erratic policy execution, low administrative capacity, corruption, and 
polarization weigh on our institutional assessment, which is nevertheless 
helped by Romania's EU membership. 
     -- We do not expect meaningful fiscal consolidation before the 2020 
elections. 
 
We believe that the volatile political and policy environment will constrain 
the interim government, headed by Mr. Ludovic Orban , in delivering reliable 
fiscal consolidation ahead of next year's general elections. Should the 2020 
budget proposal not achieve parliamentary support in the December budget vote, 
the prospect for snap elections would rise. The likelihood of this scenario 
and its timing are difficult to predict given the fluidity of Romanian 
politics. Ultimately, we believe that an election and a reset of parliamentary 
positions would likely be required to form a government with a sufficiently 
strong mandate to move ahead with a firmer consolidation agenda. 
 
Romania's political environment remains subject to confrontational rhetoric 
and parliamentary infighting. Political dynamics are in flux because support 
for the historically dominant Social Democratic PSD party has been declining, 
culminating in the October 2019 no-confidence vote and the landslide 
re-election of centrist President Iohannis in November. Given the busy 
election calendar, we anticipate that short-term political objectives will 
continue shaping Romania's historically procyclical fiscal policy. 
 
The Romanian government has repeatedly deviated from the medium-term 
objectives stipulated in the EU's Stability and Growth Pact. The planned 
headline deficits for 2019 and 2020 suggest a longer delay in responding to 
the imposition of an EDP than we had anticipated. That said, we continue to 
regard Romania's EU membership as an important policy anchor, and we believe 
the very likely imposition of the EDP in 2020 will ultimately serve to instill 
fiscal discipline--but not before a new legislative term has commenced. For 
these reasons, our base-case scenario forecasts show fiscal deficits will 
start declining from 2021, after the general elections take place. 
 
Romania will likely close 2019 with headline growth of just under 4%, after 
consumption-led expansion. This follows average wage inflation so far this 
year of close to 15% alongside increased government that boosts demand. We 
understand that authorities plan to move ahead with a 7.2% increase in the 
minimum wage early in 2020, a measure that would likely contribute further to 
short-term overheating and an even wider current account deficit. 
 
Over the medium term, however, we believe growth will decelerate as fiscal 
impetus subsides. For our base-case macroeconomic scenario, we assume growth 
remaining close to 3% through 2022, though we acknowledge that there are 
near-term uncertainties in either direction. 
 
Over the longer term, Romania's growth prospects will remain constrained by 
the high net emigration of skilled labor and negative population growth. 
Structural reforms to address these issues appear to be lacking. High wage 
growth in recent years has not been accompanied by comparable increases in 
productivity, which has in part eroded the competitiveness of Romania's 
exports. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: External imbalances have widened, but low 
stocks provide scope for adjustment 
     -- We expect general government deficits will reach 4.3% of GDP in 2019 
and 4.0% of GDP in 2020. 
     -- The funding mix of Romania's current account deficits is shifting, as 
foreign direct investment (FDI) and capital account flows decrease. 
     -- Despite the uncertain fiscal outlook, we expect Romania's central bank  
to keep inflation expectations under control and maintain adequate foreign 
currency reserves. 
 
Romania's fiscal deficit is widening more rapidly than we originally 
projected. In its November budget revision, the new government has announced a 
deficit of 4.3% of GDP for 2019 compared with the planned 2.8% deficit of its 
predecessor. The deterioration stems in part from weaker-than-expected tax 
revenues but is primarily due to payment of arrears to suppliers. We believe 
pressures on Romania's budget will persist through 2022. The composition of 
the budget and structure of the deficit suggest imbalances are significant, 
with spending on wages and pensions now standing at well over 80% of tax 
revenue. We consider the fiscal choices made thus far particularly 
problematic, given the country's challenging demographics. 
 
Weaker fiscal performance stems from the pre-electoral context, which 
constrains the interim government's room to maneuver. We have revised our 
forecasts to include in 2020 fiscal expenditures of 1% of GDP, related to the 
pension law and only partly mitigated by government's potential offsetting 
measure. For 2021, we assume the elections will provide the government with a 

10 Dec 2019 16:57 ET 
Press Release: S&PGR Revises Romania Outlook To -2-


mandate to change material elements of the pension increases anticipated in 
the July pension law. Absent such measures, we project that Romania's fiscal 
deficit will climb to about 6% of GDP by 2022, with government debt sharply 
higher as a share of GDP, implying an increase in interest expenses and 
further strain on its external position. 
 
Yields on government securities showed fluctuations over 2018-2019, with an 
increase in the cost of government borrowings. This, in our view, reflects the 
country's higher financing needs and greater uncertainty regarding fiscal 
policy. The widening of government deficits in 2019-2020 has amplified 
short-term financing requirements. With mounting uncertainty on the prospects 
of fiscal stabilization, this situation could lead to a further rise in 
funding costs and a higher interest bill. Romania's government debt stood at 
35% of GDP in 2018, with government liquid assets representing approximately 
5% of GDP. The maintenance of this fiscal reserve buffer will continue to help 
limit refinancing risk, alleviating the effects on access to financing in the 
event that foreign investment starts dwindling. 
 
Romania's current account deficits will likely remain elevated through 2022, 
mirroring the ongoing consumption-led growth and evolution of the government's 
fiscal position. Strong domestic demand and softening exports will result in 
deficits exceeding 5.0% of GDP on average over 2020-2021, in our base case. 
Perhaps more importantly, we observe that the current account deficit is 
increasingly covered by debt-financed inflows, since FDI and capital account 
flows are moderating. Compared with 2017, deficit coverage by these flows 
declined to around 70% in 2018 from over 90% and have reduced further in 2019 
as the current account deficit widened. Moreover, we note a lack of foreign 
greenfield investments, suggesting that investors might be increasingly 
hesitant due to the rapid wage growth, lack of infrastructure development, and 
continuing political and policy uncertainties in Romania. This will likely 
keep Romania's external debt on an upward trajectory. 
 
The leu's value is determined under a managed float in an inflation-targeting 
regime, with a target of 2.5%, plus or minus 1 percentage point. We forecast 
an inflation rate of 4.0% in 2019, and believe that the inflationary 
environment will keep the spotlight on monetary policy, due to the need to 
firmly anchor inflation expectations. Consumer price index-based data shows 
that the real effective exchange rate has been stable since the end of 2016. 
However, wage-adjusted real effective exchange indicators suggest 
overvaluation. 
 
We have observed that the National Bank of Romania  (NBR) has countered 
depreciation pressures on the leu through intervention in the foreign currency 
market, in particular through November which saw a meaningful net outflow of 
reserves. Failure to anchor fiscal policies will pressure the leu, further 
complicating the central bank's mission. Over 2019, the NBR has been adamant 
that an exchange rate correction as a way to handle the external deficit is 
not on the table. We expect the NBR to uphold monetary policy credibility, 
anchor inflation expectations, and keep foreign currency reserves at a solid 
level. We forecast a controlled exchange rate correction through 2021 in our 
base scenario as the outlook for fiscal consolidation remains uncertain. 
Elevated exchange rate volatility could have severe repercussions on public- 
and private-sector balance sheets, in particular because about half of 
Romania's government debt is denominated in foreign currency. Moreover, an 
estimated 40% of financial sector deposits are denominated in foreign 
currency, as well as roughly one-third of sectorwide loans.s 
 
Romania's predominantly foreign-owned banking sector remains sound, in our 
view. The system's loan-to-deposit ratio declined to about 80% at year-end 
2018 from its peak of 137% in 2008. Lending growth has remained positive for 
the past two years, with loans to households and loans denominated in Romanian 
leu increasing strongly, though this trend has recently decelerated. 
Nonperforming loans had dropped to less than 5% of total loans by Dec. 31, 
2018, from over 21% at midyear 2014. Liquidity and solvency ratios remain 
strong, and banks have maintained their profitability despite low interest 
rates.

In accordance with our relevant policies and procedures, the Rating Committee 
was composed of analysts that are qualified to vote in the committee, with 
sufficient experience to convey the appropriate level of knowledge and 
understanding of the methodology applicable (see 'Related Criteria And 
Research'). At the onset of the committee, the chair confirmed that the 
information provided to the Rating Committee by the primary analyst had been

make an informed decision. 
 
After the primary analyst gave opening remarks and explained the 
recommendation, the Committee discussed key rating factors and critical issues 
in accordance with the relevant criteria. Qualitative and quantitative risk 
factors were considered and discussed, looking at track-record and forecasts.

title: CEE MARKETS-Leu jumps from six-week lows, bond yields rise at auctions
text:
* Leu gains; central bank may have intervened 
    * Romanian government may alter new taxes
    * Hungary, Romania sell bonds at increased yields
    * Forint hits 10-month high, British Brexit vote watched

 (Adds government bond auctions in Bucharest and Budapest)
    By Sandor Peto and Luiza Ilie
    BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, March 14 (Reuters) - The leu
rebounded on Thursday from the six-week low it reached late on
Wednesday, after what market participants said may have been
possible intervention by Romania's central bank.
    Romanian government bond yields rose to multi-week highs and
the finance ministry sold five-year bonds at an average yield of
4.47 percent, up 18 basis points from a sale four weeks ago.
      
    Romanian asset prices have been jittery in the three months
since the government announced new taxes on various businesses,
including banks.
    The government is expected to work out changes to the levies
by next week to prevent a downgrade of its credit rating outlook
to negative from stable by Standard & Poor's.
    The leu gained 0.3 percent against the euro to
trade at 4.768 at 0930 GMT, off Wednesday's six-week lows at
4.78. 
    "The historically high turnover (on Wednesday) is supporting
the idea of official offers coming in to protect the Romanian
leu," Bucharest-based ING Bank analysts said in a note.
    Romania's overnight ROBOR interbank interest rate
 was bid at 1.41 percent, unchanged from Wednesday
and still near three-month lows.
    The yield on the five-year benchmark Romanian bond
 was bid higher by 7 basis points in the secondary
market at 4.32 percent.
    Government bond yields rose 1 to 2 basis points in the
region's main markets, tracking Bunds.
    The Hungarian government sold 106 billion forints ($381.08
million) worth of bonds at its bi-weekly auction and top-up
tender, boosting its original 65 billion forint offer.
 
    Yields rose from an auction held two weeks ago. But after
the sale they retreated by about 1 basis point in the secondary
market, indicating that demand remained strong.
    Regional currencies were mixed as investors waited for a
third British parliamentary vote this week on its planned exit
from the European Union, this time on whether to delay the March
29 deadline.  
    The forint gained 0.2 percent against the euro to
314.32, setting a 10-month high amid expectations the Hungarian
central bank will start to tighten policy at its meeting on
March 26.
    Poland's zloty weakened, trading at 4.3045 versus
the euro. 
    In equities markets, the stocks OTP, the region's
biggest independent lender which reported record earnings for
2018 two weeks ago, rose more than 1 percent to a record high.

title: CEE MARKETS-Leu jumps from 6-week lows, tax debate stays in focus
text:
* Leu firms, central bank may have intervened -dealers
    * Investors watch how Romanian government will alter new
taxes
    * Currencies mixed, British Brexit vote watched closely
    * Polish central bank sometimes intervenes, its chief says

    By Sandor Peto and Luiza Ilie
    BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, March 14 (Reuters) - The leu
jumped on Thursday, rebounding from 6-week lows set late in the
previous session, in what market participants said was possible
intervention by Romania's central bank.
    Romanian asset prices has been jittery in the past three
months since the government announced new taxes on various
business sectors including banks.
    The government is expected to work out changes to the levies
by next week to prevent a downgrade of its credit rating outlook
to negative from stable by Standard & Poor's.
    The leu firmed a quarter of a percent against the
euro through the 4.77 psychological line, to trade at 4.768 at
0930 GMT, off Wednesday's 6-week lows at 4.78. 
    The Romanian central bank has a track record of managing the
currency in the market sometimes. One Bucharest-based dealer
said the central bank was probably behind the leu's rebound.
    "The historically high turnover (on Wednesday) is supporting
the idea of official offers coming in to protect the Romanian
leu," Bucharest-based ING Bank analysts said in a note.
    Romania's overnight ROBOR interbank interest rate
 was bid at 1.41 percent, unchanged from Wednesday
and still near 3-month lows.
    Given the uncertainty over S&P's rating, an auction of
5-year Romanian bonds on Thursday "seems to have come at the
wrong time", but the government could sell the full amount if it
allows some rise in the yield, the ING note added.
    The yield on the 5-year benchmark Romanian bond
was bid higher by 8 basis points in the secondary market to 4.33
percent.
    Hungarian yields rose 2-3 basis points ahead of the
government's auction on Thursday as the market digests a rise in
the sale at the bi-weekly auctions to above 100 billion forints 
($359.69 million), one trader said.
    Regional currencies were mixed as investors were looking at
the impact of the third British parliamentary vote this week
concerning its planned exit from the European Union, this time
on whether to delay the March 29 deadline.  
    The forint firmed slightly, trading near
Wednesday's 10-month highs amid expectations that the Hungarian
central bank will start to tighten policy at its meeting on
March 26.
    Poland's zloty eased a touch, but remained stuck
at the 4.3 psychological line versus the euro.
    Polish central bank governor Adam Glapinski said the bank
has sometimes intervened in the foreign exchange market but
these interventions have been limited.
    DM TMS Brokers analyst Konrad Bialas said the stability of
Poland's economy and monetary policy had kept the zloty very
stable in the past months, rather than interventions.

title: Icelandair Flies Near Debt Covenants Breach -- Market Talk
text:
0812 GMT - Icelandair 's last profit warning has already cost its CEO the job and now the airline says its debt covenants are at risk. The carrier said it had opened talks with more bondholders owning more than 50% of its debt about terms. It may request a waiver of covenants or change terms.(robert.wall@wsj.com)

0807 GMT - Poland and Romania decide on Wednesday whether to raise interest rates or not. UniCredit says both will likely remain on hold, with the National Bank of Poland holding the rate at 1.5%, likely throughout 2019, and National Bank of Romania keeping the rate at 2.5%. Poland's central bank is unlikely to raise rates "for as long as the European Central Bank 's deposit rate remains negative, and as long as inflation stays within the 1.5-3.5% target range." Romania's central bank is intervening in the foreign exchange market "to keep the currency stable to ensure inflation moderates." EUR/PLN is down 0.2% at 4.2890 and EUR/RON is flat at 4.6664. Both decisions are due later in the day. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0805 GMT - Aston Martin bond yields fall after shares in the luxury-car maker were priced at GDP19 per share at its initial public offering on the London Stock Exchange , valuing the firm at GBP4.33 billion. Yields on Aston Martin 's 5.75% April 2022 sterling-denominated bonds fall as low as 4.93% from 4.967% in early trading, according to Tradeweb . "Today's listing on the London Stock Exchange represents a historic milestone for Aston Martin Lagonda . We are delighted by the positive response we have received from investors across the world and are very pleased to welcome our new shareholders to the register," chief executive Andy Palmer said.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0753 GMT - The Turkish lira falls after data showed annual Turkish inflation jumped to 24.52% in September from 17.90% in August, lifting USD/TRY to a five-day high of 6.0912. A higher inflation number often boosts a currency because it means interest rates will rise, making money more expensive. But in Turkey--whose central bank had been reluctant in the past to raise rates to curb inflation--there are concerns that the central bank may not have raised rates rises sufficiently to prevent inflation running out of control. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has previously expressed a preference for lower interest rates. USD/TRY last trades up 1.1% at 6.0514. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0753 GMT - Taiwan's growth momentum is likely to slow after 1H's 3.2% GDP increase, says Standard Chartered , with the US-China trade dispute a key concern. The island is heavily dependent on trade, and the 2 countries are among Taiwan's largest markets. That as China is the "preferred offshore manufacturing base" for many Taiwan exporters, the investment bank reminds. It estimates that Taiwan GDP growth would be slashed by 1.8 percentage points in "the worst-case scenario of a full-blown US-China trade war." StanChart has predicted 2.8% GDP growth for all of this year; 2017's increase was 2.9%. (chester.yung@wsj.com; @chester_yung)

0747 GMT - The Singapore dollar will likely remain under pressure through mid-2019 as "gradual" gains in the greenback is seen continuing, says UOB in setting a S$1.41 target for then, versus an end-of-2018 call of S$1.39. It add that "given the backdrop of overwhelming US-dollar strength, the risk is that these point forecasts may be reached sooner than later." Meanwhile, the investment bank doesn't see Singapore's central bank tightening policy further next week amid recent economic reading having "noticeably" weakened of late. The dollar has edged higher this afternoon and is up 0.1% for the day at S$1.3745. (saurabh.chaturvedi@wsj.com; @journosaurabh)

0737 GMT - Telecom Italia bond yields fall after it said late Tuesday that it had invested EUR1.69 billion in a block of 5G internet bandwidth as part of Italy's mobile spectrum auction. It also successfully bid EUR33 million for a separate block and has already won bids for two other sections, bringing its total investment in this auction to EUR2.41 billion. Yields on Telecom Italia 's 7.75% January 2033 euro-denominated bond erase early trading gains and fall as low as 4.302% from a peak of 4.373%, according to Tradeweb.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0733 GMT - German 10-year Bund yields trade higher, indicating less investor appetite for safe havens amid the Italian turmoil, but UniCredit 's analysts say that developments in Italy will remain a key driver of Bunds near term. "In the near term its dynamic [that of Bunds] will be driven by how the mood on Italy evolves," says UniCredit . The ongoing weakness of Italian government bonds has fanned strong support for German Bunds in the past few days and other core/semi-core eurozone government bonds. The 10-year Bund yield is trading 2 basis points higher at 0.45%, while the 10-year BTP yield is trading 8 basis points lower at 3.34%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0731 GMT - The euro continues to be driven by the Italian budget projections, this time going up on reports that Italy may not pencil in another 2.4% deficit-to-GDP projection for 2020 and 2021. Against the dollar, the euro rises 0.2% to 1.1577. UniCredit says risks are contained and EUR/USD is somewhat safe from major falls. Only a break below the August lows around 1.13 would trigger a more intense sell-off. "Interestingly, EUR/CHF has so far proved more resilient than expected to increasing pressure on Italian assets, as it has failed to drop below the 1.1350 handle," UniCredit says. EUR/CHF last up 0.3% at 1.1404. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0723 GMT - The Nikkei Singapore PMI fell into contraction territory last month, sliding to 49.6 from August's 51.1, the first sub-50 reading in 2 1/2 years. The survey of the private-sector economy, conducted by IHS Markit for Nikkei, contrasts with the official PMI reading released last night, which showed a slight drop to 52.4. In the Nikkei report, it says declines in output and new orders weighed on PMI while export sales fell further. Singapore manufacturing has been widely expected to slow amid the global trade tensions. (gaurav.raghuvanshi@wsj.com)

0719 GMT - Standard Chartered trims its 2018 GDP-growth view for Hong Kong to 3.6% from 3.8%--well within the government's 3-4% forecast range--in anticipation of "looming trade challenges and higher interest rates." The investment bank notes the US-China trade fight has yet to affect the city's exports, but does expect that by year's end. Meanwhile, StanChart cuts its 2019 growth forecast to 3% from 3.4% as the expected export slowdown and likelihood of further interest-rate increases cap GDP gains. (chester.yung@wsj.com; @chester_yung)

0715 GMT - Global trade uncertainty isn't likely to hold back Singapore's central bank from tightening next week, predicts OCBC unit Bank of Singapore . It expects the MAS to "slightly increase" the policy-band slope of the local dollar's nominal effective exchange rate to 1%/year from 0.5%. "The cyclical story in Singapore continues to justify incremental MAS tightening," Bank of Singapore adds, with economic growth having been resilient since the last central-bank meeting in April. (gaurav.raghuvanshi@wsj.com)

title: CEE MARKETS-Short-term bond prices rise, Poland underperforms
text:
* Hungary's 3-year bonds draw demand after auction
    * CHF loan conversion plans remain a worry in Poland,
Romania
    * Dinar firms, central bank may intervene again

    By Sandor Peto and Ivana Sekularac
    BUDAPEST/BELGRADE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Short-term government
bonds rose in Central Europe on Friday as higher yields on the
region's paper compared to its western neighbours attracted
investors, although a possible U.S. interest rate rise left the
assets with an uncertain outlook.
    Hungary's 3-year bonds traded at a yield of 1.33 percent at
0750 GMT, compared with -0.66 percent on Germany's corresponding
paper, while the 10-year yield was flat at 2.99 percent.
    The 3-year yield was down 7 basis points from levels before
an auction on Thursday which drew huge demand.
    "That bond is attractive as its yield had surged from 1.22
percent (in the last month)," one Budapest-based trader said.
    That rise in yields came despite ratings agency Standard and
Poor's lifting the country back into investment grade on Sept.
16 in a surprise move. 
    Romania's 3-year yield was bid lower by 6 basis points at
1.49 percent, while its 10-year yield rose 3 basis points.
    Risks of a rise in Polish government spending and Warsaw's
tension with Brussels over the rule of law have kept its bond
yields underpinned, however. 
    They rose 1-2 basis points along the curve, with 10-year
papers trading at 3.04 percent.
    In both Poland and Romania, planned legislation on the
conversion of Swiss franc mortgages partly at the cost of banks
have also weighed on assets. Pressure on bonds is higher in
Poland, Raiffeisen analyst Imre Stephan said in a note.
    Poland's financial regulator KNF said on Thursday that
Polish banks would face bigger than expected costs if a proposal
to make them return excessive currency conversion spreads
charged to clients becomes law.
    Concerns over a Romanian bill on conversions, which
parliament is seen passing on Tuesday, knocked the leu 
down to 3-month lows early this week.
    Rating agency Fitch said on Thursday that Romanian banks
which have relatively large Swiss franc loan portfolios had set
aside sufficient reserves for possible conversion losses.
    The leu was flat at 0844 GMT. The Bucharest bourse's index
 touched an 8-week low, underperforming regional indices
which rose as higher than expected Chinese inflation data helped
Asian and European stocks rebound.
    The dinar firmed 0.1 percent to 122.97 against the
euro, past levels where the central bank sold it in the market
on Wednesday to prevent a strengthening. 
    The bank did not cut its 4 percent benchmark rate on
Thursday, citing an uncertain monetary policy outlook in the
world.
    It could intervene again if the dinar does not stay in the
123-124 range, traders said.
    Demand for the dinar has been boosted by mid-month VAT and
wage payments, but it is also buoyed by the government's fiscal
consolidation policies, traders said.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Czech crown firm, industrial output beats forecasts
text:
* Crown up despite central banker comment on possible weaker
cap
    * Currencies rangebound, forint and zloty off multi-year
highs
    * Hungarian bond yields rise, tracking U.S., indicating
caution

 (Adds leu retreat, new prices and comments)
    By Sandor Peto and Robert Muller
    BUDAPEST/PRAGUE, April 10 (Reuters) - The crown 
gained on Friday after the Czech Republic reported industrial
output had risen more than expected, another  sign growth in
Central European economies is accelerating.
    Czech industrial output rose 4.5 percent in annual terms in
February, compared with analysts' 4 percent forecast.
 The crown gained 0.1 percent against the euro,
trading at 27.385 at 1202 GMT.
    Czech central bank board member Lubomir Lizal said late on
Thursday the probability had grown that the bank will shift its
cap on the value of the crown from the current 27 per euro and
set a weaker value for the crown. 
    But his comments were based on conclusions from a meeting in
March and did not take into account data released this week,
Komercni Banka chief economist Jan Vejmelek said in a note.
    The forint and the zloty were off
multi-year highs reached earlier this week. The forint 
firmed 0.4 percent to 297.33 and if it closes firmer than
297.50, it can firm to 295 on Monday, one trader said.
    The yield on Hungary's 10-year benchmark government bonds
rose 10 basis points to 3.25 percent, tracking the last days'
rise in U.S. 10-year Treasuries yields, indicating caution.
    Possible further monetary easing in the region may help
short government debt maturities and weigh on currencies.
    Analysts in a Reuters poll unanimously said Poland's central
bank would keep its rates on hold at 1.5 percent when it meets
next week. 
    The zloty firmed 0.2 percent versus the euro to
4.019.
    Romania's leu eased 0.2 percent to 4.408, bucking
the regional trend. It bounced back from 4.4, the level beyond
which analysts have said the Romanian central bank could sell it
to curb its strength.
    But dealers said illiquid trade ahead of a three-day holiday
caused the retreat rather than central bank intervention.
Markets in Serbia, Bulgaria and Romania will remain closed on
Monday for their Orthodox Easter holidays.     
    Serbia's central bank lowered its main rate on Thursday by
50 basis points to 7 percent. Raiffeisen analyst Stephan Imre
said in a note that dinar-denominated bonds remained well bid
after the rate cut and bets on more to come.
    "Against this backdrop, further rate cut speculations should
lend continued support to the dinar debt market going forward,
which still offers the highest yield levels in the CE/SEE
(Central and Southeast European) region," he added.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Hungarian shares fall on Internet tax proposal as other bourses rise
text:
* Magyar Telekom shares fall 3 pct on Internet tax plan
    * Unipetrol Q3 earnings boost its shares by 4 pct
    * Dinar gains after Serbian central bank intervention
    * Leu firms mildly after Romania sells Eurobond

 (Adds Hungarian party proposal and auction, and Serbian budget)
    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Hungary bucked gains in Central
European equities on Wednesday as a government proposal for a
new tax on Internet traffic knocked down the shares of Magyar
Telekom, the country's biggest Internet services
provider.
    Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government,
re-elected with a strong majority in April, has cut personal
income taxes in the past few years but imposed higher taxes on
some corporate sectors with strong foreign ownership, including
banks and telecommunications, unnerving international investors.
    The draft 2015 tax bill filed to parliament late on Tuesday
contains a new provision for Internet providers to pay 150
forints ($0.60) per gigabyte of data traffic, although they
would be able to offset corporate income tax against the
Internet tax. 
    Hungary's ruling Fidesz party on Wednesday proposed setting
a cap on the planned tax, but the move failed to lift the stocks
of Magyar Telekom, a unit of Deutsche Telekom.
     The shares fell more than 3 percent after the market
opening and were down 2.6 percent by 1234 GMT.
    Deutsche Telekom shares eased 0.3 percent in Frankfurt,
while the bourse's main stock index rose.
    The new levy could increase Magyar Telekom's tax burden by
as much as 10.5 billion forints, the equivalent of 10 forints
per share, Budapest-based brokerage Equilor said in a note
before the Fidesz party proposal. 
    "In theory the company can pass the new burden on to
customers but that would be a business policy decision," Equilor
said, adding that the new tax also increased uncertainty over
whether Telekom will pay a dividend for 2014.  
    Budapest's main equities index fell by 0.3 percent,
in contrast with moderate rises in most other Central European
bourses, led by a 0.8 percent rise in Bucharest.
    The Hungarian debt agency scrapped a one-year Treasury bill
auction as demand was low after a decline in yields to record
lows in the past months, and many investors hoped better prices
at an 8-week bill auction on Monday.  
    Prague's main stock index rose 0.2 percent.
    The shares of Czech oil processing firm Unipetrol 
surged about 4 percent. The company posted a third-quarter net
profit of 1.4 billion crowns ($65 million), after a loss a year
ago, thanks to higher margins and rising sales. It had gained a
bigger stake in the country's main refinery. 
    The shares of Unipetrol's main owner, Polish PKN Orlen
 rose 0.8 percent, outperforming the Warsaw bourse's
main index which firmed 0.4 percent.
    
    SERBIA APPROVES BUDGET REVISION
    Regional currencies were rangebound, except for the Serbian
dinar which was firmer by 0.2 percent against the euro
at 1234 GMT, after the Serbian central bank intervened in the
market to defend the dinar on Tuesday, selling 10 million euros.
    The currency gave up part of its early gains after the
government raised its budget deficit target for the year to 5.7
percent from 4.6 percent but said it had nonetheless agreed the
"principles" of a new precautionary loan programme with the
International Monetary Fund. 
    The central bank kept its 8.5 percent interest rate, which
is the highest in the region, on hold last week as uncertainty
over talks with the IMF and the government's delay in adopting a
plan to steady its finances kept the dinar weak. 
    Finance Minister Dusan Vujovic said Serbia would issue a
Eurobond by the end of the year.   
    The leu was flat versus the euro after Romania
raised 1.5 billion euros ($1.9 billion) in a 10-year Eurobond
issue on Tuesday.

    SERBIA APPROVES BUDGET REVISION
    Regional currencies were rangebound, except for the Serbian
dinar which firmed 0.4 percent against the euro,
drifting further away from two-year lows.
    The Serbian central bank intervened in the market to defend
the dinar on Tuesday, selling 10 million euros. The bank kept
its 8.5 percent interest rate, which is the highest in the
region, on hold last week as uncertainty over negotiations with
the IMF and the government's delay in adopting a plan to steady
its finances kept the dinar weak. 
    The Serbian government adopted a draft 2014 budget revision
on Wednesday that is expected to contain cuts to pensions and
public sector wages. It was expected to announce details later
in the day. 
    The leu firmed mildly versus the euro after
Romania raised 1.5 billion euros ($1.9 billion) in a 10-year
Eurobond issue on Tuesday.

title: CEE MARKETS 2--Bonds firm, Romania keeps interest rates on hold
text:
* Romania keeps rates on hold, does not change reserve
requirements
    * Bonds advance cautiously, recovery offsets Ukraine impact

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, May 6 (Reuters) - Central European government
bonds firmed slightly on Tuesday, helped by strong economic data
from around the region that overshadowed concerns over the
situation in neighbouring Ukraine's crisis.
    Romanian bonds extended their recent gains, with 10-year
yields dropping 2 basis points to 4.91 percent, benefiting from
a regional downtrend in yields.
    Romania's central bank kept its main interest rate at a
record low of 3.5 percent as expected. It also opted not to cut
commercial banks' reserve requirements despite some expectations
that it might do to boost liquidity in domestic markets.
 
    Rates are at record lows in some parts of the region as
central banks try to support recoveries in their economies.
Romania's central bank, however, manages liquidity via market
interventions and other tools rather than through its main rate.
    "We believe the central bank will find ways to stimulate
economic growth further, even without using its more visible
instruments," said Vlad Muscalu, chief economist at ING Bank in
Bucharest.
    Governor Mugur Isarescu reaffirmed at a news conference that
the bank would lower reserve requirements in "adequate" doses at
the right time, after a surprise cut earlier this year. He also
said the bank had cut its inflation forecasts slightly.
 
    
    UKRAINE LESS OF A WORRY
    Romania has seen the fastest economic recovery in central
Europe, while inflation has been low throughout the region.
    Central European currencies were supported, while the hunt
for high-yielding debt in Europe in recent weeks buoyed debt
markets and foreign currency bonds.
    Hungary's assets outperformed their regional peers on
Tuesday after data showing retail sales there surged 8.3 percent
year on year in March, adding to signs that domestic consumption
and economic growth is recovering.
    The forint firmed 0.3 percent to 307.18 per euro. 
    The region's stock markets were mixed. Budapest's main
equities index rose 1 percent, with drug maker Richter
 shares rebounding, gaining 1.1 percent after a 3
percent plunge on Monday.
    Richter has strong sales bases in Ukraine and Russia. Its
earnings, which it will report on Wednesday, are expected to be
hurt by the fall of the rouble. 
    The markets largely turned their back on the conflict in
Ukraine on Tuesday, although the country appears to be slipping
ever closer towards war after the deadliest week since the
separatist uprising began. 
    "The markets are mostly ignoring the conflict now, which may
prove to be a mistake," one Budapest-based fixed-income trader
said.
    Hungarian bond prices reversed an early fall. Yields
returned to their recent decline, and the 3-year benchmark yield
 dropped 3 basis points to 4.05 percent.
    Polish government bonds also firmed mildly ahead of the
auction of a new series of 5-year paper on Thursday.
    "There always tends to be new demand for new paper,
especially in light of the low inflation," said Maciej Popiel
from bank PKO BP.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Assets rebound, Ukraine crisis still a threat
text:
(Adds bonds, updates markets)
    * Markets bounce back as Ukraine/Russia tension eases
    * Return of wobbles remains a threat, Ukraine is main factor
watched
    * Romania, Serbia market interventions have not eroded
reserves

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, March 4 (Reuters) - Central European assets
rebounded on Tuesday after President Vladimir Putin said Russia
saw no need to use military force in Ukraine for now. 
    Putin's comments, and an earlier order for Russian troops
involved in a military exercise near the border with Ukraine to
return to base, were seen as an attempt to ease East-West
tension and fears of war in the former Soviet republic.
    That helped lift stocks and currencies in the European
Union's emerging east, which had tumbled as Russian assets were
hit by panic-selling on Monday.
    Shares in Hungary's OTP bank, which has some 140
branches in Ukraine, led gains, firming 5.8 percent after the
previous day's plunge of 10 percent to 18-month lows.
    But the situation in Ukraine is still "a time bomb" for
central and east European markets, one Budapest-based currency
dealer said, with investors eyeing the risk that Kiev will
default on debt as well as the possibility of military conflict.
 
    "Clearly the Ukrainian issue moves everything in the region
now," the dealer added.    
    Moscow's forces remain in control of Crimea, seized
bloodlessly after Russia's ally Viktor Yanukovich was ousted as
Ukrainian president last month. In his first comments on the
crisis, Putin said all options could be used to protect
compatriots who were living in "terror" in Ukraine.
 
    The turmoil in Ukraine has been a fresh blow to emerging
markets, many of which have already had to hike interest rates
and defend their currencies this year as investors fret about
U.S. stimulus withdrawal and Chinese economic growth. 
    Exports from the EU's eastern states to Ukraine are around
only 1-2 percent of their foreign sales, but a debt default or
war could have an impact in the region's markets.
    Central European states' economic fundamentals are
relatively strong but investors have tended to sell emerging
market assets indiscriminately this year. 
    Trading on Tuesday was thin and the tone still jittery but
Hungary's forint and Poland's zloty regained
some of the ground lost the day before, firming 0.7 and 0.3
percent against the euro, respectively.
    One Budapest-based trader said local banks had bought
Hungarian government debt, mainly long-term paper yielding more
than 5 percent - a big pick up from the central bank's 2.7
percent two-week deposit rate.
    "Foreigners bought the papers, too, and there was a rebound
in Poland," the trader said. "We will see now if there are
sanctions against Russia and what their response will be. In my
view the Ukrainian story is not over yet."
    
    RISK CHANNELS
    The forint is seen as vulnerable to contagion from other
emerging markets because Hungary is the region's most indebted
state and its interest rates are low following a long series of
cuts. The country is also due to hold elections in April.
    Firms with business interests in Ukraine, such as Hungarian
drug maker Richter and Poland's PKO BP, could
also be hurt by more financial turbulence or war there.
    Some investors also believe Romanian rate cuts have been too
deep given contagion risks. The country's central bank has had
to intervene to prop up the leu following a split in
the government last month, before which the currency of the EU's
second poorest member had been stable for several months.
    Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ponta won a confidence vote
in parliament late on Tuesday, which gave him a new mandate to
push through IMF-backed reforms. 
    Prior to the vote, the leu had gained 0.2 percent
in illiquid late trade, after earlier failing to benefit from
the improved regional mood.
    Serbia's central bank has also stepped up interventions to
defend the dinar as the country prepares for early elections on
March 16, though as with Romania its foreign currency reserves
remain healthy.
    The bank is expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday given
uncertainty pending a mid-March election, pressure on the dinar
and a pickup in inflation. 
    The dinar firmed 0.1 percent against the euro on
Tuesday. The central bank had spent 50 million euros in the
market on Monday to defend the currency, the same amount raised
by the Serbian debt agency in a Treasury bill auction.
    Poland's central bank is also expected to leave its
benchmark interest rate unchanged at its monthly meeting on
Wednesday and to start raising late this year.

title: CEE MARKETS 1- FX , stocks mildly positive but Ukraine worries linger
text:
* Forint leads currency gains
    * Polish GDP up 0.6 pct q/q, little reaction
    * Hungary investments rose 14.9 pct in Q4

    BUDAPEST, Feb 28 (Reuters) - Central European currencies and
stocks opened flat to slightly stronger on Friday but traders
said cautious sentiment would persist as investors kept an
uneasy eye on developments in neighbouring Ukraine.
    Hungary's forint led currencies in early trade
with a 0.3 percent gain versus the euro, tracked by the Polish
zloty, the region's most liquid currency, which added
0.2 percent by 0911 GMT.
    Fourth-quarter Polish economic growth of 0.6 percent
quarter-on-quarter and 2.7 percent year-on-year virtually
matched flash estimates and had no market impact. Dealers did
not expect much volatility unless tensions in Ukraine's Crimea
region escalate further.
    Data showed investments in Hungary rose by an annual 14.9
percent in the fourth quarter following a 9.8 percent increase
in the third quarter in a boon to central Europe's most indebted
economy. 
    "The favourable interest rate environment and the National
Bank of Hungary's Funding for Growth Scheme have helped
kick-start investments," the Economy Ministry said in a
statement.
    Raiffeisen Bank analyst Zoltan Torok said the central bank
programme, which provides cheap loans to companies via
commercial banks, would probably give private sector investments
a further push in the coming quarters.
    "We are bouncing up and down around the 310 per euro level.
We are looking at Ukraine but right now there is some
wait-and-see attitude by investors," a Budapest-based currency
dealer said.
    "But if anything serious were to happen, we would also take
a hit," the trader said. Another dealer said the forint would
probably remain in a 309.5-311 range to the euro on Friday in
low turnover.
    Even though the region has thin trade links with Ukraine,
the neighbouring country's crisis has sent a shockwave through
the region's markets and debt default or a military conflict in
Ukraine could deepen the slide in asset prices.
    Contagion from Ukraine is the latest setback for central
European markets, which have been hit this year by risk aversion
as the U.S. Federal Reserve began slowing its money printing.
    On Friday stock markets posted modest gains, led by a 1.4
percent increase in Budapest shares. Stocks in central
Europe's biggest independent lender OTP rebounded from
Thursday's falls to gain 2 percent.
    But a fall in shares in Erste Bank, which is also
listed in Prague, dragged down stocks in the Czech Republic
 after the lender earlier reported a drop in net profit.
Erste and energy company CEZ are the biggest listed companies on
the Prague exchange. 
    The Romanian leu, which has been backed by central
bank interventions, was steady in early trade.
    Romania's President Traian Basescu may approve the latest
review of an aid deal led by the International Monetary Fund
later on Friday.
    Basescu had previously refused to approve the review of the
precautionary, 4 billion euros aid deal because it included an
additional tax on fuels and a government plan to support low
income borrowers - policies he opposed.    
    The finance ministry is also expected to unveil domestic
debt issuance plans for March. Debt managers sold 1.93 billion
lei ($586.91 million) of leu-denominated debt in February.
    "As recent political tensions seem to have gone past the
tipping point, an early RON firming to 4.50/EUR gained further
steam to 4.49/EUR at the end of yesterday's session due to a
rebound in the regional climate," INB Bank in Bucharest said in
a note.
    "The RON is nonetheless eyeing 4.50/EUR this morning and we
still expect the local currency to stick to softer ground up to
4.51/EUR today, with a rebound probable when the new government
in the making will be announced on Monday," it said.
    The Serbian dinar was unchanged after the central
bank sold 10 million euros in Thursday's session.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Leu gains as Central Europe's fundamentals prevail
text:
* C.bank's intervention last week, IMF deal support leu
    * Romania's rate easing cycle likely coming to an end
    * Hungary T-bill demand surges

    By Sandor Peto and Radu Marinas
    BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Romania's leu shrugged
off an expected interest rate cut to lead Central European
currencies higher on Tuesday, as further signs the region's
economy is rebounding from recession outweighed disappointing
U.S. economic data. 
    The leu rose as much as 0.7 percent to the euro
before the Romanian central bank cut rates by 25 basis points to
a new record low of 3.5 percent, seen as the last of a
175-basis-point easing cycle which began in the middle of last
year.
    It edged up further after the move, which flouted a recent
trend towards higher borrowing costs in emerging markets. Turkey
and South Africa both raised rates last month to support their
currencies during a massive emerging markets sell-off.
    "The cut and its size was expected and the leu did not
soften because it's being given support from money market rates
following last week's forex interventions, which trimmed
liquidity," said one Bucharest-based dealer.
    News that the Romanian government and the International
Monetary Fund had reached agreement over a review of the
country's 4 billion euro aid deal also lent the leu support.
 
    The Romanian central bank stepped into the market last week
to defend the leu, but bought the currency in much smaller
amounts than interventions in other emerging economies. The leu
has been Central Europe's most stable currency this year. 
    Romania postponed a tender on Monday to sell one-year bills,
citing global market turbulence and saying that it had already
met most of its 2014 borrowing needs. 
    Market participants said the leu, which was bid at 4.457
against the euro, looked safe despite the rate cut.
    "The unusually thin volumes coupled with discouragingly high
FX swap rates suggest the slight firming of the leu to beyond
4.49/EUR yesterday was likely fuelled by unwinding bets against
the local currency," said ING economist Mihai Tantaru said.
    "Elevated short-term rates should entertain a similar
trading pattern for the leu with 4.45/EUR the next short-term
target," he added.
    
    HUNGARY DEBT DEMAND PICKS UP
    Hungary sold more three-month treasury bills than planned on
Tuesday as investors scrambled to shorten the maturity of their
Hungarian debt portfolio, betting on a halt or reversal in
central bank interest rate cuts.
    Investors rushed to buy short-term paper before a bond
expiry worth 439.5 billion forints ($1.9 billion) on Feb. 12. 
An uncertain interest rate outlook means keeping money in
longer-dated debt is more risky. 
    The region's most liquid currencies, the zloty and
the forint, rose about 0.6 and 0.3 percent
respectively, regaining some ground after losses in the past
weeks as a sell-off in other emerging markets spilled over into
Central European markets.
    "A series of positive data arrived from CEE, particularly
Poland's strong PMI (Purchasing Manager Index)," said Piotr
Poplawski, analyst of Bank BGZ in Warsaw. 
    "Add that to weak U.S. ISM (manufacturing survey data) and
CEEs are on the rebound."
    In recent months, better economic balance and growth
prospects have mostly protected Central Europe from the jitters
in other emerging markets, but in January investors began to
ignore differences in economic fundamentals.
    A rise in January PMIs in Central Europe helped its assets
on Monday. The effect lasted even after weak economic data in
the United States triggered an overnight plunge in equity
markets around the globe.
    "Stocks are falling in the region, too, but you see we can
call that moderate compared to (more than 4 percent) fall in the
Nikkei (of Japan)," one Budapest-based dealer said.
    Bucharest's main index led the decline in regional
equities, shedding 1.2 percent. Budapest dropped 0.3
percent.
    Hungary's central bank also indicated last week that it had
room to reduce rates again after cutting them to 2.85 percent
from 7 percent, where they stood in August 2012. 
    Hungary is the region's most indebted nation, and some
investors are betting it and Russia will be the next emerging
economies forced to defend their currencies by raising rates.
    Russia's rouble hit its lowest level in nearly five years on
Tuesday. The forint joined the sharp currency rebound in Central
Europe, but investors were cautious.
    "The Hungarian forint includes a considerable risk component
regarding the uncertainty of ongoing interest rate cuts in our
view," Raiffeisen said in a note on the region's markets.

title: Romania - Factors to watch on Jan 31
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Here are news stories, press reports and events to watch which may affect Romanian financial markets on Friday.

IMF

An IMF mission is in Bucharest until Feb. 5 for talks on how Bucharest plans to plug a revenue gap triggered by a fuel tax delay. Politicians and analysts believe an agreement will be struck in the days ahead.

text:
* Zloty underpinned as BGK expected to sell euros


    * Crown off peak hit after cbank opted against intervention
    * Romania says has covered 78 pct of 2013 funding needs
    BELGRADE/BUCHAREST, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Potential support
from a Polish state bank steadied the zloty on Friday while the
crown pulled back from a three-month high reached after the
Czech central bank opted against currency interventions for now.
    Traders expect the Polish currency to be underpinned by
sales of euros by state-controlled bank BGK before a fixing on
Monday that will determine how much Poland has to pay to match
European subsidies. 
    Two market sources told Reuters they have seen unusual
activity from BGK in the past few days, something that could
continue until 1215 GMT on Monday when the European Central Bank
carries out the fixing.
    "These are not big sums but we are seeing them very often,
which is not typical," said one of the sources.
    The zloty was flat on the day at 4.228 per euro at
1320 GMT, while the crown had dropped 0.4 percent from
Thursday's close to bid at 25.679 to the euro. 
    Czech rate setters voted on Thursday for the second meeting
in a row against intervening to weaken the crown in order to
ease monetary conditions further now that interest rates are
near zero. 
    But the bank said it stood ready to use the tool if needed,
which is a threat analysts and dealers say will put a cap on
crown gains going ahead. 
    The crown was just off 25.575 per euro hit late on Thursday,
its strongest since June, as it neared the 25.50 level seen as a
line that could prompt the central bank into action.
    Dealers expect the crown to settle back into the range of
25.65-26.00 seen in recent months.     
    "The possibility of intervention is staying on the table
(and) will limit gains in the crown. We could see verbal
intervention (if the crown is) around 25.50 in the coming
weeks," Ceska Sporitelna bank said in a note.
    Elsewhere in the region, investors will keep their eye on
interest rate decisions in Romania and Poland next week. 
    While Warsaw is seen holding rates at 2.50 percent,
Bucharest, which started its easing cycle later due to stubborn
inflation, is seen shaving another quarter point, bringing
borrowing costs to a record 4.25 percent. 
    The Romanian leu was down 0.1 percent against the
euro. The Hungarian forint rose 0.3 percent and yields
regained some ground as as concerns over budget and debt
negotiations in Washington weakened the dollar on Friday. 
    But concerns also kept a lid on gains in world shares and
limited investors appetite for emerging market currencies.

will discuss its letter of intent for a new two-year, 4 billion

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Czech crown climbs after decision against  intervention
text:
* Czech central bank keeps interest rates on hold


    * Governor says likelihood of FX intervention remains high
    * Shares in Romania's Fondul hit record high on buyback plan
    BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The Czech crown extended gains
against the euro on Thursday after a central bank policy meeting decided against
intervention to weaken the currency.
    With Czech interest rates close to zero, the central bank has said for
months that it will consider intervention to help lift inflation back to target
and boost exporters as the economy recovers after edging out of its 18-month
recession in the second quarter. 
    "We did not launch them (interventions), however we agreed that the
probability is not really changing ... and remains high," Czech National Bank
Governor Miroslav Singer said. 
    By 1345 GMT, the crown was bid at 25.692 per euro, up 0.6 percent
on the day, extending gains from earlier in the session.
    "For now, so long as the economy continues to recover and inflation doesn't
drop sharply, we doubt that a majority of MPC members will vote in favour of FXintervention at upcoming meetings," Capital Economics said in a note. 
    "Either way, the bigger picture is that monetary conditions are set to
remain extremely loose until 2015 at the earliest."
    Other regional currencies were slightly weaker. The Polish zloty 
was down 0.3 percent, while the Hungarian forint and Romanian leu
 were 0.1 percent weaker.
    "Risk sentiment is a little off, given the U.S. budget debate," one
Bucharest trader said.
    Shares, which have benefited from the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision last
week to keep its stimulus intact, were mostly stronger, though traders said they
could face pressure as attention moves to fending off the possibility of a
damaging debt default. 
    Poland's broad market index led gains with a 1.3 percent advance on
the day, firming to its highest level in almost six years, supported by rising
bank shares on expectations of an economic rebound. 
    In Romania, shares in investment fund Fondul Proprietatea 
outperformed the blue chip index and reached a record high a day after
announcing plans to buy back roughly 4.4 percent of its shares at an estimated
cost of 441.6 million lei ($133.2 million).
