text:
* U.S. Fed stimulus comments support emerging FX

* Czech crown limited by intervention fears

* Hungary and Romania sell bonds (Updates throughout)

BUCHAREST/WARSAW, July 11 (Reuters) - Most emerging European currencies firmed against the euro on Thursday after the U.S. Federal Reserve said it will stick to an easy monetary policy for now, while the prospect of central bank intervention kept the Czech crown weak.

In Hungary, the state debt management agency sold 47 billion forints worth of bonds, with yields around 60 basis points lower compared to yields accepted at the previous tender.

Romania also successfully placed bonds on Thursday with healthy demand supported by the comments from the Fed that its stimulus programme would continue for a while yet.

Hungary's June inflation inched up to an annual rate of 1.9 percent, still not far off a 38-year low hit earlier this year. Central bank policymakers have signalled they had room to cut interest rates further, a move priced in by markets.

"The bank's room for manoeuvre will continue to be defined by the external environment and the extremely loose monetary policy pursued by major central banks," said Erste Bank's Orsolya Nyeste.

"There is no particular obstacle to a July rate cut as external market conditions have turned for the better since last month."

Central and eastern European assets have plunged since May when the Fed signalled it would begin to taper its monetary stimulus that had sent a flood of money into emerging Europe. But Fed chief Ben Bernanke said on Wednesday the stimulus would continue as inflation remained low and the unemployment rate high.

By 1416 GMT, the Hungarian forint was up 0.7 percent against the euro at 292.040. The Polish zloty and Romanian leu were each 0.2 percent up.

In Romania, where the leftist government is set to start talks next week on a new aid deal with the IMF and the central bank has started cutting interest rates, traders said there was renewed interest for longer-dated debt on the secondary market.

The Czech crown was 0.2 percent weaker. With rates at a record low 0.05 percent, the Czech central bank has said it could intervene in the market to weaken the crown if it needs to ease monetary policy further.

"While (the crown) has strengthened in recent weeks (because of the EUR/USD), the space for further crown gains is limited because of threats of central bank intervention," CSOB said.

Elsewhere in the region, Serbia's central bank kept its benchmark interest rate at 11 percent on Thursday, bucking market expectations for a third consecutive cut.

Serbia is among markets which have struggled recently as investors pull out on the view that the Fed will start withdrawing stimulus, making rate cuts in these countries riskier. The dinar was flat.

title: CEE MONEY-Market turmoil cuts Romania's room for manoeuvre on IMF deal
text:
* IMF to review Romania's 5 bln euro aid deal this week

* Analysts expect long negotiations for successor deal

* Continued IMF help crucial for investment

By Luiza Ilie

BUCHAREST, June 24 (Reuters) - A rapid sell-off in emerging markets has left Romania's government with an awkward choice - push ahead quickly with politically sensitive reforms or risk the loss of an IMF safety belt and a run on its currency and debt.

Romania appeared to be in a comfortable position before the U.S. Federal Reserve rocked markets by signalling it will reduce monetary stimulus, sending developing country assets - including Romania's - tumbling.

A debt tender failed last week for the first time in almost a year, and the leu has lost roughly 5 percent against the euro since the start of May, the most of any central European currency.

A 5 billion euro International Monetary Fund-led aid deal provides some guarantees for investors, even though Bucharest has not drawn on the funds. But it expires at the end of June and the government has still to reform inefficient state firms, sell assets and use more EU development funds.

While the IMF may broadly agree that Romania has met its commitments in the current deal given it stuck with austerity to bring the budget gap under 3 percent of national output, its lack of long-term reforms will complicate negotiations over a new backstop.

"This is a high risk aversion moment in the region and risks associated with a sudden stop of the IMF agreement are fairly high," said Mihai Patrulescu, senior economist at Unicredit Tiriac Bank in Bucharest.

Analysts said investors place great value on the presence of an IMF deal which gives them more confidence that the government will pursue reforms and maintain budget discipline.

DEAL REVIEW

Romania has had IMF-led aid deals since 2009 and has made large fiscal adjustments to exit the EU's excessive deficit procedure, a scrutiny process for the bloc's heavy spenders.

But subsequent governments have delayed privatisations and the overhaul of healthcare and infrastructure, while absorption of EU development funds has been weak, at roughly 15 percent. Local administrations are still struggling to pay their bills.

The IMF will likely need to see progress in these areas before agreeing a new deal, and the leftist cabinet of Prime Minister Victor Ponta may be reluctant to act swiftly as selling assets and raising healthcare costs would erode support.

Although the government has roughly 70 percent of parliament seats and remains popular in opinion polls, the four-party ruling coalition is relatively unstable and with a presidential election looming in 2014 it may be unwilling to sacrifice its support with unpopular measures.

Premier Victor Ponta and President Traian Basescu have both said they want a successor aid deal, as does central bank Governor Mugur Isarescu who said it would provide safety in the face of volatile global markets. Still, some government officials have complained that some of the IMF's requests were unrealistic.

After selling loss making rail freight carrier CFR Marfa last week, Transport Minister Relu Fenechiu said the privatisation was done "at gunpoint" because of IMF deadlines. The lender first asked Romania to sell the carrier in 2010.

Negotiations may also be derailed by cabinet plans to raise army pensions, lower value added tax and hire more people in the public sector, all of which would pressure finances if enforced.

"Neither side will rush through negotiations," said Daniel Hewitt, emerging Europe economist at Barclays Capital. "But it is possible to work out a set of measures the government is willing to take and the IMF is willing to accept."

CREDIBILITY

Earlier this year, the IMF extended Romania's aid deal by three months, giving it more time to fulfil its commitments.

The cabinet has largely met those, culminating with the sale of a majority stake in CFR Marfa. It also sold a stake in gas grid operator Transgaz and picked advisers for several IPOs due later this year.

But the CFR Marfa sale illustrates Romania's struggles to reform companies that are still plagued by communist-era management techniques and inefficiency.

Two former bidders, who withdrew saying the short deadlines made it impossible to accurately assess the carrier, say they will file legal challenges against the sale, which still needs approval from the competition watchdog.

"Overall, the IMF has seen the agreement as a success, except when it comes to reforming state-owned enterprises," said Vlad Muscalu, a senior economist at ING Bank in Bucharest. "A third deal would aim to tackle that."

The government has a comfortable funding situation, having covered more than half its needs for 2013 and building a buffer fund that could cover the rest of the year. But the currency remains vulnerable and a sharp fall could compel the central bank to intervene to soften any violent market moves.

Even more importantly, Romania needs the IMF's seal of approval to attract much needed investment. Foreign direct investment stood at 322 million euros in April, a sliver of Poland's 2.1 billion euro first-quarter foreign investment.

"Romania has a lot to do, it is so far behind," Barclays' Hewitt said. "Reforms are very delayed." (Reporting by Luiza Ilie; Editing by Toby Chopra)

text:
(Updates prices)

* Currencies little changed in quiet trade

* Slowing inflation revives chance of Czech intervention

* Investors await Polish court ruling on Wednesday

By Jason Hovet and Marcin Goettig

PRAGUE/WARSAW, Feb 11 (Reuters) - The Czech crown dipped on Monday after data showing slower inflation revived the possibility that the central bank could turn to currency interventions to ease policy further.

The zloty also weakened. Two of Poland's most dovish monetary policy setters said they saw limited scope for more interest rate cuts although analysts said the market was still pricing in two rate cuts over the next 12 months.

By 1518 GMT the zloty had inched 0.2 percent lower to 4.155 in light trade. The crown eased 0.1 percent.

Market participants are also awaiting a court verdict expected in Poland this week that could affect monetary policy in the region's largest economy if it forces Jan Winiecki, who has blocked aggressive policy easing, to leave the bank's rate-setting council.

The court is scheduled to rule on whether Winiecki libelled a former central bank governor. Winiecki disputes the charges. If the court rules against him, the Senate, or upper house of parliament, will name a replacement.

The ruling could be delivered on Wednesday.

The government has been calling on the bank to cut rates further to support the economy and the ruling coalition has the majority in the Senate.

"The court ruling may negatively impact the zloty. The key question is who would replace Winiecki if he was dismissed," said a Warsaw-based currency trader.

In Hungary, the forint eased 0.2 percent to 291.19 per euro, unmoved after Moody's ratings agency kept the country's rating in "junk" territory with a negative outlook due to weak growth prospects for the contracting economy.

Moody's warning on Hungary comes just as the most indebted central European country readies for a possible foreign currency bond issue after Budapest's talks with the IMF about a financing backstop collapsed last year due to policy differences.

Central European economies are struggling to get or stay out of recession as the region suffers slowing trade with the crisis-hit euro zone and weaker consumer sentiment at home thanks to government belt-tightening.

Markets will look ahead to fourth-quarter gross domestic product readings in the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania on Thursday.

Data on Monday showed that the annual Czech inflation rate fell below the central bank's (CNB) 2 percent target for the first time in 15 months, which analysts said pointed to the need for easier monetary policy.

Czech policymakers have made clear since cutting rates to "technical zero" in November that intervening against the crown would be the next preferred way to ease policy to help the recession-hit economy.

"With the crown rebound after the board meeting last week, the monetary conditions are actually somewhat tighter at this moment," Danske Bank analyst Stanislava Pravdova said.

"We think the CNB should step up its rhetoric again (or it risks) seriously undershooting its inflation target."

The crown has gained 2 percent since the central bank signalled on Wednesday that further monetary easing was less urgent, quashing expectations it would intervene soon to weaken the currency.

Romania's leu - which has gained 3 percent since December while other currencies in the region have dropped in that time because of falling interest rates - was down 0.1 percent at 4.397 to the euro on Monday.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Crown hits high as  intervention  risk fades
text:
(Adds detail on Romania)

* Crown firms as intervention fears ease on cbank comment

* Romania yields rise, push leu to one-month low

* Forint recovers from weak data, investors await fx bond

By Krisztina Than and Sam Cage

BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, Feb 7 (Reuters) - The Czech crown extended strong gains on Thursday after the central bank eased fears it would intervene soon to weaken the currency, while a rally in Romanian debt stalled and knocked the leu.

The crown extended gains from the previous session, when the central bank said recent weakness in the currency meant further monetary easing was less urgent, and rose a further 0.5 percent by 1429 GMT to 25.228 per euro, having hit a one-month high.

With rates at a "technical zero" since November, Czech policymakers have made clear that intervening against the crown would be their next preferred way to ease policy in order to spur spending to boost the recession-hit economy.

"For a market which has been speculating for months now on FX interventions (the bank's comments have) been a hit," Komercni Banka fixed income trader Dalimil Vyskovsky said.

"The currency has strengthened massively in a short time and rates have jumped on both IRS and bonds. We think the move might soon prove to be exaggerated, though."

Czech central bank Governor Miroslav Singer on Wednesday squashed expectations for an intervention that the bank had flagged earlier, saying further monetary easing may still be needed but looked less urgent.

Ceska Sporitelna analyst Martin Lobotka recommended locking in profits on a recent short EUR/CZK recommendation.

"In the coming months, the bank will wait to see whether leading indicators translate into a better macro picture and will hold the crown between 25.20 and 25.70," he said in a note.

ROMANIA RALLY STALLS

Thursday also saw a rally stall in Romanian debt which had sliced 100 basis points from yields after a convincing December election win for the leftist government eased political uncertainties. The leu was also lower.

Inclusion in a key JP Morgan emerging market debt index had also supported Romanian bonds, but yields have now started to rise again as traders lock in profits.

The finance ministry sold five-year paper on Thursday at 5.79 percent, a higher cost of funds than the 5.4 percent secured at the last auction on January 17.

ING said the recent weakening in bonds could be a buying opportunity and forecast yields on three- and five-year paper would fall back to 5.3 percent.

The rally in bonds had pushed the leu to a one-year high in January but it has started to slip back and fell 0.4 percent to hit a one-month low of 4.415 per euro.

"The leu was the best performer so far this year among CEE peers so a correction had been expected," said a Bucharest dealer.

The Polish zloty and the forint tracked the crown higher, with the Hungarian currency rebounding from an initial fall to 294.94 after industrial output figures showed the biggest annual fall in more than three years.

The forint firmed 0.4 percent versus the euro to 292.9 and the government bond market also shrugged off the figures. Hungary sold more than planned at auctions on Thursday, with the market waiting on a foreign currency bond issue in which Hungary may seek to raise as much as $2 billion.

title: CEE MARKETS 2- FX  up on US data, forint extends gains
text:
* PMI data props Hungarian forint

* Zloty strengthens after underperforming CEE

* Serbian dinar up on govt-related company subsidy

By Jason Hovet and Radu Marinas

PRAGUE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Central European currencies rose on Friday on benign US payroll data and the forint extended its three-day firming streak due to fresh signs of respite for Hungary's recession-hit economy.

U.S. job growth rose modestly in January and gains in the prior two months were bigger than initially reported, supporting views the economy's sluggish recovery was on track. [ID:nL1N0B138D

"The data, I'd say have a neutral or mildly positive impact," said Piotr Bujak of Nordea in Warsaw.

The Hungarian currency led gains in emerging Europe until midday after data showing Hungary's seasonally-adjusted Purchasing Managers' Index jumped to 55.9 in January from a revised 49.1 in December.

A reading above 50 signals growth in manufacturing and similar surveys showed Polish and Czech manufacturing surveys, which use different methodology than the Hungarian survey, remained stuck below the 50 mark.

By 1400 GMT, the zloty was 0.6 percent up at 4.165 per euro and the forint rose 0.4 percent to 291.44, at similar token with the Czech crown to25,599.

"The zloty has been underperforming other CEEs over the past few weeks, so now it has more potential to gain amid better attitude to CEE as a whole, even despite improvement in Poland's PMI weaker than in Czech and Hungary."

Central Europe's economies are struggling as austerity measures are dampening consumer sentiment and because of slower trade with the crisis-hit euro zone, and central banks are loosening monetary policy, which is weighing on currencies.

The Romanian leu was 0.3 percent up at 4.365.

Dealers said Serbian dinar firmed 0.2 percent to 111.07 due to greater corporate euro sales and government-subsidised lending for small and medium enterprises worth about 120 million euros.

CONCERNS REMAIN

The forint has lost 3.7 percent since Dec. 1, leading a drop in the region, as it has also been hit by investor concerns that a new central bank governor, due to take office in March, could use unorthodox monetary tools to boost the economy.

Government officials have tried to soothe concerns this week, and Prime Minister Viktor Orban said on Friday that the leadership change needed to be as smooth as possible.

CIB analysts said that "considering technical factors as well despite a slowdown in the positive correction in the forint by the end of yesterday, there is a chance that the near two-month weakening trend in the currency will be broken."

"Risk sentiment is slightly more supportive, but flows are very low so I would not read much into the current action. I think in February we will remain well-behaved until the (foreign currency) bond is sold," a Budapest-based trader said referring to Hungary's first foreign bond issue since 2011, which could be launched in the coming weeks.

Central banks in much of the region meet next week, with Poland expected to cut interest rates. In the Czech Republic, rates are already at a "technical zero" and investors will look for clues as to whether the central bank will turn to currency interventions as its next policy tool.

Only Romania has kept interest rates steady, held back by inflation concerns that should continue as the country deregulates power and gas prices under pressure from the EU and IMF. The Romanian central bank also meets next week.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-CZK near six-month low on  intervention  talk
text:
* Czech crown falls as central bank flags intervention again

* Polish bonds fall on suggestion of pause in easing

* Leu firms to 9-month high on IMF deal hope

* Hungary raises bond sale, some think central bank to buy

(Updates throughout)

By Sandor Peto and Dagmara Leszkowicz

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Fears of central bank intervention knocked the Czech crown, while Polish bond yields rose sharply on Thursday after its central bank suggested it might halt cuts to borrowing costs.

Czech central bank Governor Miroslav Singer on Wednesday reiterated the bank's position that it is ready to intervene to weaken the crown currency if monetary policy needs to be eased further after interest rates were cut close to zero.

The crown fell to a six-month low against the euro, but regained some ground later. At 1436 GMT it was bid at 25.619, 0.5 percent weaker from Wednesday.

A Prague dealer said the early weakening was fuelled by Singer's comments and a break through a technical level at 25.6-65 to the euro.

"There were foreign names heavily buying (euros) this morning between 25.650-750. On the other hand we see increased selling activity from local corporates," the dealer said. "It will probably at least slow down further crown weakening."

The crown is near levels where the central bank could intervene, according to the 25.62 consensus estimate in a December Reuters poll, although a wide range of analyst estimates, from 24.5 to 27, showed high uncertainty.

Polish bonds continued to weaken for the second consecutive day as the central bank signalled a pause in an easing cycle.

The Monetary Policy Council cut interest rates for the third time in a row on Wednesday, bringing the key rate to 4.0 percent but said it would probably soon pause its easing campaign.

Since then, bond yields have jumped by some 20 basis points at the shorter end of the curve and market players say it may just be the beginning of the trend.

"Risk that there will be a sharper sell-off on the bond market has grown markedly after yesterday's (comments) by the central bank," said one Warsaw-based fixed income dealer.

Poland's 12x15 forward rate agreements are pricing in a total of 75 basis points more of interest rate cuts over a year and if the bank decides to end the cycle, many investors will decide to close their positions, market players say.

Hungary meanwhile increased the size of its first 2013 government bond sale by half as expectations that rates will fall and that the central bank might start buying bonds boosted investor demand.

Romania also sold more of its debt on Thursday thanks to greater political stability and prospects of a new International Monetary Fund deal.

TIME FOR FALLS?

Hopes an international credit line will be secured have also boosted the leu which gained some 0.6 percent to the euro, hitting a nine-month high.

It has broken the level of 4.4 percent it had tested repeatedly since late December, when a clear election win gave the government a mandate to negotiate a new IMF deal.

Prime Minister Viktor Ponta makes a speech at 1600 GMT in which he may give details of the credit talks with the IMF and this year's budget, which has not yet been passed by parliament.

Other currencies in the region were in the red on Thursday, with Hungary's forint down some 0.8 percent and the Polish zloty 0.3 percent weaker.

The two currencies were the region's top gainers last year, rising 9.5 percent and 7.7 percent respectively as investors sought healthy returns from high-yielding assets.

But easier monetary policy and - in some cases - countries' willingness to weaken their units has cooled the market's appetite for CEE assets and market players say scope for further strengthening is limited.

"I would tend to think that HUF, PLN and CZK would lead regional currencies weaker - watch also for possible intervention by the BNR in Romania to help stem recent appreciation and just take the heat out of hot money inflows," Timothy Ash, economist at Standard PLC wrote in a note.

title: CEE MARKETS 4-Czech crown rebounds after mild cbank comments
text:
(Adds Czech central bank news conference, new prices)

* Czech cbank keeps rates on hold as expected

* Crown rebounds as cbank does not mention fx intervention

* Leu slips as Romania delays IMF-agreed privatisation

* Positive global mood underpins other FX, stocks

By Sam Cage and Sandor Peto

BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST, Dec 19 (Reuters) - The crown regained ground on Wednesday to trade flat on the day after the Czech central bank kept interest rates on hold near zero but stayed mum about market intervention to weaken the currency.

Investors watched closely whether the bank would step up its earlier rhetoric on possible crown selling. But Governor Miroslav Singer did not signal intervention at a news conference after the rate decision.

Romania's leu meanwhile slipped from three-month highs after the new government delayed sales of state assets agreed with the International Monetary Fund, raising doubts about its commitment to a new IMF pact.

Progress in U.S. budget talks increased investors' risk appetite, supporting other emerging European currencies and equities.

The Czech central bank kept its two-week repo rate

unchanged at 0.05 percent after slashing the benchmark rate earlier this year to support the recession-hit economy.

The bank's economic forecast has shifted from balanced to slightly anti-inflationary, but the change is small, he said.

"The forecast assumes looser monetary conditions, (moving to) the bottom, around the middle of the next year," Singer said, but he declined to forecast any monetary policy measures.

Erste Group said in a note that the central bank "did what it could and now it can pretty much sit and wait."

Dealers have said that investors would start to buy euros near crown levels at 25 against the euro. The crown was bid at 25.177 against the euro, off intra-day lows at 25.248.

"I think people want to see intervention and cannot cope with the fact that it will not come soon," a Prague dealer said.

Other central banks in the region have also lowered borrowing costs to counter economic slowdown.

ROMANIA'S IMF DEAL THREATENED

The leu eased 0.1 percent to the euro to 4.47.

"On the one hand, (the move in the leu reflects) commercial needs at the end of the year, and on the other the news that IMF-agreed privatisations have been postponed has taken a toll," said a Bucharest dealer.

Leftist Prime Minister Victor Ponta, whose government is set to be approved by parliament on Friday following a Dec. 9 election, had assured investors he would replace Romania's 5 billion euro IMF deal, which expires in early 2013.

But the government's announcement that it had postponed the sale of minority stakes in several state-controlled companies by a year, to end-2013, and a proposal to split the finance ministry, could complicate that process.

The IMF has regularly criticised the European Union's second-poorest member for failing to sell and reform its inefficient and oversized state sector, which holds back an economy that is only slowly emerging from a deep recession.

A positive global mood underpinned the Polish zloty

and the Hungarian forint amid expectations of more aggressive monetary stimulus from the Bank of Japan and signs of progress in resolving the U.S. budget logjam.

The zloty hovered around its highest since early October, rising 0.3 percent to 4.076, and the forint was up 0.4 percent, recouping some of this week's losses ahead of a meeting where the central bank cut its base rate.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Forint, zloty down on rate cut prospects
text:
* Hungary's c.bank seen cutting rates next week after low CPI

* Czech cbankers point to crown weakening intervention

* All eyes on more stimulus in the U.S.

* Romania expects PM nomination after Sunday vote

BUCHAREST, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint and Polish zloty fell against the euro on Wednesday driven by rate cut expectations, while the Czech crown shrugged off central bank comments pointing to intervention aimed at weakening the unit to support a fragile economy.

Prospects of Hungarian and Polish rate cuts outweighed expectations the Federal Reserve will announce a fresh round of bond buying with newly created money later on Wednesday, which were supporting riskier assets worldwide.

The forint and zloty are up 11 and 9 percent respectively year to date, having benefitted from a yield chase by investors outside western markets.

But traders said Tuesday data showing Hungarian inflation fell to 5.2 percent in November should bolster arguments for a fifth consecutive rate cut by the central bank.

"Next rate meeting takes place on Tuesday and given the lower inflation, the rather stable forint, despite recurrent cuts, as well as continued dovish comments from MPC members, we expect another cut by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent next week," SEB said in a note.

"We anticipate further cuts in the beginning of 2013 to front-load the easing cycle and expect the rate to bottom at 5.25 percent."

Poland too has cut its key rate twice this year to 4.25 percent, the lowest since May 2011.

On Wednesday central banker Andrzej Kazmierczak, seen as one of the staunchest hawks among policymakers, said it was too early to speak about further cuts. But Governor Marek Belka said on Tuesday the bank was "very likely" to cut rates further to boost the slowing economy.

Market interest rates fully price in further cuts totalling 125 basis points over the next twelve months in Warsaw.

By 1045 GMT, the forint and zloty were each down 0.2 percent to the euro.

CZECH INTERVENTION

Elsewhere in the region, Czech central bank Vice-Governor Vladimir Tomsik said interventions against the crown were the most efficient tool for further monetary easing, after the bank cut its main rate to a record low 0.05 percent last month.

Even the bank's most ardent hawk and monetary policy easing opponent weighed in on Wednesday saying she would support intervention on condition benefits to exporters would outweigh risks from higher prices.

Czech short-end yields dipped to fresh record lows, but the crown was up 0.1 percent.

"As long as there are voices from the central bank saying they will intervene if necessary, then we should not be surprised if it really happens," Komercni Banka analyst Jan Vejmelek said in a note.

"So far I have the feeling that market players are rather underestimating this risk."

Romania's leu was 0.2 percent stronger but still volatile as investors wait to see who President Traian Basescu will ask to form a government after Prime Minister Victor Ponta's coalition won two-thirds of seats in a parliamentary election.

The ruling leftist alliance has said it wants Ponta to be reappointed, but analysts said Basescu, locked in a power struggle with the prime minister, may try to split the parties by nominating someone else.

text:
* Polish 5-yr bond yields at record low

* Czech c.bank governor says bank would intervene if needed

* Romania sells planned 250 mln lei in 3-yr bonds

(Updates throughout)

By Jason Hovet and Dagmara Leszkowicz

PRAGUE/WARSAW, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Polish 5-year bonds hit record lows on Thursday on expectations the country's central bank will soon cut borrowing costs, while the Czech crown recouped early losses tracking a stronger euro.

Earlier, the crown fell after central bank governor Miroslav Singer said the bank may intervene to weaken the currency if there was a risk of long-term deflation pressure.

Currencies across the region were mostly firmer in afternoon trade though traders said worries over Spain persist.

Expectations of lower interest rates in Hungary and Poland are pointing to weaker currencies in those regions and bond yields are near record lows in Poland and the Czech Republic.

"Rally on Polish bonds continues and every single effort of setting against the trend ends up badly," said Bartlomiej Wit, chief fixed income dealer at ING Bank Slaski.

By 1316 GMT the crown, the Polish zloty and Hungary's forint each added some 0.2 percent to the euro while Romania's leu edged some 0.2 percent lower.

Minutes from the Czech central bank's Sept. 27 meeting, released last week, showed that the governing board was still divided over whether to intervene against the crown and employ more monetary easing to prop up the recession-hit economy.

Years of austerity are taking a toll on the Czech economy and other economies in the region are fighting to get out of or avoid recession. The export-driven region is also struggling with slowing trade with the euro zone.

In Poland, a speech by Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Friday was keenly awaited, as he is expected to announce some measures to try to stimulate growth.

In Hungary, the forint was steady, shrugging off data showing the headline inflation rate jumped to 6.6 percent, the highest in over four years. Hungary has cut its interest rates, the highest in the European Union, for two months in a row.

Hungary sold nearly 1.5 times as much 12-month paper as originally planned and average yields fell 23 basis points from the previous auction two weeks ago. Yields on the secondary market also fell, and the government plans to launch a new three-year euro-denominated bond.

Budapest, which is still wrangling with the International Monetary Fund over a financing deal analysts say is needed to bring its borrowing costs back down to manageable levels, has not tapped international markets so far this year.

"Regardless of the high inflation data, which surpassed already high market projections, expectations for interest rate cuts have not diminished," said a Budapest fixed income trader.

"If Hungary wants, it can come out with a euro bond, and if storm clouds are gathering, there is still the IMF as an alternative."

Romania sold a planned 250 million lei in three-year treasury bonds, with the average accepted yield some 26 basis points lower compared to the level accepted at the last tender of the paper in February.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Leu bounces off record low, zloty hits 1-yr peak
text:
* Dealers cite c.bank intervention boosting leu

* Romania govt shuffle keeps political tension high

* Zloty hits fresh 1-year peak, yields little changed

* Crown trails after second straight output decline

By Jason Hovet

PRAGUE, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu rebounded 1 percent off a record low on Monday, with dealers saying the central bank had intervened to give it some respite from a months-long political clash that has paralysed policy and drawn criticism from abroad.

Other emerging European currencies also gained, led by a jump in the Polish zloty to a one-year high due to strong demand for Polish bonds. The Czech crown, however, trailed after data showed industrial output declined for a second straight month.

Recession-hit Romania paid a higher price for its debt on Monday. It sold a planned offer of 700 million lei in one-year paper at a 5.66 percent average yield, 37 basis points higher than at a sale in June.

Markets were keen to see the results at the tender, Romania's first market foray since a July 29 referendum to impeach suspended President Traian Basescu.

After a delay, Romania's Constitutional Court will decide on Aug. 31 whether to validate the referendum, in which a large majority voted to dismiss Basescu, but turnout fell short of a required threshold.

Prime Minister Victor Ponta's government wants his rival Basescu removed, arguing he has overstepped his powers.

The power struggle has raised doubts over Romania's International Monetary Fund standby aid deal that has helped it weather the volatility of the euro zone debt crisis but comes with strict policy requirements.

By 1445 GMT, the leu rose 1.4 percent to 4.51 to the euro, well off an all-time low of 4.651 hit on Friday.

"I think depreciation bets will soften from now on, after the central bank (intervention)," said a Bucharest trader.

The central bank declined to comment.

On Monday, Ponta replaced five ministers in his cabinet after the resignation of an interior minister. Earlier, central bank Governor Mugur Isarescu urged the Balkan country's leaders to reduce the political tension, but added that, given the turmoil, the exchange rate was "almost reasonable".

"It doesn't make sense for them to intervene too much at this point," a second trader said. "We need to at least know the referendum outcome, otherwise they can only provide short-term support."

ZLOTY TESTS 4.0 LEVEL

In other trade, Serbia's dinar dipped 0.1 percent after government moves to step up control over the central bank prompted a second resignation at the bank.

In the rest of central Europe, currencies and bonds have gained as investors favour their higher yields compared with negative yields in some safer western European states.

Demand pushed Polish five-year bond yields to record lows, boosting the zloty to a one-year peak for a second session. It

tested the key 4.0 level, up 0.5 percent since Friday. Yields were up a notch on 5- and 10-year paper.

"The market is bullish mainly thanks to the demand for Polish bonds," said a Warsaw-based trader.

The Hungarian forint gained 0.3 percent while the Czech crown reversed early losses. Stock markets rose for a second day, led by Prague's 1.6 percent rise.

Hungarian three-year bond yields fell below 7 percent for the first time since July 20, down 5 basis points.

Hungarian assets have rallied since last month, when Budapest got talks with the IMF over a credit deal underway. Analysts expect a financing backstop will help ease borrowing costs for central Europe's most indebted country.

The region relies heavily on the euro zone, which is in its third year of crisis, for trade and banking. Data on Monday showed Czech output declined for a second straight month in June, but foreign trade showed a large surplus.

"Foreign trade data may be viewed as good news for the Czech crown but development of industrial orders should sour the sentiment," said Radomir Jac, chief analyst for Generali PPF Asset Management.

title: UPDATE 1-Romania president accuses government of power grab
text:
* Government trying to suspend, impeach president

* President says govt seeks control of judiciary

* Political row pressures currency, debt costs

* Thousands rally in central Bucharest

(Adds rallies, quotes, currency)

By Sam Cage and Luiza Ilie

BUCHAREST, July 5 (Reuters) - Romania's president accused the government on Thursday of using an attempt to impeach him as a way of grabbing control of the judiciary and other state institutions.

The leftist Social-Liberal Union (USL) government is set to use its parliamentary majority to vote on Friday to suspend right-winger Traian Basescu. A referendum would then be held on his impeachment within a month.

The impeachment threat is part of a wider political clash that has paralysed lawmaking and raised doubts over Romania's ability to keep to a 5 billion euro International Monetary Fund-led aid deal - hurting the currency and increasing debt costs.

Basescu told parliament: "The major objective of this suspension is to put the justice system and state institutions under the control of parties in the USL."

Some 2,000 supporters of the opposition Democrat-Liberals (PDL) backing Basescu gathered in downtown Bucharest, shouting anti-government slogans. In another square, people backing Prime Minister Victor Ponta shouted: "Out with Basescu."

In power since May, after the previous, centre-right government collapsed, the USL, led by Ponta, Romania's third prime minister in four months, is favourite to win an election late this year.

Opponents accuse him of trying to cling to power, but many people are tired of an austerity drive enforced by a centre-right government in 2010.

"We are witnessing a systematic attack on state institutions 


... now they attack presidency and the final target is to
subordinate justice," newly elected PDL leader Vasile   Blaga
told the gathering.     


The USL passed a law to make it easier to impeach Basescu, whose position is ceremonial but who influenced the previous government's austerity policies. In the impeachment request, USL lawmakers said the president broke the constitution and pressured judges.

The new law, still pending judgment in the constitutional court, would make it possible for a simple majority of voters to impeach a president in a referendum, rather than requiring a majority of the entire electorate.

In late afternoon, the government approved a decree setting a simple voting majority for referendums. It is not clear whether the decree or the court verdict, likely due on Monday, will prevail.

Both reverse previous legislation by the PDL, which has close links to the president and is now in opposition. The PDL had switched the referendum rule to a majority of the electorate after a previous attempt to unseat Basescu in 2007.

Basescu would probably lose the referendum and his post if the new legislation is enforced, but easily survive if the old threshold is kept.

POWER GRAB

Ponta did not attend the parliamentary debate on Thursday, seeking instead to reassure investors.

"I am not in parliament for a political debate but I am here with you because I feel that in this type of political battle it is essential to maintain economic balance," Ponta told a meeting of investors, according to news agency Agerpres.

The USL has come under severe pressure itself. Ponta faces calls to resign over plagiarism charges and the government had to back down from an attempt to replace judges on the constitutional court, after international criticism.

The president of the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, issued a statement expressing "deep concern (at) various attempts to exercise pressure on the Constitutional Court of Romania and to undermine its independence".

The leu struck a new record low on Thursday beyond 4.492 per euro, while yields rose at a two-year Romanian bond sale, reflecting rising investor concern.

Dealers said the central bank might have intervened to support the currency.

"Romania looks now rather like Ukraine or Belarus than a CEE state. It looks everyone wants to get out and the central bank seems to be present on the offer side as it wants to prevent sharp swings," a dealer at a foreign bank in Bucharest said.

title: CEE MARKETS 3- FX  up, but euro worries keep pressure
text:
* Big order lifts crown, weakening seen again

* Greece, Spanish banks keep investors cautious

* Forint nears big 300 level, leu back on path to low

By Sam Cage and Jana Mlcochova

BUCHAREST/PRAGUE, May 18 (Reuters) - Central European emerging currencies recovered from lows on Friday, mirroring the euro's brief recovery, with one Budapest trader saying panic had subsided over the prospects of Greece being forced to leave the euro.

The Czech crown, which fell to a fourth-month low this week, recovered the most ground in what one dealer attributed to euro "sell" orders from two big London names. By 1358 GMT the crown

was bid up 0.6 percent up at 25.3 to the euro.

A Prague-based dealer, however, predicted fresh pressure on the crown. "We could see (EUR/CZK at) 26 again - not today, but in a short time," a Prague-based dealer said.

Czech bonds were steady, supported by expectations of a rate cut as soon as next month after the economy slid deeper in recession in the first quarter.

Hungarian bond yields retreated by about 5 basis points from early levels along the curve with Budapest stocks bouncing back to lead regional market gains with 1.4 percent.

Warsaw and Prague were 0.7 and 0.1 percent up respectively while Romania's fell 1.1 percent.

"Panic over Greece has subsided, expectations are shifting into a more positive direction and Greece may not leave the euro zone," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said.

But the trader added that Greece - which holds fresh elections on June 17 - and the euro zone would remain the dominant market-moving factor next week.

Hungary's forint and the Polish zloty have each shed more than 4 percent since a May 6 election left Greek politics in disarray and raised questions about its future in the euro zone, central Europe's most important banking and trading partner.

Hungary's forint was off morning lows, and traded flat on the day, close to the 300 per euro level which it has tested several times since January but failed to break.

It briefly hit 299.7 per euro earlier in the session.

"The level of 300 to the euro provides psychological support, the question is whether it will be able to stop further weakening of the forint, especially if the euro/dollar moves lower again," a Budapest based dealer said.

Hungary hopes to start aid talks with the International Monetary Fund in June on a loan from the Fund and EU to help avert a potential funding crisis. The country's borrowing costs remain high after years of controversial government policies, including the crisis taxes, which have made investors wary.

With the existing windfall tax on telecoms firms already under challenge in European courts, parliament approved on Friday a new charge on phone calls, effective from July 1, to help plug a budget gap in central Europe's most indebted state.

Elsewhere, the Polish zloty rose 0.5 percent to 4.333. It has found some relief from expectations the central bank could intervene.

Romania's leu was flat on the day at 4.44 per euro, close to an all time low hit earlier this week.

"Local politics doesn't help - it feels like 2008 reloaded. The whole world falls apart and Romanian politicians are promising higher wages and pensions," said a Bucharest dealer.

In Serbia, the dinar continued to slide a day after the central bank sold 50 million euros to stem declines, with investors cautious before a presidential runoff on May 20.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development said on Friday lacklustre growth in emerging European economies could turn into recession if the euro zone crisis escalates.

"The risk that emerging Europe as a whole will re-enter recession within the next 12 months is viewed as high," the EBRD said in a statement accompanying the growth forecasts.

"The collapse of the [Romanian] government was very unexpected. Many banks were short EUR/RON," he says. "If we don't get a new government in the next two weeks, the central bank may allow RON to depreciate to 4.4 against the euro, but it could well reach that level on its own as some London banks heavily sell the leu," he adds. title: PREVIEW-Romania c.bank to cut rates for 4th month
text:
* Bank meets Thursday, March 29, no specific time set

 * Expected to cut rates by 25 bps to 5.25 pct

 * For full poll see or  

 By Ioana Patran

 BUCHAREST, March 23 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank will likely cut interest rates for the fourth month running next week and once more before the middle of the year, but caution over the impact of global fuel prices and a parliamentary election may make it pause thereafter.

 Official borrowing costs in the European Union's second poorest member state are already at an all-time low of 5.5 percent as the bank seeks to reboot an economy still only recovering slowly from a collapse in 2009 that forced it to seek IMF support. 

 All but one of 16 analysts polled by Reuters said the bank would cut rates by another quarter-point at its March meeting and 12 said it would cut again before the end of the second quarter.

 Those moves are justified by an expected fall in inflation to another record low this month, after reaching 2.6 percent in February, leaving "real" interest rates still relatively high.

 "The economy needs stimulus for growth and of course lower interest rates help financing the public deficit, reducing the cost of public debt," said Georgiana Constantinescu, analyst at Credit Europe Bank in Bucharest.

 A cold snap earlier this year when temperatures plunged below minus 20 degrees Celsius and snow storms blocked roads, railways and ports has hurt output and could push the economy into negative territory in the first quarter.

 Romanian exporters are facing falling demand from the euro zone, its main trade partner, and the economy is facing a second consecutive quarterly contraction that would put it briefly back into recession. 

 The government expects growth of 1.5-2 percent for the whole of 2012, down from a 2.5 percent expansion last year. 

 All but four of the sixteen analysts polled by Reuters expect the central bank to deliver another quarter point cut after the March 29 meeting, bringing borrowing costs to 5 percent by the end of the second quarter 

 However, some said the central bank could stop its easing cycle after its March meeting, as inflationary risks stemming from fuel prices, a weak leu currency and an upcoming parliamentary election were tilted to the upside.

 "We are mulling a revision of our reference rate forecast as global oil prices are amplified by a weak leu and electoral pressures loom throughout the next eight months," said Mihai Patrulescu, economist at Bancpost in Bucharest.

 "At the next week's meeting we could see the last cut this year."

 Romania's leu hit a 21-month low last week against the euro and traders said the central bank has intervened indirectly to curb its move.

 The leu, emerging Europe's most stable currency in 2011, has failed to benefit from a sharp rebound in riskier assets so far this year as investor interest was limited mainly by the threat of potential central bank intervention to stem volatility.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Leu flirts with 21-month low, Fitch warns Hungary
text:
* Leu close to 21-month low after rate cuts

* Dealers say Romanian cbank supporting currency

* Fitch says could cut Hungary if no IMF deal

(Updates with Fitch report, new prices)

By Sam Cage and Michael Winfrey

BUCHAREST/PRAGUE, March 16 (Reuters) - Emerging European currencies inched lower on Friday, with Romania's leu hovering near a 21-month low and the forint under the microscope after rating agency Fitch said Hungary could face another credit downgrade.

Currency investors were on alert for further central bank intervention in both Romania and Serbia, where the dinar

has fallen due to uncertainty over the outcome of parliamentary elections scheduled for May.

The leu was the emerging European Union's most stable currency as the euro zone debt crisis raged in 2011, but it has failed to benefit from a sharp rebound in riskier assets this year on a brightening global economic outlook.

Poland's zloty and the Hungarian forint have led the region's currency gains this year, each rising more than 8 percent, with the Czech crown following.

The leu, however is down 1.25 percent in that time. It was virtually flat on the session at 4.38 per euro at 1351 GMT, less than 1 percent off an all-time low of 4.4023 hit during Romania's own funding crisis in 2010, when the government austerity measures forced the economy into a deep recession.

"It looks exciting, finally, for the EURRON. Volumes yesterday and today were at least four times larger than the average of the previous 2-3 weeks," said a Bucharest dealer.

The central bank has cut interest rates to a record low 5.5 percent and bond yields have fallen across the curve, to 6.29 percent on five-year paper. The bank also intervened via third parties to prop up the leu at 4.39 per euro on Thursday and was also active on Friday, dealers said.

"Behind this weakening move could be slightly looser control of the central bank and it could be a signal that the RON is likely to trade in a wider range - probably one between 4.32-4.42/EUR," said ING analyst Vlad Muscalu.

FITCH ON HUNGARY

Hungarian markets, the most volatile in the region in 2012 as the government struggles to secure a new credit line from the European Union and IMF, were closed and the forint was down around 0.1 percent on the day in offshore trade.

The country has come under fire due to a string of policy decisions from Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government that critics say have flouted budget rules and could undermine democracy.

EU finance ministers moved to freeze almost half a billion euros in development funds this week unless Budapest could present it with a credible fiscal plan by June.

That drew an angry retort from Orban, who told tens of thousands of supporters at rally on Thursday they would not be treated as second-class European citizens.

Fitch said it expected Orban to bow to EU pressure to set out a credible fiscal reduction plan this spring so it could start aid talks and unfreeze the development funds.

But even if it does, doubts will remain about whether Budapest can submit to the IMF's strict conditionality, Fitch said, adding failure to secure the loan could prompt a downgrade to Hungary's credit rating, which is already in 'junk' territory.

The Czech crown was down 0.1 percent at 24.522 per euro, and the Polish zloty was 0.3 percent weaker at 4.135.

Poland's central bank also supported its currency last year as the problems in the euro zone - emerging Europe's main trade and banking partner - hurt the zloty, and Governor Marek Belka said he believed it had reduced volatility by intervening.

"The biggest concern is the euro zone," Belka said during an economic forum in Prague, adding that Poland's relatively high level of foreign currency loans continued to be a cause for worry.

Dealers say Serbia's central bank has also intervened to support the dinar this week. The outcome of May's election could have a major impact on the Balkan country's EU candidacy and talks over a backstop loan from the International Monetary Fund.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Forint leads gains in  FX , Romanian leu falls
text:
(Updates prices, adds Romania)

* Romanian leu down 0.3 pct vs. euro, hits 20-mth low

* Polish yields rise for 2nd day, zloty off lows

* Crown firm, forint up as local markets closed

By Jason Hovet and Marcin Goettig

PRAGUE/WARSAW, March 15 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint led gains in central European currencies on Thursday as they rebounded thanks to a stronger euro, getting a break from a bout of profit taking this week that has halted a rally since the start of the year.

The Romanian leu bucked the trend, however, falling to a 20-month low versus the euro as a looming economic slowdown and interest rate cuts are making the currency less attractive.

Central European stocks were mixed, while Polish bond yields rose 4 basis points, up for a second day after higher-than-expected inflation data this week dampened expectations that the central bank would cut interest rates later this year.

By 1459 GMT, the forint had gained 0.6 percent to 290.83 to the euro, while the Polish zloty, the region's most liquid currency, was up 0.4 percent.

"In the mid-term the zloty may appreciate somewhat, but I would not expect strong gains as we are in the phase of slowing economic activity and elections in Greece are around the corner," said Dorota Strauch, an FX analyst at Raiffeisen Bank Polska. Greek election could revive worries about Greek debt and tame global risk appetite.

In Hungary, local markets were closed for a national holiday with rallies expected to be held both for and against Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government, which is struggling to get a credit line from the European Union and International Monetary Fund to ease borrowing strains.

Unease over Budapest's attempts to counter EU and IMF criticism of its central bank legislation - which is holding up aid talks - has prompted many investors to be more cautious on eastern Europe, where exports are being hit by the debt crisis in its key export market, the euro zone.

Elsewhere, the Czech crown added 0.5 percent to 24.521 to the common currency.

The crown is playing catch-up with the forint and the zloty's more than 8 percent gains this year, but dealers say it would be difficult to break firmer than its five-month high of 24.500.

"There is still nice (euro) support around 24.500/550, and I see quite good demand to buy (euro) below 24.600," Komercni Banka dealer Lubos Kolarik said.

"There are also nice offers above 24.630/640, so there has been some nice volume in this range that is two-way at the moment. People rather tend to buy dips than sell rallies."

Czech bond yields rose on the long end. Rates are also up, tracking euro markets but also getting a lift from comments from central banker Kamil Janacek on Wednesday saying the record-low base rate could rise this year.

LEU FALLS

The Romanian leu fell 0.3 percent to the euro, hitting a multi-month low of 4.388 to the euro.

"I think we are seeing a combination of deleveraging flow with people closing out short EUR/RON bets," said Peter Attard Montalto, an economist at Nomura International.

"People saw a divergence between Romania CDS and EURRON and thought RON should rally but it didn't, so now closing out and hitting stops," he also said, adding he expected central bank intervention to support the currency next week.

The leu has been the most stable emerging European currency over the past two years - as the euro zone debt crisis has made currencies in the region volatile - partly due to the threat of intervention by Romania's central bank.

Despite the weakening currency, Romania sold 1.03 billion lei ($307 million) in five-year treasury bonds on Thursday, double the planned amount. The average yields fell 46 basis points from last month's tender, following the central bank's interest rate cuts.

The bank cut interest rates to a record low of 5.5 percent in February, further beefing up its support for a fragile economy that may suffer its second consecutive quarterly contraction in the first quarter of 2012.

In Serbia, the central bank intervened in the currency market for the third consecutive day on Thursday to halt a weakening of the dinar against the euro, dealers and traders said.

Investor concerns are rising over who will win elections in Serbia in May. Whoever takes power could have a profound impact on policies ranging from Serbia's candidacy for the European Union to its negotiations over a 1 billion euro ($1.3 billion) backstop loan from the International Monetary Fund. title: UPDATE 2-Cold snap undermines Romania's slow recovery
text:
* FinMin says q/q contraction possible in Q1

* Would be technical recession after Q4 contraction

* Maintains full year forecast 1.5-2 pct growth

* Govt mulls easing austerity before Nov election

(Adds analyst comment, details)

By Luiza Ilie

BUCHAREST, March 9 (Reuters) - Romania's economy may suffer its second consecutive quarterly contraction in the first quarter of 2012, dragged into recession by freezing temperatures and heavy snow which hit output, Finance Minister Bogdan Dragoi said on Friday.

The economy shrank by more than 7 percent in 2009, when Romania was forced to seek a 20 billion euro ($26.5 billion) International Monetary Fund bailout and enforce austerity measures to maintain investor confidence.

Its recovery has been slow, with last year's 2.5 percent expansion doing little to make up the lost ground. The effects of the euro zone debt crisis mean the government expects growth of 1.5-2 percent for the whole of 2012.

Temperatures plunged below minus 20 degrees Celsius in January and February and snow storms blocked roads, railways and ports and even buried many houses in southern Romania, while the army had to rescue stranded travellers.

"It is possible we will see technical recession in the first quarter. But the bad weather has not hurt productivity and output, it only blocked the transfer of goods," Dragoi said.

"In the first quarter we see ... a marginal (GDP) drop compared with the fourth quarter."

There was also a quarterly contraction in the last three months of 2011. The ministry still expects the economy to grow between 1.5 and 2 percent on an annual basis in the first quarter.

The news had little impact on the leu, which has been the emerging European Union's most stable currency as the euro zone debt crisis has raged, partly due to the threat of central bank intervention.

LOOMING ELECTION

Romania has completed its IMF bailout and has a new deal in place worth 5 billion euros, to be tapped only if needed.

With a parliamentary election due in November, Romania's government - struggling at less than 20 percent support in opinion polls - is examining ways to ease austerity, which included cutting public employees' wages by a quarter and raising sales tax by five percentage points to 24 percent.

On Tuesday, Romanian President Traian Basescu said the newly appointed government should consider ways to restore public sector pay to pre-austerity levels by June, a move Dragoi said would add 2 billion lei ($609 million) for the 2012 budget.

Cutting social security contributions by five percentage points, another possibility to improve living standards in a country where some villages and even city districts have no running water or sewerage, would have a budgetary impact of about 2.3 billion lei, Dragoi added.

He said the government will stick to its deficit target of 1.9 percent of gross domestic product for this year.

The two measures together would amount to some 0.7 percent of GDP. The IMF has said there is not enough money to increase salaries and pensions, for now at least, but has previously given Romania some leeway because of its generally strong commitment, after cutting the budget gap to 4.4 percent of GDP last year from 6.5 in 2010.

"The markets may penalise the government if they decide to raise wages or pensions or cut social security contributions," said Ionut Dumitru, chief economist at Raiffeisen Bank Romania.

"Taking such measures at a time when the economy is performing worse than expected may be seen as a slippage. They need to be very careful about what they decide." ($1 = 3.2823 Romanian lei) ($1 = 0.7534 euros)

BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--Romanian foreign-exchange reserves fell to EUR31.74 billion in November from EUR32.2 billion a month earlier, central bank data showed Friday, in the wake of central bank intervention to support the leu.

Market participants attributed the decline in reserves to repeated interventions by the central bank in an effort to prevent the leu from weakening too much against the euro. They estimate the central bank sold over EUR200 billion in the first half of November to prop up the national currency.

Foreign-exchange inflows rose to EUR1.1 billion in November, from EUR383 million in October. Total outflows reached EUR1.55 billion, down from EUR1.8 billion the previous month.

The central bank's gold holdings were steady at 103.7 metric tons, but their value adjusted for international gold prices increased to EUR4.27 billion, from EUR4.1 billion in October.

Romania's overall international reserves totaled EUR36.02 billion in November, down from EUR36.3 billion a month earlier.

The payments due on public and publicly guaranteed external debt in December amounted to EUR108.3 million, the data showed.

title: Emerging Europe Central Banks Vulnerable To Mounting Attacks
text:
--Emerging European currencies fall victim to euro-zone debt crisis concerns

--Central banks in this region seen with less firepower than other emerging markets to fight currency weakness

--Currency market interventions, however, may continue as these currencies underperform

By Erin McCarthy


   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Having spent much of the past two years trying to weaken their currencies, emerging-market central banks are now trying to do the opposite, for which they are increasingly tapping the foreign currency reserves they accumulated through those previous actions.

Some of them, especially those in Eastern and Central Europe, may find that the war chests they built up aren't deep enough to fight off an intensifying attack by speculators as fears of another global crisis grow.

Poland and Romania's central banks have been seen intervening in the foreign exchange market to prop up their currencies recently, while Turkey's central bank holds daily foreign exchange-selling auctions to help its currency. Despite these efforts, the attacks on their currencies keep growing.

The selloff is global, with nervous investors shifting en masse into dollars and safe havens such as the yen. But the problems that poses aren't felt universally.

Latin American countries such as Brazil and Chile and Asian nations such as South Korea and Taiwan all went on aggressive dollar-buying campaigns when the dollar was in constant decline against their currencies. That has left them in better shape now to address the problem of an ascending dollar, less vulnerable to speculators' attacks, and thus less of a natural target. Even Mexico, which has largely kept out of markets, has about $76 billion of reserves combined with a $72 billion flexible credit line arrangement with the International Monetary Fund.

But emerging European currencies are under much more pressure, mostly because of their ongoing exposure to the euro zone debt crisis, which crimped their capacity to amass the reserves needed to arrest the mounting attacks on their currencies.

In any intervention, these countries' central banks will have to pit themselves against global investors who likely won't find their reserve levels or other policy tools all that impressive. This will especially be a problem for economies whose reserve levels are marred by large economic imbalances, like Turkey's massive current account deficit and Hungary's high levels of foreign currency debt.

"There aren't too many economies out there that we should be able to expect good things from a currency intervention," said Michael Lee, senior portfolio manager of the Wells Fargo Advantage International Bond Fund.

Hungary holds about $53 billion in reserves, tiny compared to Brazil's $352.9 billion. That weakness, combined with high levels of foreign currency debt--which means a weak forint puts households and banks holding such debt under pressure--has seen investors running for the door from the forint.

With such meager reserves, the Hungarian forint's only defense may be a substantial one-time rate increase, which could hamper already bleak growth. And if it cannot get financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund, as it requested earlier this month, the forint could head for another freefall.

Turkey is in a similar boat. After holding foreign-exchange selling auctions and directly intervening in the market in October, its central bank ultimately tightened monetary policy with a back-door rate hike, whose effect has since seemingly waned. With about $95 billion in reserves, Turkey must still tread very cautiously, since reserve depletion can unnerve foreign creditors, whose financing helps fund its massive current account deficit.

And even Poland, which has better economic fundamentals and sturdier reserve levels at about $110 billion, is struggling to fight the market. Its bank stepped into the market Wednesday to fight off speculative flows hurting the zloty, bringing the euro down as low as PLN4.4423. But the intense selloff across risk assets ultimately erased the effect of the intervention within hours, leading some to bill it as a failure.

Still, some market watchers say emerging Europe's central banks could catch a break, since dangerously illiquid markets and high trading costs may keep speculators out of the market altogether. Instead, investors may chase currencies whose central banks are standing back. These include the South Africa rand, which has dropped nearly 22% against the dollar since September.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com [ 23-11-11 2117GMT ]

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Forint up after CPI but euro zone crisis weighs
text:
(Updates price movements)

* Bonds show no reaction to higher CPI data

* Crown off multi-month low, zloty weak in holiday trade

* GDP data next week expected to show impact of euro crisis

By Jason Hovet and Sam Cage

PRAGUE/BUCHAREST, Nov 11 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint firmed on Friday after higher-than-expected inflation data, but the widening euro zone debt crisis continued to weigh on other emerging European currencies.

The forint and the crown have struggled in the past week as the euro zone crisis spiralled into a new, more dangerous phase with attention now turned to Italy's debt mountain.

Gross domestic product data, due across the region next week, will indicate how much the euro zone's problems are slowing growth in emerging Europe, whose economies are dominated by exports to their western neighbours.

Higher inflation in Hungary fuelled the case for the bank to raise interest rates, a dealer said, helping the forint

rise 0.6 percent to 310.75 to the euro. But the currency stayed within sight of its all-time low of 317.45 hit in March 2009, a level it has been approaching this week.

The government has said it will wait for Germany to officially change its economic outlook before revising its own growth projection of 1.5 pct for 2012, which most analysts say is too optimistic.

"Of course the market will be interested in the GDP figure, if it is too bad relative to the consensus, people will ask why the government waits to change its forecast," a foreign exchange dealer said.

Hungarian inflation ticked up to 3.9 percent in October, higher than analysts expected. With the forint inching towards a new low, analysts have said emergency rate hikes, like the 300 basis point rise implemented at the start of the 2008 financial crisis, cannot be ruled out.

"We see a clear risk of an emergency hike to stem HUF weakening. In our baseline scenario, however, we have unchanged rates until a rate cut in H2 2012," said Bjarke Roed-Frederiksen of Nordea Markets.

Debt markets, however, showed little reaction to the inflation data, with Hungarian yields falling by up to 11 basis points from highs hit on Thursday.

"Sentiment is slightly better although there is a lot of news knocking about," a bond trader said. "Nobody cares about inflation right now, because growth is so subdued and fears over growth are so strong that there are no real concerns about inflation."

By 1400 GMT, the zloty was down 0.5 percent at 4.424 to the euro with local markets closed for a national holiday. The central bank intervened to support the zloty in September and October.

Dealers have also suspected Romania's central bank of intervening at times. The leu was up 0.1 percent at 4.347 per euro.

CZECH RATES

The crown was down 0.3 percent at 25.7 per euro and set for its biggest weekly loss in two years after outperforming this year the forint and the Polish zloty, which have both shed more than 10 percent since Jan. 1.

Unlike Poland or Hungary, the Czechs are facing little inflationary pressure, leaving space for rate cuts in the face of a weaker economic outlook as trade with the euro zone slows.

The Czech currency was near its lowest level since June 2010 after losing 2.5 percent in the past week. Prior to this week's weakening, the crown, seen as the region's safe haven currency, was the only currency in central Europe still trading above its level at the start of the year.

Dealers say London hedge funds have been behind the crown's weakening this week. In the past two weeks, the Finance Ministry, central bank and European Commission have sharply cut their Czech growth outlook for next year to 0.7-1.2 percent.

Czech central bank vice-governor Vladimir Tomsik was the lone voter in favour of a 25 basis point interest rate reduction at the board's Nov. 3 meeting. The board left the bank's base rate unchanged at a record low 0.75 percent, minutes showed.

At the meeting, the bank's governing board agreed that risks and uncertainties to the outlook were extremely high, mainly due to the euro zone debt crisis.

"This morning's minutes from the MPC's Nov. 3 rate meeting kept to a dovish tone, but ultimately said all policy options were on the table until further developments are seen in the euro area, which could offer the unit a bit of support," 4Cast said in a note.

"Overall, in this uncertain environment, relief is only seen to be temporary and EUR/CZK downside is seen to be limited."

title: CEE MARKETS 3- FX  down ahead of key euro summit
text:
(Adds fresh bond prices)

* Eyes on EU summit as debt crisis weighs on CEE

* Currencies soften after recent selling pressure

By Jason Hovet and Radu Marinas

PRAGUE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - European emerging

currencies edged down against the euro on Wednesday and the forint fell to its lowest level since April 2009 with investors cautious

ahead of a crucial EU summit tasked with endorsing a plan to tackle the euro zone's debt crisis .

The incoming head of the European Central Bank threw the euro zone a lifeline hours before the summit on Wednesday by signalling the bank would go on buying troubled states' bonds to combat market turmoil.

Mario Draghi delivered the message that financial markets have been waiting for about the ECB's intentions as leaders of the 17-nation single currency area struggled to produce a comprehensive plan to resolve the bloc's sovereign debt woes.

[ID: nLDE79O03J ]

" In the next days and weeks we will watch whether European leaders have some concrete message to markets ," a Budapest-based trader said.

The forint fell 1.2 percent from its opening level to 302 against the euro by 1433 GMT , pressured by falls in the single European currency and fears over a potential ratings downgrade.

By 1448 GMT, the forint eased further, to 302.60 per euro according to Reuters data.

"The latest news about the euro zone bailout package were not good," a currency dealer in Budapest said.

Hungarian bonds eased after comment s from Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy about the risk of a downgrade of sovereign debt rating by one agency . [ID:nL5E7LQ394 ]

P olicymakers in central Europe foresee slowing economies and lower state revenues next year due partly to the euro zone's debt troubles. This has put a drag on currencies that, apart from of the Czech crown, have lost ground in 2011.

Hungary's Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy said on Wednesday the economy needs a boost if it is to reach a goal of 1.5 percent growth in 2012.

His comments echoed the tone of Czech Finance Minister Miroslav Kalousek, who said on Tuesday the government may have to come up with more savings measures next year to keep to its budget deficit goals.

The Czech crown fell 0.6 percent to 24. 05 per

euro.

Hungary's central bank, caught in a policy bind of rising risk premiums and a weak forint, held its key rate at 6 percent on Tuesday. Markets see chances of a hike ahead even with the slowing economy.

"I'm not convinced they can do without a rate hike for much longer, be it an emergency hike or a slow trickle of hikes," a Budapest dealer said.

PROSPECTS DIM

The forint has led a retreat in the region's currencies since Sept. 1, falling more than 8 percent as Europe's policymakers struggle to reach agreement on the best way to contain a sovereign debt crisis that began two years ago in Greece.

"It is clear that the market is no longer expecting the comprehensive solution that was preannounced a few weeks ago," KBC said.

"So, it is not excluded that the wait-and-see mode might continue as there won't be enough 'hard stuff' to react to."

Poland's zloty traded 0.5 percent down at 4.36 on the day. Romania's leu

edged down 0. 4 percent.

A Bucharest dealer said risk of leu intervention held the currency in place after central banks in Romania and Poland stepped in over the past month to rescue currencies from lows.

"The market is calm due to the central bank interventions the other days and if there is no client to take the lead," a Bucharest dealer said.

Romanian budget data on Tuesday showed the state can easily meet its IMF-agreed target of a deficit of 4.4 percent this year, but prospects for next year are less certain.

"This should not be a major worry, yet, although a weaker growth outlook increases the risk for fiscal slippage next year," BNP Paribas said in a note.

Central European stock markets were mixed, hovering

around Tuesday's levels , while the Czech bourse

was up 0.4 percent.

title: INSTANT VIEW 3-Romania annual inflation slows to 3.5 pct in Sept
text:
BUCHAREST, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Romania's inflation fell sharply to 3.5 percent in September from August's 4.3 percent, beating market expectations and entering the central bank's target band, indicating it may have room to start cutting interest rates.

Analysts say slowing inflation, helped by steep falls in food prices, coupled with lower global growth forecasts may mean rates could be cut from the current 6.25 percent, although risks for inflation remained strong in the medium term.

The central bank, which targets inflation at 2-4 percent this year and next, has kept rates flat at a record low since May 2010, but still the highest among emerging EU states.

Consumer prices were down 0.2 percent on the month with food prices falling some 1.2 percent. Non-food prices rose 0.2 percent while services were up 0.6 percent, the National Statistics Board said on Tuesday.

MARKET REACTION

The Romanian leu was a touch weaker against the euro, trading at 4.323 at 0730 GMT, compared with levels around 3.3190 seen before the data release.

MARKET FORECAST

A median forecast of 14 analysts polled by Reuters earlier this month showed Romanian inflation at 3.9 percent year-on-year in September. Monthly forecast was 0.2 percent.

KEY FIGURES
