 CPI (pct change)             SEPTEMBER       AUGUST
 yr/yr                        3.5               4.3
 mth/mth                     -0.2              -0.4
 ============================================================


ANALYST COMMENTS:

DEALER WITH FOREIGN BANK IN BUCHAREST

"The leu is a touch weaker because, at least in theory, a sharp drop in inflation leads to expectations of rate cuts."

"But in practice, I think the market would like a 4.4 level to the euro gradually. And so the leu weakens slightly without central bank intervention."

"I say without intervention because Romania's economic recovery is export driven."

NICOLAIE ALEXANDRU-CHIDESCIUC, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT ING IN BUCHAREST

"It is good news but a closer look at the details shows the drop stems from volatile elements."

"Inflation will continue to fall in the coming months and it is possible to see rates lower than 2 percent in March-April 2012."

"But this disinflationary trend is not sustainable and it would likely be easily reversed even if next year records a normal harvest, not a poor one."

"We will see inflation rise in June-July."

"What's debatable is how high inflation can go. For instance, for the end of 2012, we have a forecast close to 4 percent."

"Even before the data release we were expecting an interest rate cut from the central bank in February 2012."

"For now this pronounced drop in inflation is purely temporary. It couldn't be seen as a trend that will consolidate in the medium term. There are still significant risks to inflation."

"In theory, a drop so pronounced in inflation would lead to lower longer-dated money market rates. It is also possible that the central bank may be a little more relaxed about a weaker leu currency, given the slowdown in exports, but nothing excessive."

CATALINA MOLNAR, SENIOR ECONOMIST, RBS ROMANIA

"Inflation falling to 3.5 percent is below our expectations as the favourable effect from a drop in vegetables and fruits prices was stronger than we anticipated."

"The effect of a good crop was expected to have an impact in the autumn months, but not at this magnitude. Considering this, our end of the year inflation forecast is now down to 3.5 percent and considering it includes an aggressive scenario of hikes in heating prices, we might even see lower a year-end inflation."

"We must be aware that the favorable impact from the food sector on inflation from this year could come back as a boomerang next year as inflation could rise again to above 4 percent in the summer and autumn period due to an unfavorable base effect."

"Considering all these, the maneuvering room the central bank has to cut rates is rising and we might even see a rate cut to 6 percent at the last central bank meeting from this year."

"Next year, considering a medium inflation forecast of 3.5 percent and a persistent negative output gap, the central bank could continue cutting rates to 5.5 percent."

DAN BUCSA, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT UNICREDIT TIRIAC BANK

"Inflation surprised to the downside for the fourth month in a row. Volatile prices fell further on very good crops. It is surprising that sharp RON depreciation during September had very limited effects on inflation."

"The new inflation reading means that the inflation target will probably be met (3.7 percent our corrected forecast for end 2011)."

"Annual core 2 inflation fell to 3 percent and core 3 (excluding tobacco and alcohol) went down to 2.7 percent in September, increasing the probability of rate cuts."

"Despite the very good inflation numbers, we don't expect a rate cut in November, unless there is comprehensive action from Euro Zone leaders to quench risk aversion."

"We maintain our call for the first cut in early 2012, with the possibility of a hastier cutting cycle especially if economic growth is weak in the first half of 2012."

title: Eastern Europe Steps Up  Currency -Supporting  Interventions
text:
-- Poland sending strong message to the market as it intervenes for third consecutive trading day

-- Russia's central bank also intervenes

-- Romania's central bank also suspected of intervening to prop up the Leu

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Authorities in Eastern Europe cranked up their efforts to prop up their currencies Monday, as Poland intervened for the third consecutive trading day and Russia also piled in to support the ruble.

Poland's central bank bought its domestic currency against the euro, while the Bank of Russia is suspected of selling at least $400 million, as well as shifting its trading band--which it uses to contain currency volatility--five kopeks weaker, after news that Greece would miss its deficit targets this year triggered another sell-off in emerging market currencies.

Romania's central bank is also suspected of intervening Monday, according to one dealer as central banks in emerging markets step in to stem currency weakness, which can pose inflationary problems, by lifting the cost of imported goods.

Moreover, for those countries burdened with large amounts of foreign currency-denominated debt, currency weakness is particularly harmful as these debts become much more expensive to pay back.

That is especially the case for Poland, whose central bank kept up its fight Monday to defend the zloty, something for which it has more than enough reserves to do, market participants say.

"The National Bank of Poland has enough ammunition with its $100 billion of foreign-exchange reserves to stay in the game for some time and [it] could be successful," said Murat Toprak, a foreign exchange strategist at HSBC in London.

That being said, the job won't be easy.

"It will be very difficult for the Polish authorities to reverse the trend because foreign investors will use the intervention to scale down long positions in Polish bonds," said Bartosz Pawlowski, head of foreign exchange and interest rate strategy for the Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa region for BNP Paribas in London.

Currencies in Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe and Africa have been under heavy selling pressure in recent weeks as a toxic combination of global economy fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries led investors to fold their bets in emerging markets on a colossal scale.

Greece concerns ramped up that pressure Monday forcing central banks in the region into action again. The trading band of the ruble against the central bank's dollar-euro basket now spans 32.55 to 37.55, said Mikhail Anisimov, head of forex at VTB Capital in Moscow. That comes after the Russian central bank spent $2.36 billion defending the ruble, believed to be the biggest one-day dollar sale by the regulator since the financial crisis and oil-price decline that started in 2008.

At 1558 GMT the euro was trading at RON4.315 against the Romanian leu, down around 1% on the day. Against the Polish zloty, the single currency was trading at PLN4.3868, down from session highs hit earlier of PLN4.4401.

-By Clare Connaghan, Dow Jones Newswires; 44 20 7842 94966; clare.connaghan@dowjones.com (Katie Martin in London and William Mauldin in Moscow contributed to this item) [ 03-10-11 1618GMT ]

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Slight return of risk appetite lifts CEE assets
text:
(Adds bonds, updated stocks and FX)

* Forint leads fx firming; CEE stock indices up 3.5-4 pct

* Traders eye possible Romania cbank intervention

* Govt bond yields slump, making curves less steep

* Euro crisis can keep regional markets volatile

By Sam Cage and Sandor Peto

BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The zloty and forint led emerging European currencies higher on Tuesday, benefiting from the return of some appetite for riskier assets and underpinned by the possibility of further central bank intervention to support currencies in the region.

Stock markets tracked a rebound in Asian shares from multi-month lows on hopes euro zone officials will act to corral Greece's debt woes -- though traders and analysts said any relief from recent losses may be temporary.

Hungarian government bond yields declined by 18-38 basis points from multi-month highs, with long-term yields falling more. Poland's bond yield curve also got less steep as long-term yields fell by about 10 basis points.

"I think this is a correction and high volatility will stay," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said. "I don't think that there is a final resolution to the European debt crisis. What we can see is a ray of hope."

The euro zone is central Europe's key trading partner, making the region vulnerable to the currency bloc's debt crisis even though debt levels in central Europe are relatively low.

By 1342 GMT the zloty was 0.8 percent higher at 4.381 per euro, moving further away from the 27-month low of 4.537 that prompted the central bank and the state to intervene on Friday to support the currency.

Hungary's forint gained 1.3 percent to 285.95 against the euro, and one Budapest-based dealer noted some flows which also pushed down the zloty against the forint to support levels at 65.20-30.

The zloty has fallen 9 percent since mid-year and the forint about 7 percent. The region's safe-haven unit, the Czech crown

, shed less than 1 percent and the leu -- defended by the Romanian central bank -- eased 1.5 percent.

On Tuesday the crown gained 0.7 and the leu 0.1 percent.

Romania's central bank was last seen in the market on Sept. 22.

"Central bank vehicles were on the offer towards 4.3100 the other days, but I am not very sure it was an intervention per se," said a Bucharest dealer. "I think they would step in around 4.3200 more aggressively and if not there, 4.3500."

The region's main national equity indices rose by 3.5-4 percent after deep losses in the past weeks.

ZLOTY, FORINT RISKS

In times of risk aversion investors sold the forint and the zloty almost indiscriminately and differentiated between the two units only occasionally.

A rebound of the zloty would cut state debt, reducing the likelihood that the Polish government will need painful fiscal measures to keep the debt below constitutional limits.

"The fall in the debt-to-GDP ratio assumed in the debt strategy is surely positive for bond prices, but one has to keep in mind that elections are key now and it will be the new government that will decide on the budget," said Bartlomiej Wit, the head of fixed income trading at ING Bank Slaski in Warsaw.

Concerns about public finances have been a key factor weakening the zloty. Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski budget plans would stay on track even if growth slows to 3 percent next year and there was no risk of public debt exceeding the key threshold despite the recent weakening of the zloty.

The government on Tuesday approved a budget that envisages economic growth of 4 percent and average annual inflation of 2.8 percent, but final approval by parliament hinges on the outcome of an election set for Oct. 9.

Rostowski said the debt strategy assumed an average zloty rate at 4.35 per euro.

Hungarian assets also face risks as the government has just launched a scheme to allow households to repay foreign currency loans at discount exchange rates, forcing commercial banks to swallow big losses.

"My feeling is that this issue will get more attention when queues line up at banks and people start to think that it will be more than 10-15 percent of borrowers who want to repay debt," the Budapest bond trader said.

title: UPDATE 2-Stronger Romania leu backed by fundamentals-cbank
text:
* C.bank adviser says recent rise supported by economy

* Leu currency hits 10-month high versus euro

* Analysts say comments suggest leu may rise more

(Releads, adds more analyst comment, detail)

By Radu Marinas

BUCHAREST, March 22 (Reuters) - Romania's leu hit a 10-month high against the euro on Tuesday after an adviser to central bank governor Mugur Isarescu said recent gains in the currency reflect increasing economic strength.

"The leu is very much in line with fundamentals," Lucian Croitoru told Reuters by telephone, in a rare comment by the central bank on the currency.

The leu hit 4.1325 against the euro after his comment, its highest since May 4, 2010, and 0.6 percent higher on the day <EURRON=>.

Analysts said it could gain further, helping tame inflation fuelled by surging food and energy prices on global markets.

Regional peers' strong currencies had allowed them to keep interest rates low as their economies recover strongly from the 2008 crisis, although Poland and Hungary have already raised rates and the Czech Republic is expected to follow.

Analysts and dealers say the central bank intervened in February to support the leu on foreign exchange markets, raising doubts about whether 2011's 2.5 percent gain against the euro was supported by signs of economic recovery.

Romania suffered a deep recession but the economy has shown signs of life this year, while the government has completed a 20 billion euro International Monetary Fund-led bailout and agreed a new precautionary deal.

The central bank had been expected to cut interest rates to stimulate growth after holding them at a record low of 6.25 percent since May 2010 but some analysts have recently revised that view as a result of imported inflation.

Analysts said Croitoru's comments suggested there was room for further leu appreciation, particularly with the government looking more secure after surviving a fifth no-confidence vote last week and pushing through IMF-backed reforms.

ING said the currency could firm towards 4.05 per euro. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

"This proves what I've already been saying, that we would witness more appreciation of the leu against the euro," said ING analyst Nicolaie Alexandru-Chidesciuc.

The leu hit a five-month high against the euro, the main reference for regional currencies, in late February after what dealers said was covert intervention by the central bank to try to counter rising prices.

"The (leu) firming has been initially engineered mostly by central bank interventions. Consequently, the leu has benefited from positive reports about Romania," said Alexandru-Chidesciuc.

The central bank raised its end-2011 inflation forecast to 3.6 percent from a previous 3.4 percent last month, but held fire on more support for the country's struggling economy after a jump in prices caused by a rise in value-added tax last year.

"I do believe that in the new context of higher inflation with quite powerful pressures manifested, exchange rate appreciation could temper inflationary expectations," said Ionut Dumitru of Raiffeisen Bank in Bucharest.

Dumitru now sees the leu reaching 4.15 per euro at the end of June, after revising an early March prediction. <RO/POLL1>

"Romania looks better, fundamentals have been improving," Dumitru said. "Probably the central bank now has a higher degree of comfort to rein in inflation."

The IMF board will meet on March 25 to debate Romania's request to rubber stamp the new 5 billion euro aid agreement.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Crown hits 22-mth high;  intervention  helps leu
text:
* Crown breaks resistance past 2010 highs

* Dealers say Romania cbank behind leu outperformance

* Hungary Econ Ministry reiterates budget pledge, bonds rise

(Recasts with crown, updates throughout)

By Marius Zaharia and Jason Hovet

BUCHAREST/PRAGUE, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Czech crown broke resistance levels to a 22-month high on Tuesday and the Romania leu outperformed thanks to likely central bank intervention even as weak stock markets dragged on other currencies.

A poor reading of Germany's ZEW economic sentiment indicator dragged on the region with investors worried the fragile export-driven recovery in emerging Europe may hit the wall, especially if fiscal cuts begin to hamper growth. Hungarian assets were boosted by comment from the Hungarian Economy Ministry cleared some confusion over Hungary's pledge to reduce its budget deficit next year, and whether it hinged on EU accounting changes.

The ministry said on Tuesday the country is committed to cutting its 2011 budget deficit to below 3 percent of gross domestic product regardless of a decision in Brussels on a proposed change in pension accounting rules. [ID:nBUD005497]

Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy was also cited as saying the deficit reduction could be achieved without austerity.

Hungary government bond prices reversed an early decline and yields dropped back near three-week lows.

But the leu led gains in the region, rising 0.7 percent to a September high around 4.23 to the euro. Five dealers said the central bank was behind the move, with two estimating a tiny 100-150 million euros may have been sold. [ID:nLDE68D0W7]

"It moved more than 150 pips, with banks that are the usual intervention instruments selling (euros) at a timing very similar to past interventions, before the fixing," a dealer said.

The reasons for any intervention were unclear, as the leu traded within the 4.2-4.3 per euro range seen as the central bank's "comfort zone". Another dealer suspected the bank may fear second-round effects on inflation from a July VAT hike.

The central bank, which is suspected of constantly intervening in the market against both sharp weakening or firming since late 2008, was not available for comment.

CROWN PATH CLEAR


 The crown -- central Europe's top performer with a 7 percent
gain this year and beating a 4 percent rise for the zloty --


broke 2010 highs around 24.630/620 per euro, which had provided resistance for the past month.

Dealers said the crown has benefitted from increased foreign demand for Czech bonds and treasury bills, which have dropped to historic lows since June on government austerity pledges. This has helped make the crown a safe haven currency in central Europe when risk appetite is low.

The crown added 0.5 percent to 24.516 per euro by 1449 GMT.

"We are starting to move in one direction," a Prague FX dealer said. "(The crown) is also getting good flow from the (debt) papers market."

The Hungarian forint rose 0.6 percent and extended a fifth straight session with gains after pledges to cut the deficit last week. This has helped bonds but dealers said a further drop of yields on secondary markets could be difficult.

"I don't think that yields could fall significantly further," a trader said. "Much stronger (investor) confidence would be needed for that, with the forint firmer than 280 or even near 275."

title: UPDATE 1-Romania Aug inflation quickens, just below fcast
text:
* Heightens cbank dilemma of balancing inflation, recovery

* Most analysts see interest rates unchanged till end 2010

* Leu shows little reaction to data

(Adds more details, currency, comment)

By Sam Cage and Luiza Ilie

BUCHAREST, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Romania's annual inflation quickened in August due to a hike in value added tax, heightening the central bank's problems with controlling prices while trying to give the depressed economy a helping hand.

Prices rose 7.6 percent from a year ago, just below analysts' average forecast but up from 7.1 percent in July, when the VAT increase was first implemented. Inflation was 0.2 percent on the month <ROCPI=ECI>.

Bucharest is struggling to bring its fiscal deficit down to keep a 20 billion euro International Monetary Fund-led bailout deal on track and maintain investor confidence, and it chose to hike VAT by 5 percentage points to 24 percent to boost revenues.

"Given the upward path of inflation we feel that the central bank will leave interest rates unchanged," said Melania Hancila, chief economist at Volksbank in Bucharest.

"Although a deepening of the economic crisis created the premises for monetary policy easing, the central bank is forced to hold fire due to increased risks and high inflation."

A median forecast from analysts polled by Reuters earlier this month put inflation at 7.7 percent on the year. The central bank, which targets inflation at 2.5-4.5 percent in 2010, sees end-year price growth at 7.8 percent. <RO/POLL1>

While the economy nudged out of recession in the second quarter, the government, IMF and analysts all expect gross domestic product to shrink in the second half as the higher VAT and wage cuts hit spending.

Most analysts expect the central bank to keep interest rates unchanged until the end of the year.

The National Statistics Board said costs for food items rose 0.4 percent on the month in August. Non-food costs were flat, while services rose 0.4 percent. Inflation was 0.2 percent on the month.

Romania's leu was little changed after the data and traded at 4.272 per euro by 0822 GMT, 0.1 percent higher on the day <EURRON=>.

The currency is driven mainly by political risk, as the fragile coalition government struggles to defend its austerity measures and grip on power, and large swings are expected to be fought with covert interventions by the central bank.

(Editing by Patrick Graham)

By Marius Zaharia

BUCHAREST, March 10 (Reuters) - The rebound in the EU's emerging currencies may hurt economic recovery this year and policymakers look set to fend off investors by keeping interest rates low and threatening market intervention.

Although the currencies of Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania are still well below pre-crisis highs, weak demand for the region's exports in the euro zone has officials worrying that excessive strength could hurt growth.

Drawn by a solid economic outlook, investors propelled the zloty and the crown to 15-month and four-month peaks this week, while the forint and leu have been helped by their official interest rates of 5.75 and 7 percent.

The zloty surge, a 23 percent gain in 13 months, has prompted two ministers to talk down the currency this month and central bankers there have cast doubt on the timing of rate hikes that would raise the zloty's allure. [ID:nLDE6281MH]

For a graph of currency moves in the region, click on: http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/310/EZ_CEEFX0310.gif ("http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/310/EZ_CEEFX0310.gif")

Romania's central bank governor also signalled last week he was concerned the leu could firm too far, spreading fear among dealers that the bank could intervene between 4 and 4.1 lei per euro, virtually freezing the currency. [ID:nLDE62313Q]

"We are at a stage where they are afraid that their currencies are going too strong," said Gyula Toth, EMEA economist and strategist at UniCredit in Vienna.

"You have a situation when there is a constant inflow of currency into the country, and from this perspective they will have to fight quite heavily (against FX firming.)"

UNDESIRED FIRMING

Analysts think Poland and Czech Republic will hike rates twice in the second half of the year, and markets expect Romania to cut by one percentage point in 2010 and Hungary by 25-75 basis points, depending on developments after an April election.

But according to a Reuters poll <CEEFXPOLL01>, all of the currencies are expected to appreciate this year.

Even turmoil tied to debt-stricken Greece is seen helping, as it has pushed some investors away from troubled euro zone periphery states into more solid-looking economies further east.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Waldemar Pawlak said a zloty level of around 4.0 per euro was desirable, a statement bringing to mind the government's forays into the foreign exchange market last year when it tried to keep the zloty from weakening by converting European Union development funds.

The Czech central bank discussed intervention against crown firming last year and analysts said they could do so again if the unit approached 25 per euro. [ID:nL58899]

"In Romania there was already a hint the central bank might intervene. In the Czech Republic... we saw verbal interventions last year and those might come back, and in Hungary it is already possible to see verbal intervention," said Elisabeth Gruie, FX strategist at BNP Paribas in London.

She believes markets are pricing in excessively high levels for rates and sees no hikes in the region this year, a thought echoed by others.

"Strong currencies in the end will tend to delay rate hikes," said Timothy Ash, an analyst with RBS in London.

INVESTMENT FLOWS

Raising rates would attract more flows into straight FX plays. Otherwise, if investors are not going to get more gains from currencies, they may switch more focus to debt and equities trades.

BNP Paribas sees more flows into regional debt than FX instruments in the short term, and Barclays is especially upbeat on Romanian bonds, as rates have more room to fall there and the country is pursuing budget cuts backed by the International Monetary Fund.

Low currency volatility would also redirect flows to other emerging markets such as Asia or Latin America, which are more tolerant to FX strength.

If growth does stay strong, governments may also have more political room to carry out further fiscal reforms, although elections this year across the region may prove a bigger barrier to any such tightening of public purse strings.

Locking in a competitive advantage against euro zone countries and shoring up growth will also benefit incumbent administrations.

"If you're looking for a soft patch and not a double dip recession, FX strength already starts to become an issue," said BNP Paribas's Gruie. (Editing by Michael Winfrey and Patrick Graham)

title: IMF sees contraction of 4.1 pct in Romania in 2009
text:
WASHINGTON, May 4 (Reuters) - The Romanian economy is likely to shrink some 4.1 percent this year, the International Monetary Fund said on Monday, after approving a $17.1 billion stand-by loan to cushion the impact of global turmoil.

The loan is part of a 20-billion-euro package aimed at helping Romania, a new European Union member of 22 million people, ride out recession and prevent a financing crisis. The Fund also said it "broadly" agreed with the Romanian central bank's policy of smoothing out foreign exchange movements via intervention in the currency market.

"There is some room for intervention, it's not an unlimited room for intervention," Jeffrey Franks, the IMF's mission chief to Romania, said. (Reporting by Justyna Pawlak and Marius Zaharia in Bucharest; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: Romania leu bucks regional weakness, mkt cites cbank
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Romania's leu bucked the regional weakening trend on Friday and dealers said the currency was helped by the Romanian central bank's largest intervention so far this year.

The Hungarian forint <EURHUF=> fell 2.2 percent, the Polish zloty <EURPLN=> dropped 1.8 percent and the Czech crown <EURCZK=> weakened by 1.3 percent, while the leu <EURRON=> firmed 0.6 percent.

"The central bank sold euros through commercial banks to bring the leu from 4.34 to 4.29 per euro," one dealer with a local bank said. "It heavily sold euros between 1200 and 1300 (1000-1100 GMT) and it sold some more at different times throughout the day."

Over the last several months, dealers have suspected the central bank intervened occasionally as economic concerns and uncertainty over fiscal policies following November's parliamentary election weighed on the leu.

Piraeus bank analysts wrote in an afternoon note that Friday's intervention was the most consistent from the start of the year and it was aimed at defending the 4.35 level.

"It sold 300-400 million euros," a dealer with a foreign bank in Bucharest said. The leu has been one of the most battered currencies in eastern Europe this year, hitting successive record lows against the euro last week as investors feared financing risks stemming from Romania's vast budget and current account deficits.

Romania is seen as one of the most risky economies in emerging Europe in the wake of the global financial crisis, and is the only European Union country rated below investment grade by some rating agencies.

At 1255 GMT, the leu <EURRON=> traded at 4.3050 per euro, compared with an intra-day low of 4.3405 per euro and a high of 4.2920. Last week it hit a record low of 4.3530.

The bank has admitted to only a small amount of leu-buying in October as the financial crisis pummelled global markets. (Reporting by Marius Zaharia, Editing by David Stamp)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Russia devalues rouble again, Romania leu down
text:
* Russia allows rouble to weaken for 3rd time in 4 days

* Romania leu falls despite recovery from historic lows

* Ukraine-Russia gas row enters second week

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Russia on Wednesday allowed its rouble currency to weaken yet again as emerging assets struggled to extend gains beyond the Asian session.

Romania's leu slipped after the central bank stepped in to stop the currency's slide to historic lows while a gas dispute between Russia and Ukraine that has squeezed supply to Europe entered its second week with few signs of easing.

Emerging European shares were mostly weak but the benchmark MSCI Emerging Markets Index <.MSCIEF> was up for the first time in six successive sessions, reflecting strong Asian gains, to inch 0.68 percent higher to 554.64 by 1120 GMT.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> were 2 basis points tighter to trade at 668 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

Worries over the global economy continued to dominate sentiment -- Wednesday data showed euro zone industrial production falling for the seventh straight month -- with some emerging market governments to revise 2009 economic targets.

Turkey, which remains in talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for a loan, has cut its 2009 growth target to below 1 percent from 4 percent, according to a newspaper report. [ID:nLE115983]

Hungary's prime minister said the country's economy would shrink much more in 2009 than earlier thought and force the government to redraw its economic plans. [ID:nLE315552]

"There's uncertainty about the world economy, how much of a fiscal stimulus would come from the U.S. with the new president taking office, whether the lowering of interest rates by central banks around the world will succeed in stimulating the world economy," said Nigel Rendell, emerging markets strategist at Royal Bank of Canada.

"People also realise there is going to be less money going into emerging markets this year because major economies will be issuing a lot of bonds."

EMERGING CURRENCIES

Russia, which has been among the biggest casualties of an emerging markets selldown, posted figures showing a record net capital outflow of $129.9 billion last year, a third more than forecast. [ID:nLD448601]

Russia's finance ministry has said that its 2009 budget could be recalculated to take into account the impact of the fall in oil prices. Moscow staged the third mini-devaluation of the rouble in four days, allowing it to fall 1.4 percent against its euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> from the previous session to trade at 36.29.

Analysts say the unit is set to fall further to reflect weakening oil prices and an economic slowdown.

"We expect the central bank to depreciate the currency to at least 38.00 versus the euro-basket," said BNP Paribas in a client note.

The sparring between Russia and its smaller neighbour Ukraine over gas has done little to improve the risk perception of the Russian economy.

Russian gas flow to Europe remains disrupted with Moscow accusing Kiev of deliberately siphoning supply meant for European customers. Russia turned off supplies to Ukraine on Jan. 1 over a contract dispute. [ID:nLD73352]

The cost of insuring Russian sovereign debt rose, with the country's five-year credit default swaps quoted at 680-690 bps, 6 bps higher than previous close.

Most emerging European currencies were weaker, with the Czech crown among the day's biggest losers.

The crown fell some 1.5 percent against the euro <EURCZK=>, hit by Wednesday's figures for November showing the largest fall in the country's industrial output since 2001.

Falling euro zone demand has added weight to calls for swift and bold interest rate cuts in the country. [ID:nLE296066]

"The Czech automobile industry, which is of huge importance for the total economy, is suffering seriously from the global crisis in the automobile sector ... The automobile industry also has huge importance for the Slovak, Polish and Hungarian economies. We therefore also expect very disappointing industrial production numbers for Poland due to be released next week," said Danske Bank in a report.

Central bank intervention on Tuesday helped Romania's leu to recover after it hit a historic low of 4.3530 against the euro on Tuesday but the currency remained weak.

The leu <EURRON=> pared earlier losses against the euro to trade 0.3 percent down against the common currency and is expected to test record lows in the weeks ahead.

"Government funding capacity is deteriorating rapidly," noted BNP Paribas. (Additional reporting by Kylie MacLellan; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: Romania  leu firms vs euro, dealers cite cbank  intervention
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Romania's leu regained some ground against the euro on Tuesday after falling nearly 1 percent to hit an all-time low earlier in the session, with dealers citing covert central bank intervention.

The leu has been the most battered currency in central and eastern Europe so far this year as investors sold it rapidly on the back of concerns about vast budget and current account deficits while the central bank remained sidelined.

They said the bank had been intervening regularly before Christmas to keep the leu below 4.0, but it stopped afterwards.

"It started again," one dealer said. "It intervened through several banks at around 4.35 per euro and it brought it below 4.3 and after that some players stopped losses, which has pushed it at 4.25."

At 1402 GMT, the leu <EURRON=> traded at 4.2542 per euro, compared to an all-time low of 4.3530 hit earlier in the session. The unit was up 1.5 percent on the day.

The central bank declined to comment on the talk of intervention.

"The central bank gives very rarely comments on the intervention subject," Adrian Vasilescu, an adviser to central bank governor Mugur Isarescu, told Reuters. "We have no comment."

Dealers said the central bank intervened with small volumes, but it breathed some life into the market and trading intensified.

"Everybody was expecting this moment, players were interested to see how far the central bank would let the leu fall," another dealer said. "Things are more clear now, I expect the leu to shy away from record lows for the rest of this week."

Most currency traders said Tuesday's inflation data, which beat market expectations, had little impact on the currency. Prices rose 6.3 percent in December, from 6.7 percent in the previous month and compared with the 6.6 percent consensus. (Reporting by Marius Zaharia; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: CEE MARKETS 3-C.bank boosts Romania's leu; IMF lifts forint
text:
(Updates throughout)

PRAGUE, Jan 13 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu recovered strongly on Tuesday as dealers cited central bank intervention and the Hungarian forint also jumped, helped by IMF assurances Hungary was on track with its $25 billion aid package.

The currencies rebounded after nearing new lows in earlier trade, which helped erase losses in emerging European currencies despite persistent concerns about the region's economies.

Mounting evidence the global economic slowdown will take a heavy toll on emerging Europe and falling risk appetite have hung on currencies in the past week, renewing a weakening trend started in the second half of 2008. A dragging Russia-Ukraine gas row has also added to concern. [ID:nLD708539]

Dealers cited central bank intervention in Romania, helping lift the leu <EURRON=> 1.9 percent to 4.233 per euro. It was the first sign of the central bank since December. [ID:LD353441]

In Hungary, the forint was up 1.8 percent from Monday's domestic close at 276.5 per euro by 1507 GMT, which pushed bond yields down. Earlier, the forint closed in on the 286 level, last hit in October when the escalating financial crisis battered central Europe.

The forint had fallen sharply in the past few days due in part to market speculation the IMF would scold Hungary over a lack of progress on the terms of an aid deal struck in October to allay external financing concerns.

But in Budapest on Tuesday, the fund's head Dominique Strauss-Kahn said Hungary was making progress. [ID:nLD334802]

"(The 286 level) might be hard to break from a technical standpoint. Both of these facts together have created a correction in the forint," said Ulrich Leuchtmann, head of foreign exchange research as Commerzbank in Frankfurt, referring also to IMF comments.

CONTAGION

The leu and forint remained down 5.2 percent and 4.7 percent respectively in 2009. Analysts have said Romania, with a large current account deficit, may need its own aid package to restore confidence.

"Investors have lost confidence in the currency," one Bucharest dealer said.

Currency weakness and nagging inflation have limited the central bank's scope for joining the regional trend of cutting rates to counter collapsing demand for the area's exports.

Data on Tuesday showing Romania's annual inflation rate eased to 6.3 percent in December from 6.7 percent may lift some concerns. [ID:nLD37336]

In other trade, the Czech crown <EURCZK=> edged up to 26.63 per euro. Poland's zloty led losses with a 0.7 percent drop to 4.12 the euro, and more weakness was expected.

"We see high probability of a weaker zloty because economic conditions are deteriorating fast, and the central bank is ready to use non-conventional measures to support the financial system, which may have a negative impact on the zloty," said Shahin Vallee, currency strategist at BNP Paribas.

The Serbian dinar <EURRSD=>, which has also hit new lows in the past week, was up 0.5 percent at 91.87 per euro in choppy trade, helped by a central bank sale of 12 million euros.

title: EURONOMICS: Euro-Zone Bailouts Seen Hurting Emerging Econs
text:
MILAN (Dow Jones)--Governments and central banks have begun to bring relief to the credit crisis in Western Europe, but they may have transferred the burden to economies on the European periphery.

"The crisis in Western Europe and the U.S. is easing, but there's no easing in Eastern Europe, where it looks like the credit crunch is only intensifying," said Lars Christensen, chief analyst at Danske Bank in Copenhagen.

Weaker Western banks may have been saved by government rescue packages, but now their incentive is to channel resources towards buying back the new shares issued to receive that temporary assistance.

"The effect is to transfer the credit crunch from the banks to the corporates and also emerging-market economies," said Simon Smollett, an analyst at Calyon in London. "Emerging-market economies will find their money markets will tighten and their currencies still continue to slide, because the demand from Western banks is a return of capital."

Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia and Turkey appear at risk of joining Hungary and Ukraine as economies in line for international assistance. None of these countries has a sovereign credit rating strong enough to allow credible bank rescue plans along the lines of those launched by euro-zone governments.

Instead, they're proceeding in a piecemeal fashion. This week, Serbia raised deposit insurance to avoid a run on its banks, Kazakhstan's central bank announced a $5 billion fund to support local banks, and Bulgaria's central bank eased reserve requirements on lenders under its purview.

Turkey's central bank has tried to broker interbank lending in foreign currencies to mitigate a liquidity squeeze. Its government is now offering a tax amnesty for Turks wishing to repatriate savings to the country.

In Romania, the central bank intervened directly in foreign exchange markets Friday. That helped foil an "attack against the leu," Governor Mugur Isarescu told local press Tuesday.

The battle rages on, though, as interest rates on Romania's money market remain far above the central bank's 10.25% policy rate, already the highest in the 27-member E.U. Isarescu is pleading with banks not to use the local Robor interbank lending rate as price guidance for loans, saying rates of around 18% are skewed by market turmoil. But banks are unlikely to comply, analysts say, given that overnight rates have spiked to 60% and above.

That spike has helped support the leu but "will crush the local banking system and then leave them even more exposed in a few weeks' time," said Calyon's Smollett.

That was not the goal of the Western bank rescues. Moreover, if Eastern European economies begin to flail and cut back sharply on imports, the euro-zone slowdown will be exacerbated.

Ultimately, Eastern European countries with large external deficits - especially those highly exposed to short-term or hard-currency debt - need to boost their savings after years of rapid, credit-fired growth.

"You can't avoid the hangover," said Danske Bank's Christensen. The usual ways to do that are tightening fiscal policy or hiking interest rates. "There will be an economic slump, but you kind of want a slump because these economies have been growing too fast," he said.

Outside institutions such as the International Monetary Fund or the European Central Bank may be able to offer help, but such assistance comes at a price.

Ukraine this week announced plans to force down its budget deficit, which almost certainly points to a cutback in the capital spending aimed at boosting long-term growth. The central bank is also signaling that it will let the hryvnia, which usually tracks the U.S. dollar, weaken.

Such moves probably amount to gestures of reciprocity for expected help from the International Monetary Fund, said Alexander Pecherstyn, an economist for ING in Kiev.

In the same vein, Hungary announced a tougher fiscal stance the same day as the European Central Bank's unprecedented offer of liquidity to unclog that country's frozen money markets.

Pressure for the ECB to do the same for neighbors may grow if emerging-market funding pressures persist, Goldman Sachs says. But Goldman argues that's an unlikely outcome for outliers such as Romania and Bulgaria, and all but off the table for countries outside the European Union.

-By Christopher Emsden, Dow Jones Newswires; +39-02-58-21-99-05; chris.emsden@dowjones.com

title: TRADE IDEA-Erste recommends closing euro/Romanian leu short
text:
BUCHAREST, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Erste bank recommended on Friday investors close short positions in the euro against the leu at 3.72 per euro, saying the Romanian unit has little room to firm because global financial woes enhanced worries over external vulnerabilities.

Romania is seen as one of the most vulnerable countries in the region because of its vast current account deficit and its high proportion of hard-currency lending, coupled with lax fiscal and income policies.

"There is a low probability of further recovery of the leu amid gloomy global context," Erste said in a report.

"The deepening of the global financial crisis, coupled with the lax fiscal policy ... determined a sharp depreciation of the local currency against the euro ... The fall of the leu could only be halted by the central bank which intervened in the forex market and brought the exchange rate below 3.75 per euro."

The leu reached its lowest level in almost four years at 3.9860 per euro <EURRON=> on Oct. 6, but regained some of its losses in recent days as dealers cited several covert central bank interventions. (Reporting by Marius Zaharia; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: Romania c.bank ready to curb big leu swings
text:
BUCHAREST, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank is ready to intervene on the foreign exchange market to counter large swings in the leu currency, governor Mugur Isarescu said on Tuesday.

"We are sending a clear signal: we do not agree with extremely big variations of the exchange rate," Isarescu told parliament.

"When their amplitude gets higher and when volume of trading is low, what has happened in the last days, we have what we call anomalies. We are ready to intervene directly or indirectly to counter them."

But he said that the central banks should not enter markets too frequently. (Reporting by Marius Zaharia)

title: Romania cbank may prop up leu near 4 per euro-analysts
text:
BUCHAREST, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) could intervene this week to support the leu and shore up its inflation targets after the currency sank around 10 percent over the last month to an almost four-year low, analysts said on Monday.

With the leu bid at weaker than 3.9 per euro -- nudging a four-year low -- analysts have increasingly alluded to testing a "BNR put", in which they believe the bank will feel obliged to prop up the leu <EURRON=> at around 4.0 or 4.1 per euro.

It would be necessary, they say, to prevent a possible banking crisis. Because 55 percent of Romanian loans are in foreign currencies, firms and households could have trouble paying back loans if the leu slides more against the euro.

"The BNR has a lot to lose if EUR/RON rises substantially above the psychological level of 4.00. Therefore, the bank is likely step into the market, potentially already (this) week," said JP Morgan analyst Miroslav Plojhar.

Emerging European currencies have been pummelled as investors avoid risk and hoard cash following the downfall of major financial institutions, but none more than the leu.

On Monday morning, it shed 1.8 percent to 3.944 against the euro, following heavy losses at the end of last week.

Romania's more developed ex-communist peers -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- have seen their currencies slip 3.4 to 4.5 percent since Sept. 12 when U.S. bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, but analysts said their banks would keep to the sidelines because they were still relatively strong.

For Romania, the financial crisis has heightened concerns, voiced by rating agencies and the International Monetary Fund, that the country is more vulnerable than its peers because of a vast current account deficit, high rates of hard currency borrowing and inadequate fiscal and wage policies.

The fear is the Romanian economy could be destabilised if global cash flows and foreign investment dry up and are no longer sufficient to plug the double-digit external deficit.

"They should intervene to stop the depreciation because otherwise this will have a major impact on inflation and will throw inflationary expectations in the air," said Ionut Dumitru, head of research at Raiffeisen Bank in Bucharest.

Inflation is expected to fall to around 6 percent in December, still above the central bank's 2.8-4.8 percent target.

The bank kept its benchmark rate on hold at 10.25 percent at its last meeting in September, but analysts said another hike may be on the cards due to pledges by major parties to loosen fiscal policy ahead of a Nov. 30 parliamentary election.

Elsewhere in the region, Serbia's central bank intervened to tame dinar losses after Ukraine stepped in to buy local currency at 5 hryvnias to the dollar <UAH=> on Friday.

"We've seen interventions in Ukraine, Serbia. The next to come is Romania," said Elisabeth Gruie, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. (Editing by Victoria Main)

An adviser to the central bank declined comment. "On this subject we don't say anything. We don't say yes, we don't say no, we don't say maybe," Adrian Vasilescu, an adviser of central bank governor Mugur Isarescu, told Reuters.

title: FOCUS: Romania's  Central Bank  Chief's Job Is Getting Harder
text:
Spare a thought for Romania's central bank governor, Mugur Isarescu.   

The country's economy is slowing, inflation is soaring, a weakening currency is slamming corporate profits and hopes of fiscal restraint are faint given national elections due to be held later this year.   

"We have to relieve the pressure on monetary policy," he said Tuesday at a seminar in Bucharest, where he also warned that inflation, currently on course to accelerate to 8% next month, has to be tamed this year or the country would have to shelve hopes of adopting the euro in 2014.   

Isarescu, one of the longest-serving central bank governors in the world, has been sharing his thoughts to all and sundry in recent days, offering a deluge of commentary to local media and even making a rare appearance on the country's main television show devoted to money matters.   

He'll be back on the podium Wednesday, meeting with the heads of Romania's banks, many of whom have complained that the National Bank of Romania has a communications problem.   

The agenda isn't public but almost certainly will focus on matters beyond the short-term interest rate the central bank sets, according to people in Romania's financial sector.   

Erste Bank (EBKOY) Chief Executive Andreas Treichl, Raiffeisen International Bank (RIBH.VI) Chairman Steven van Groningen and Patrick Gelin, CEO of BRD-Societe Generale (BRD.RO) have all made stinging accusations in the local press, arguing that the central bank needs to be open to dialogue rather than prone to issuing diktats.   

The claims come as Isarescu, in his various media forays, has signaled that he is mulling the feasibility of new regulatory measures, such as raising reserve requirements for consumer loans, or imposing rules that require credits to be extended only in the currency by which the borrower receives income.   

Such measures are quite likely, said Florin Citu, deputy head of financial markets for  ING Groep NV's (ING) Romanian operations. "It's their favorite way of implementing monetary policy: direct measures of control," he said.   

While controversial, such measures are being increasingly tried out in emerging Europe, although mainly in countries such as Croatia, Montenegro or Bulgaria whose currencies are closely tied to hard currencies.   

Such "alternative" measures shouldn't be branded as unorthodox, because the manipulation of reserve requirements is an old tool, one the Bank of Spain has used inside European Monetary Union for mortgage lenders, said Ivailo Vesselinov, an emerging-markets analyst for Dresdner Kleinwort in London.   

"The innovation here is really just trying, perhaps out of necessity, to use all available tools," he said.   

"But there's nothing to say that the institutions of emerging economies can't lead the way, even if it's not so much setting a trend as it is them being at the appropriate state of the cycle to try these measures," he added. "They could, of course, subsequently be followed by other countries."   

One caveat, though, is that the National Bank of Romania is required by statute to target inflation.   

As inflation rose to 7.5% in January - up from 3.7% in the spring of 2007 - the central bank has hiked its main interest rate to 9%, up from 7.5% and the highest central bank rate in the European Union. But inflation has continued to shoot up and many analysts say more tightening is inevitably on the horizon.   

Currency Quandary 
    

However, higher rates risk pushing up the value of the Romanian leu, an effect Isarescu argues could widen the trade and current-account deficits and stoke still more inflationary pressures.   

Yet Isarescu also said Tuesday that letting the leu depreciate is "not the best medicine" for reining in the current-account deficit, which ended 2007 at a whopping 14.3% of gross domestic product, up 66% from the year before. He added that the leu's current rate should prevent further widening of the external deficit.   

After rising more than 15% against the euro in the 12 months ending last July, the leu has since given back all that gain and a bit more.   

One effect of the slide has been to whack corporate profits, notwithstanding economic growth of more than 5% a year.   

The 35 non-financial companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange posted a net cumulative loss of RON88.6 million (EUR25.4 million) in the fourth quarter of 2007, compared with net cumulative profit of RON280 million (EUR80.4 million) in the same period a year before. The main reason was the soaring value of debt liabilities contracted in foreign currencies, mostly the euro.   

Isarescu has been loquacious of late in warning borrowers to keep their currencies in the leu to avoid risks.   

But only one bank - the state-owned CEC or Romanian Savings Bank - has warmly embraced the idea, announcing last week it will stop allowing retail borrowers to be exposed to currency risk.   

But with national credit growth rates of more than 50% a year, far greater than the increase in deposits, it isn't at all clear how CEC would be able to fund new loans. Most Romanian banks have foreign shareholders and hence strong avenues to access euro-based funding.   

For the very same reason, a central bank regulation restricting lending to leu-based loans would likely bring credit growth to a screeching halt - an outcome that would very likely bring inflation down quickly, albeit at the cost of substantial economic pain.   

But while talking up the virtues of the leu, Isarescu is at the same time vocally trying to calm jittery foreign-exchange markets by suggesting the current rate is sustainable. Given his frequent reminders that the National Bank of Romania can - and sometimes does - intervene in the currency markets, that message is potent.   

"Foreign-exchange market intervention and the message that banks should only lend in RON are two conflicting messages," said ING's Citu, an economist who formerly worked at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. "The current policy is just creating more problems than they solve."   

A policy mistake by the National Bank of Romania at this point could spur a more rapid adoption of the euro as the currency of choice in private transactions, a nightmare scenario for the central bank, said Citu.   

To be sure, Isarescu has competition in the policy space that doesn't make his job any easier.   

Finance Minister Varujan Vosganian has been making the rounds, too, publicizing his view that he hopes to stabilize the EUR/RON at around 3.50, up around 5% from the current level and a rate he said would help both importers and exporters.   

Speaking on television Tuesday, Vosganian also took his chance to upbraid Isarescu for the latter's frequent criticism of Romania's fiscal policy, saying the central bank "has to analyze its own policy first." The minister added that he himself "never made statements on the bank's policy."   

Isarescu has been regularly pleading for the government to refrain from the gigantic wage hikes it has been giving to public-sector workers, which have pushed up prices across the border, more than erased productivity gains and hurt the country's terms of trade and have, above all, fueled a mad rush for more credit as Romanians became optimistic about their future income inside the European Union.   

Achieving such restraint won't be easy for a government that lost its parliamentary majority last year and will face voters by November. Indeed, Vosganian has said that Romania is "now in a crisis caused by too much money."   

-By Christopher Emsden, Dow Jones Newswires; +39-02-58-21-99-05; chris.emsden@dowjones.com

title: Romania leu at one-week highs on cbank comments
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 17 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu retraced this week's losses to reach a one week high against the euro on Thursday, helped by recent comments by central bankers that the currency was still attractive, dealers said.   

On Wednesday central bank deputy governor Cristian Popa said the leu's fall to almost three-year lows this week had gone too far, while an adviser of the bank's governor said the leu remained attractive after a recent interest rate hike.   

After hitting a near five-year high versus the euro last summer, the leu has been emerging Europe's punch bag because of Romania's current account gap of around 14 percent of GDP and the absence of a policy response to it.   

"The central bank's verbal interventions made Romania look more positive for now, showed some unhappiness in Bucharest about the weak leu and this is a good sign," said one dealer with a foreign bank in Bucharest.   

"But the current account is still huge so the leu will not firm too much for too long."

title: Romania  has option to  intervene  on  fx  market-cbanker
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 16 (Reuters) - The Romanian central bank reiterated on Wednesday its policy to reserve the right to intervene on currency markets and said such moves would not be announced in advance.   

 The bank's chief economist Valentin Lazea said economic problems such as a vast trade deficit differentiated Romania from its eastern European neighbours and were behind a recent decline in the leu currency to three-year lows versus the euro.   

 "The bank operates with the interest rate first of all," Lazea was quoted as saying by Rompres news agency.   

 "But the central bank said it is keeping the option to use other instruments, if need be, including direct interventions on the forex market, except that, of course, they will not be announced in advance."   

 The leu has been emerging Europe's punching bag since hitting an almost five-year high against the euro in the summer of 2007. It hit a near three-year low of 3.7240 <EURRON=> earlier this week on worries about economic fundamentals.   

 On Wednesday, it traded at 3.7020 per euro.   

 The Romanian central bank has not intervened officially since September 2005 when it moved to weaken the leu. The bank has declined to comment on rumours of intervention since. Traders have said they suspected covert central bank buying of lei late last year when the leu was falling sharply in November.   

 "We must start from the fact that the recent leu fall ... isn't reflected in other central European countries," Lazea said.   

 "This means Romania has a certain problem ... the foreign deficit ... which in turn reflects a more structural problem. Economic growth in Romania is based particularly on consumption, whereas in central European countries it is based both on consumption and exports."   

 Voracious demand last year, Romania's first in the EU, has bloated the current account deficit to an expected 14 percent of gross domestic product and has pushed inflation to 6.6 percent in December, well above the central bank's 3-5 percent target.   

 The central bank hiked its benchmark rate 50 basis points to 8 percent earlier this month and analysts widely expect it to continue the tightening cycle when it meets next in February.  (Reporting by Luiza Ilie; Editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: Romania Leu Opens Steady Amid Mixed  Central Bank  Signals
text:
BUCHAREST (Dow Jones)--Romania's currency opened stable Friday and the mixed signals from the central bank's refinancing auction late Thursday will hold the leu at current levels for now, say traders. 

 "The results of the refinancing auction were too confusing to interpret," said a trader with a foreign bank in Romania. "I think the leu will remain steady." 

 The leu opened Friday at between 6,900 and 7,000 to the dollar. 

 The central bank offered 300 billion lei in its weekly refinancing auction for banks in overdraught Thursday but dem totaled 582 billion. The central bank offer last week was 500 billion lei. 

 The trader said the demand shows a scarcity of lei on the market. However, the central bank at the same time cut refinancing interest rates to 205% yearly on 15-day loans from 220% in last week's auction. 

 This weeks auction showed the same mixed signals as last week's auction when the rate dropped from 226% the previous week and the offer dropped from 600 billion lei. 

 Another trader said central bank officials told him Thursday they were "ready to buy dollars at between 6,900 lei and 6,950 lei." 

 "The central bank will definitely intervene if they see asks at 6,850 lei or below," he said. "This was made very clear to me." 

 Howe he said the leu will likely remain stable Friday without central bank intervention. 

 Several traders say the National Bank of Romania (NBR) has phoned them during the week saying it was ready to buy dollars. 


Another trader predicted the leu could strengthen slightly over the
next week or so as large companies sell dollars to pay taxes in April.

BUCHAREST, March 7 (Reuter) - Romania's leu closed Friday stronger at 6,800/7,200 to the dollar against 7,000/500 in early trading as a midday with help from a midday central bank (BNR) intervention, traders said. 

 "Inflows on the money market helped the dollar in early trading when it climbed to 7,500/8,000, but the central bank stepped in immediately to mop up leu funds," said one trader. 

 "It was a clear attempt to support the leu," said another, estimating that the BNR sold some $7.0 million and bought around $2.0 million. 

 BNR officials confirmed the central bank's actions on Friday but declined to confirm the size of the intervention, which it called "a test." 

 "I wouldn't call it an intervention, it was rather a test," said BNR spokesman Adrian Vasilescu, without elaborating. 

 Some dealers speculated that the BNR was poised to lash out at banks that had not extended their rollover T-bills on offer on Friday. Results of Friday's subscription were not available. 

 Short-term money market rates fell to some 215/230 percent from near 300 percent in the early hours as the market digested Thursday's drop to 226.31 percent from 426.5 percent in the average auctioned credit rate. 

 On Friday, the BNR also postponed for the second week in a row announcing a new method of computing the reference exchange rate for the leu currency but gave no reason for the delay. 

 Traders said the delay might affect the banks, because minimum reserves on banks' hard currency deposits, held in leu currency with the central bank, are converted at that rate. 

 "This will trigger an artificial rise in reserve targets as the 7,744 level of the reference rate is by far weaker than the market rates," said one dealer with a state bank. 

 Last month, the BNR gave up computing the leu's reference rate after restoring local dealer licences to 24 banks, which are now market makers along with four others.

title: Romania  c.bank says building  intervention  fund.

BUCHAREST, March 22 (Reuter) - The central bank will amass an intervention fund to allow it to play an active role in its reformed, market-maker-based, local foreign exchange market, National Bank of Romania vice governor Vlad Soare said. 

 "The central bank will be more involved in that market," Soare told Reuters after announcing that the bank will limit interbank foreign exchange dealer licences to four banks.  Soare denied that the changes were an attempt to hold the value of the leu currency which slid around 65 percent in a year due to current account problems. 

 He said he expected some continued depreciation of the currency in line with inflationary expectations of around 20 percent this year, down from 27 percent last year. 

 "This doesn't mean somebody is trying to stabilise the rate of exchange," Soare said. 

 He said he had warned both the new market makers and the broker banks that while being responsible and disciplined they could not try to peg the currency back. 

 "The rate of exchange will be further depreciated in line with what we expect from inflation," he said. title: IMF approves extra $280 million loans for Romania.
text:
WASHINGTON, Dec 21 (Reuter) - The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that it approved an extra $280 million in loans for Romania to help the country rein in rising consumer prices and a ballooning trade deficit. 

 The additional money will come in the form of an extension of an existing IMF "standby" credit for Romania through April 1997, it said. 

 Romania's monthly inflation rate accelerated in November to its highest level this year, 4.1 percent, from 3.5 percent in October. Since last December, prices have risen 23 percent. 

 The rise has been fuelled by a steep drop in Romania's currency, the leu, brought on by a widening of the trade deficit. Romania's central bank intervened on the Bucharest foreign exchange market on Tuesday to support the leu. 

 The IMF said its loans will be used to back up an economic programme aimed at reducing inflation to less than 20 percent in 1996, cutting the trade deficit and significantly building up foreign currency reserves at Romania's central bank.

title: Romanian leu closes firm on 2,800, money market up.
text:
BUCHAREST, Dec 13 (Reuter) - The Romanian leu closed more or less unchanged and firm at 2,800 to the dollar, with dealers saying the drought of hard currency seemed ready to break. 

 "I think the volume is starting to come back," said a trader at one of the big four state-owned banks which have worked with the central bank to reinforce the fragile leu. 

 The state bank trader said customer and inter-bank volume rose sharply on Wednesday to between $15 million and $18 million, up from perhaps $10.0 million a day in recent days. 

 "I think they were expecting it to go weaker but the rates are stabilising so they started to sell. There is still a lack of liquidity but it is starting to move," he said. 

 Romanian dealers have complained for weeks about a chronic lack of hard currency. Though dollar hoarding is usual with the approach of winter it has been greater than normal, helping drive the leu sharply lower over the past two months. 

 Even private commercial banks, cynical about the dual role played out between the central bank and the state-owned banks in supporting the leu, said the currency seemed somewhat firmer. 

 While the state banks continued to quote the currency at 2,549/30 the commercial banks displayed significantly weaker rates. ING Bucharest, for example, was on 2,750/50. 

 "I'd say the close today is really 2,800-2,820," said a trader at one private commercial bank. "I think it will go step by step and will be firmer as the week goes by." 

 Commercial dealers said activity was minimal. 

 The big four state-owned banks acknowledge they have been working more or less in concert with the National Bank of Romania which has threatened to intervene if the currency drops below 2,600. 

 So far the interevention has been limited to phone calls to remind dealers where their real interests lie. 

 The message has yet to get to the retail exchange shops which, despite government warnings they will be shut down, prefer to sell the leu at 3,000 to the dollar. 

 That and the 2,800 level on the inter-bank market makes the National Bank's reference rate, computed as a weighted average based on reports from traders, of 2,554 look a little out of kilter with the activity of the real market. 

 State bank dealers, however, said there was greater purchasing volume available at around 2,600 than the 2,800 offered by some of the commercial banks. 

 Dealers said they were pleased to see rises in money market rates a week after the central bank raised refinancing rates 5.0 points to 65 percent. One-week money rose to 54.89 percent from 54.69 and 12-month rates to 52.69 percent from 52.39.

 Dealers said the market was opaque at best with no-one trading at anything close to the rates advertised. Trading was more or less confined to client-related transactions. 

 One dealer at a state-owned bank acknowledged his institution was effectively underpinning the currency. 

 "We do not wish to weaken the Romanian currency," he said. 

 "At the moment there are different opinions (between traders) about where the currency should be. I think that our state ownership gives us a particular view." 

 He said his bank felt it could serve its clients adequately around the 2,600 level for the leu. 

 The National Bank of Romania has said it will intervene at the 2,600 level to support the currency and the government has said it is the level that it and the IMF wants. 

 Commercial bank dealers said the real market was closer to 2,800/50 but that virtually no inter-bank work was happening.

title: Romania  PM says  currency  stable, no  intervention .
text:
BUCHAREST, Dec 5 (Reuter) - Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu said he believed Romania's leu currency had stabilised after a sharp fall and that central bank intervention was not needed. 

 "The exchange rate got stabilised and there is no intervention from the National Bank," Vacaroiu told Reuters. 

 Despite complaints from foreign exchange traders that dollar supplies have dried up and that pressure on the leu remains, Vacaroiu insisted the local inter-bank market was working. 

 The government had allowed a one-off 10 percent depreciation in consultation with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) taking the leu from around 2,400 two weeks ago to around 2,600. 

 While private exchange houses, whom he accused of serving the "subterranean" economy, have since pushed it further, Vacaroiu said he believed the currency was more or less stable. 

 "In my opinion as an economist, this is an equilibrium exchange rate. It is a stable exchange rate now," he said. 

 A steady depreciation over the past 18 months of about 1.0 percent a month gathered pace with the leu falling a nominal 36 percent at exchange houses in a matter of weeks. 

 Over the past year the leu has halved nominally on the interbank market to 2,850 from 1,800. With inflation forecast at 25 percent this year that makes a 30 percent real depreciation. 

 While leu weakness and dollar hoarding are traditional ahead of the icy Romanian winter the fall has been much sharper than last year, eroding hard won confidence in the local unit. 

 Vacaroiu said the fall had been exacerbated this year by the illegal activity of exchange houses but more fundamentally by a tripling in the trade deficit to a forecast $1.5 billion, built in large measure, according to the premier, on capital imports. 

 "Imports exceeded exports and we had a trade balance deficit," he said in an interview. "Of course, in the case of an economy such as Romania's, which is coming out of the crisis and is being modernised -- if it wants to enter Europe it should modernise from an economic point of view -- it's normal." 

 Private economists, however, say they fear the current account deficit is structural and funded too short term. It has been a major factor in difficult negotiations with the International Monetary Fund on an extended stand-by agreement. 

 Far from intervening to sell dollars, Vacaroiu said the central bank was more likely to buy dollars -- as it has already done in recent weeks -- to reinforce its hard currency reserves. 

 "The National Bank, in cooperation with myself, has the task to consolidate its hard currency reserves and it buys on the market, so there is no question on intervening," he said. 

 Vacaroiu said he was generally satisfied with the operation of an inter-bank market created about 18 months ago but which private bankers say is manipulated by state banks on behalf of the powerful central bank and government. "The entire foreign exchange market on the screen is real," he said. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264

title: Romania  central bank  says will smooth  forex  market.
text:
BUCHAREST Nov 15 (Reuter) - Romania's central bank, confirming it intervened in the currency market on Tuesday, said it was prepared to do so whenever necessary to "smooth out inter-bank market". 

Foreign exchange manager at the National Bank of Romania, Adrian Grigoriu, told Reuters the bank was adopting an active policy to ensure the market operated smoothly. 

 "We will intervene both by selling and buying to smooth out the inter-bank market," Grigoriu said. 

 He confirmed dealers reports that central bank had bought dollars on Tuesday saying the aim of its move was to reinforce foreign exchange reserves. He declined to give details. 

 "We also wanted to test the market as on Monday there were no inter-bank deals," Grigoriu said. 

 He said the market responded quickly to the call for quotes on the dollar and behaved "professionally" offering both buy and sell quotations and abiding by central bank rules on offering continuous prices during the trading day. 

 Dealers earlier said that the bank had intervened on Tuesday using a tactic to underpin the leu by exposing some big players to greater risk and to show market that there was liquidity. 

 The leu was steady at around 2,500 to the dollar in the inter-bank market on Wednesday despite earlier predictions that it would fall to 2,700. The leu has fallen to 2,500 to the dollar from 2,200 over the past month, accelerating a steady depreciation over the past year of about 1.0 percent a month. 

 Tuesday's was the first acknowleged central bank intervention for about three months. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264

title: Romania central bank intervened  Tuesday - dealers.
text:
BUCHAREST, Nov 15 (Reuter) - Romania's central bank intervened on the local currency market on Tuesday using an unorthodox tactic to buy dollars at a rate firmer than that generally quoted on the market, dealers said. 

 "The central bank bought dollars on Tuesday at a price higher than the exchange rates on the market," said one dealer. 

 Dealers said the tactic effectively underpinned the local leu currency by exposing major banks which were long on the dollar to greater risk and show there were dollars available. 

 The leu has fallen sharply over the past month affected by low hard currency offer on the inter-bank market and facing a traditional pre-winter period of dollar-hoarding. 

Central bank officials were not available for comment. But dealers said the National Bank of Romania had bought about $6.0 million late in trading on Tuesday. They said the bank called several dealers asking for a spot quote on the dollar/leu cross. 

 Apparently thinking that the central bank wanted to sell dollars to support the leu, the dealers offered firmer exchange rates than they were generally offering to buy dollars. 

 Dealers declined to give the rates but the leu was steady at around 2,500 to the dollar in the inter-bank market today despite earlier predictions that it would fall to 2,700. 

 "I don't know exactly what is behind the central bank's move but it seems it wanted to hit some major players by testing the market," one dealer said. 

 The same dealer said the tactic had successfully proven that there were dollars available on the market but the banks were contributing to the dollar hoarding by going long. 

 The leu has fallen to 2,500 to the dollar from 2,200 over the past month, accelerating a steady and planned depreciation over the past year of about 1.0 percent a month. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264

title: Romania central bank intervenes  to prop up leu.
text:
BUCHAREST, Feb 9 (Reuter) - Romania's National Bank (BNR) sold dollars on the local foreign exchange market on Wednesday to prop up the leu, an official said today. 

 "We sold dollars late on Wednesday to pump liquidity into the market to support the leu," BNR deputy manager Adrian Grigoriu told Reuters, declining to specify the amount sold. 

 Late on Wednesday, the central bank announced the leu's reference rate at 1,796 to dollar, down from a previous 1,797 level. The BNR's reference rate is computed as a weighted average based on foreign exchange operators' reports. 

 Dealers were not immediately available to comment on the BNR intervention but on Wednesday they said they expected the leu's reference rate to slip below 1,800 this week. 

 Commercial banks quoted the leu within a range of 1,794/99- 1,799/07 per dollar on Thursday, close to Wednesday's levels. 

 "We will intervene again to temper the market if necessary," Grigoriu said without elaborating. 

 Wednesday's intervention confirmed dealers' fears that the BNR would step into the market this week to keep the leu at what they called "a social exchange rate". 

 Dealers said a leu/dollar rate below 1,800 would send electricity costs up, triggering further price hikes. 

 "We do not agree with (leu's) depreciation as it will encourage non-competitive companies to use it to cover their deficiencies," Finance Minister Florin Georgescu recently said. 

 Georgescu said the BNR had enough hard currency resources to keep the leu's exchange rate stable. 

 BNR's foreign exchange reserves were $591.5 million last December, when Romania's total reserves topped $2.1 billion. -- Mirela Eremia, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264

title: Romanian leu edges down, dealers see weakness.
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 26 (Reuter) - Romania's leu edged down to 1,778/90 to the dollar on the interbank market after clinging to 1,775/85 over recent days. 

 Dealers said it might end the week a little weaker. 

 "The leu might end the week a whisker weaker if the National Bank does not step in the market," said Cosmin Calinescu, Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare chief dealer. 

 Calinescu said he had not detected any central bank intervention this week. On Monday, dealers said the BNR sold dollars last week to keep the leu stable at 1,774 to the dollar. The National Bank of Romania has not confirmed the intervention. 

 Dealers said there was a shortage of hard currency on the interbank market but they declined to make long-term forecasts on the leu's exchange rate. 

 "Market players are unwilling to sell hard currency at current rates and buyers on the other hand are reluctant to bid higher," one of them said. 

 Traders were pessimistic about the state of the local market, saying that trading between banks was almost "dead". 

 Dealers said they believed the BNR has resources to keep the domestic market balanced but they wondered for how long. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264

title: Romania  dealers see lower leu without  intervention .
text:
BUCHAREST, Jan 3 (Reuter) - Romania's leu currency may depreciate against the dollar this week unless the central bank (BNR) intervenes, dealers said. 

 "Without central bank intervention I see the leu down at around 1,800 to the dollar," a dealer said. 

 On Tuesday the leu opened around 1,775/85 to the dollar, down from its 1,770/85 level at Friday's close. 

Central bank governor Mugur Isarescu told Reuters on Thursday that the bank preferred to see a gradual movement of the leu. 

 But he said the bank was ready to step into the market if necessary as it did in December, when it spent $20-30 million to support the Romanian currency. 

 Traders said there was a shortage of dollars on the market. 

 "The dollar became attractive lately as gains from interest on lei deposits fell over the past months. People have to protect their lei and they do not have so far other alternatives which could offer higher earnings," a dealer said. 

 Dealers generally declined to commit themselves to any long-term forecasts as they were waiting commercial banks' reactions to a cut in central bank interest rates on Tuesday. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
